docs.title: Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
Prof. Sharat Batra · University of Minnesota · batra052@umn.edu

Welcome to Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook — an open, interactive course resource designed for undergraduate students at the University of Minnesota and beyond.

This textbook covers the core principles of microeconomics through clear explanations, real-world examples, mathematical models, and interactive simulations. Each chapter builds on the last, taking you from the foundational ideas of scarcity and choice all the way to international trade and behavioral economics.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• How individuals and firms make decisions under scarcity
  • How markets coordinate supply and demand to set prices
  • How different market structures (competition, monopoly, oligopoly) affect outcomes
  • How markets can fail and what policy can do about it
  • How insights from psychology reshape our understanding of economic behavior

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
This course introduces the fundamental principles of microeconomics — the study of how individuals, households, and firms make decisions in the face of scarcity, and how these decisions interact through markets. Students will develop analytical tools to understand resource allocation, price determination, market structure, and government policy.

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • Apply the core economic concepts of scarcity, opportunity cost, and marginal analysis
  • Model supply, demand, and market equilibrium graphically and mathematically
  • Analyze how different market structures affect prices, output, and social welfare
  • Evaluate the causes and consequences of market failures
  • Apply microeconomic reasoning to real-world policy questions

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Define economics and distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics
  2. Explain scarcity, choice, and the concept of opportunity cost
  3. Apply marginal analysis to decision-making
  4. Construct and interpret a Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
  5. Identify the role of incentives and trade in economic reasoning

Meet Professor Owl

Hello! I'm Professor Owl, a Great Horned Owl who has spent countless semesters helping students make sense of microeconomics, one trade-off at a time. I'll show up in six different moods as you read this book:

  1. Welcome — I'll open each chapter and tell you why it's worth your attention.
  2. Thinking — I'll pause with you at the big "aha" moments.
  3. Tip — I'll hand you a shortcut, like a secret passed between students.
  4. Warning — I'll flag the mistakes nearly everyone makes, before you make them.
  5. Encourage — when the material gets genuinely hard, I'll remind you that's normal.
  6. Celebration — when you've truly mastered something, we'll celebrate it together.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Every choice has a trade-off — and I promise only to spend yours when it's worth it.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Economics?
docs.text:
Economics is the study of how individuals, firms, and societies allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. Because resources — time, money, land, labor — are limited, every economic agent must make choices. Economics provides the tools to analyze those choices systematically.

Two Branches of Economics

  • Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers: households, firms, and specific markets. Why does coffee cost more than water? Why do nurses earn less than surgeons?
  • Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: total output, unemployment, inflation, and economic growth. Why did GDP fall during COVID-19? What causes inflation?

This textbook focuses on microeconomics.

docs.title: The Fundamental Problem
docs.text:
Scarcity means that resources are limited relative to human wants. This is the central fact of economic life. Because we cannot have everything, we must choose. Every choice involves a trade-off — getting more of one thing means getting less of another.

Scarcity in everyday life

You have 24 hours in a day. If you spend 3 hours studying economics, those 3 hours cannot also be spent sleeping, working, or watching TV. Time is scarce; you must allocate it.

docs.title: Opportunity Cost
docs.text:
The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up when you make that choice. It is the true cost of any decision.

\[\text{Opportunity Cost} = \text{Value of the Next-Best Alternative Foregone}\]

Opportunity cost of college

The full cost of attending college is not just tuition and books. It also includes the foregone wages you could have earned by working instead. For a student who could earn $35,000/year, the opportunity cost of a four-year degree includes $140,000 in foregone income — even if tuition is free.

Key insight: Opportunity costs are often hidden. Economists think about all costs — not just the ones that show up on a bill.

The Cost You Can't See

Notice that Maria's painting and the airline's empty seat share something: the real cost was never on a receipt. Once you start asking "what am I giving up?" instead of "what am I paying?", you're thinking like an economist.

docs.title: Sunk Costs
docs.text:
A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered. Rational decision-making requires ignoring sunk costs and focusing only on future costs and benefits.

The sunk cost fallacy

You bought a $15 movie ticket but the film is terrible. Should you stay to "get your money's worth"? No — the $15 is gone regardless. The only relevant question is: Will the next two hours of my life be better spent watching this movie or doing something else?

docs.title: 1.3 Marginal Analysis
docs.text:
Economists think at the margin. A marginal change is a small, incremental change. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefits of an action to its additional costs.

The Rule: Pursue an activity as long as the marginal benefit (MB) exceeds or equals the marginal cost (MC).

\[\text{Optimal choice: MB} = \text{MC}\]

docs.title: Example: How many hours to study?
docs.text:
Suppose each additional hour of studying raises your exam grade, but with diminishing returns:

Study Hours Marginal Benefit (grade points gained) Marginal Cost (value of time foregone) 1st hour 20 5 2nd hour 15 5 3rd hour 10 5 4th hour 5 5 5th hour 2 5

The optimal choice is 4 hours — where MB = MC = 5. Studying a 5th hour costs more than it's worth.

Marginal thinking in business

An airline has a flight from Minneapolis to Chicago that is half-full. Should it sell the remaining seats at a discount? Yes — as long as the discounted fare exceeds the marginal cost of adding a passenger (essentially zero for an already-flying plane). The fixed costs of the flight are sunk.

docs.title: Diminishing Marginal Returns
docs.text:
As you do more of something, holding everything else constant, the marginal benefit typically falls. This is the principle of diminishing marginal returns (or diminishing marginal utility for consumers).

  • The first slice of pizza is wonderful. The fifth is less enjoyable.
  • The first hour of studying helps a lot. The tenth hour adds little.

docs.title: 1.4 The Production Possibilities Frontier
docs.text: The Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) is a model that illustrates the trade-offs facing an economy (or individual) that produces two goods using fixed resources.

docs.title: Constructing the PPF
docs.text:
Consider a small economy that can produce only wheat and computers, using all available labor and capital.

Production Possibility Wheat (millions of bushels) Computers (millions of units) A 0 30 B 5 27 C 10 21 D 15 12 E 18 0

Plotting these combinations traces the PPF — a curve bowing outward from the axes.

docs.title: Key Features of the PPF
docs.text:
1. Points on the curve — efficient: all resources are fully employed.

2. Points inside the curve — inefficient: resources are idle or wasted (e.g., during a recession).

3. Points outside the curve — currently unattainable with existing resources and technology.

4. The slope of the PPF = the opportunity cost of producing one more unit of a good.

If the PPF Feels Slippery, That's Normal

"Increasing opportunity cost" trips up almost every new economics student — it's genuinely counterintuitive the first time. Sketch the wheat-and-computers table above again by hand; the bowed shape will click once you see the numbers yourself.

docs.title: Why Is the PPF Bowed Outward?
docs.text:
The outward bow (concave shape) reflects the law of increasing opportunity costs: as you produce more of one good, you must give up increasing amounts of the other. This happens because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods — the most productive wheat farmers are moved to computer production last.

\[\text{Opportunity Cost of Computers} = \frac{\Delta \text{Wheat}}{\Delta \text{Computers}}\]

As we move from A to E (producing more wheat), the opportunity cost of each additional bushel of wheat rises.

docs.title: Shifts in the PPF
docs.text:
The PPF shifts outward when:

  • More resources are available (e.g., population growth, capital investment)
  • Technology improves (higher productivity for one or both goods)

Technological progress

If a new variety of wheat doubles agricultural productivity, the PPF shifts outward along the wheat axis — the economy can now produce more wheat without sacrificing any computers.

docs.title: Comparative Advantage and Specialization
docs.text: Two individuals (or countries) can both gain by specializing in the good for which they have the lower opportunity cost and then trading. This is the principle of comparative advantage (covered in depth in Chapter 16).

docs.title: 1.5 Economic Models and Assumptions
docs.text:
Economists build models — simplified representations of reality — to isolate and study specific relationships. A model deliberately ignores some details to focus on what matters most.

Common economic assumptions:

  • Ceteris paribus ("all else equal") — when analyzing one variable, hold others constant
  • Rational behavior — individuals make choices to maximize their well-being given constraints
  • Equilibrium — markets tend toward a state where supply equals demand

Models are not perfect — they are useful

A map of Minneapolis that showed every building, tree, and pothole would be unusable. A useful map simplifies. Economic models do the same thing: they sacrifice realism for insight.

docs.title: Positive vs. Normative Economics
docs.text:
Positive Normative Nature Descriptive — what is Prescriptive — what ought to be Example "A minimum wage increase reduces employment for low-skill workers." "The minimum wage should be raised to $15/hour." Verifiable? In principle, yes No — depends on values

Economists try to keep these separate. A positive analysis of the minimum wage does not tell you whether to support it; that depends on your values and how you weigh trade-offs.

Spotting Positive vs. Normative Fast

Here's a fast test: if you could, in principle, settle the claim with data, it's positive. If settling it requires someone's values, it's normative. Run every statement in Problem 5 through that test before you check the solution.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Scarcity The condition in which resources are limited relative to wants Opportunity Cost The value of the next-best alternative foregone Sunk Cost A past cost that cannot be recovered and should be ignored Marginal Analysis Decision-making by comparing marginal benefits to marginal costs Marginal Benefit (MB) The additional benefit from one more unit of an activity Marginal Cost (MC) The additional cost from one more unit of an activity Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce Efficiency Producing at a point on the PPF (no waste) Law of Increasing Opportunity Costs As more of a good is produced, its opportunity cost rises Comparative Advantage The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer Ceteris Paribus Latin for "all else equal" — a modeling assumption Positive Economics Analysis of what is (factual, testable) Normative Economics Analysis of what ought to be (value-based)

docs.title: Problem 1 — Opportunity Cost
docs.text:
Maria is a dentist who earns $150/hour. She decides to spend a Saturday afternoon (4 hours) painting her living room rather than hiring a painter who charges $40/hour.

a) What is the explicit cost of painting the room herself? b) What is the opportunity cost of painting the room herself? c) From an economic standpoint, is it rational for Maria to paint the room herself?

Solution

a) The explicit cost is $0 — she is not paying anyone.

b) The opportunity cost is the foregone dentist income: 4 hours × $150/hour = $600.

c) The total economic cost of Maria painting is $600 (opportunity cost) compared to $160 (paying the painter). It is not rational from a purely economic standpoint — she should hire the painter and spend those 4 hours working as a dentist.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Sunk Cost
docs.text:
You paid $80 for a non-refundable ticket to a concert. On the day of the concert, you feel slightly ill and estimate that attending will give you $30 of enjoyment, while staying home and resting will give you $60 of enjoyment.

a) Should you attend the concert? Why or why not? b) Does the $80 ticket price affect your decision?

Solution

a) You should stay home. The relevant comparison is: $30 (attending) vs. $60 (resting). Resting gives you more utility.

b) No. The $80 is a sunk cost — it is gone regardless of what you do. Rational decision-making ignores sunk costs.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Marginal Analysis
docs.text:
A firm's data on weekly output is shown below:

Workers Total Output (units) Marginal Product Marginal Revenue ($10/unit) Marginal Labor Cost ($200/worker) 1 50 50 $500 $200 2 95 45 $450 $200 3 130 35 $350 $200 4 155 25 $250 $200 5 170 15 $150 $200 6 180 10 $100 $200

a) How many workers should the firm hire? b) What principle guides this decision?

Solution

a) The firm should hire 4 workers. At 4 workers, the marginal revenue product ($250) still exceeds the marginal cost ($200). Adding a 5th worker costs $200 but generates only $150 in revenue — a net loss.

b) The MB = MC principle: hire as long as the marginal benefit (marginal revenue product) exceeds the marginal cost (wage).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Production Possibilities Frontier
docs.text:
An economy produces only food and clothing. With all resources devoted to food, it can produce 120 units. With all resources devoted to clothing, it can produce 60 units. Assume the PPF is a straight line.

a) Draw the PPF and label the intercepts. b) What is the opportunity cost of 1 unit of clothing in terms of food? c) What is the opportunity cost of 1 unit of food in terms of clothing? d) If the economy is producing at (60 food, 30 clothing), is it efficient?

Solution

a) The PPF runs from (0 food, 60 clothing) to (120 food, 0 clothing) — a straight line.

b) Opportunity cost of 1 unit of clothing = 120/60 = 2 units of food.

c) Opportunity cost of 1 unit of food = 60/120 = 0.5 units of clothing.

d) The point (60, 30) lies exactly on the PPF (it satisfies the constraint: 60/120 + 30/60 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1). This is an efficient point.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Positive vs. Normative
docs.text:
Classify each statement as positive or normative.

  1. "The United States spends about 18% of GDP on healthcare."
  2. "The government should provide universal healthcare."
  3. "Rent control reduces the quantity of housing supplied."
  4. "Housing is a human right and should not be subject to market prices."
Solution
  1. Positive — a factual, measurable claim.
  2. Normative — a value judgment about policy.
  3. Positive — a testable prediction of economic theory.
  4. Normative — a statement about values, not facts.

You've Learned to Think Like an Economist

Look back at where you started: you can now name a hidden cost, resist a sunk-cost trap, apply MB = MC to a real decision, and read a PPF. That's the entire toolkit this book builds on — every choice has a trade-off!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 2: Supply and Demand, we use these foundations to build the most powerful tool in economics — the supply-and-demand model.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the law of demand and construct a demand curve
  2. Explain the law of supply and construct a supply curve
  3. Identify the determinants that shift supply and demand curves
  4. Find the market equilibrium price and quantity
  5. Analyze how supply and demand shifts change equilibrium
  6. Explain the concepts of consumer surplus, producer surplus, and market efficiency

Welcome Back!

Welcome back! This chapter hands you the single most useful tool in all of economics: supply and demand. Once you can read these two curves, you can explain rent spikes, gas shortages, and ticket scalping — every choice has a trade-off, and this chapter shows you how markets sort them out.

docs.title: 2.1 Markets
docs.text:
A market is any arrangement that facilitates the exchange of a good or service between buyers and sellers. Markets can be physical (a farmers' market), virtual (Amazon), or decentralized (the labor market). The price that emerges in a market coordinates the decisions of buyers and sellers without any central authority directing them.

Markets everywhere

  • The market for Minneapolis apartment rentals
  • The market for computer science graduates
  • The New York Stock Exchange
  • The global market for crude oil

docs.title: The Law of Demand
docs.text:
Demand refers to the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity that consumers are willing and able to buy, holding all else equal.

The Law of Demand: When the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls (and vice versa), ceteris paribus.

\[Q_d = f(P, \overline{I}, \overline{P_r}, \overline{\text{Tastes}}, \overline{E}, \overline{N})\]

where \(P\) is price (variable) and the bars denote factors held constant.

The demand curve is a downward-sloping line (or curve) showing the quantity demanded at each price.

docs.title: Why Does Demand Slope Downward?
docs.text:
Two effects explain the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded:

  1. Substitution effect: When the price of coffee rises, consumers substitute toward tea. The good becomes relatively more expensive.
  2. Income effect: When the price of coffee rises, consumers' purchasing power falls — they can afford less of everything, including coffee.

Two Effects, Same Direction

Notice that both effects point the same direction: a higher price makes a good relatively more expensive (substitution) and makes you poorer in real terms (income). That's why the law of demand holds so reliably.

docs.title: The Demand Schedule and Curve
docs.text:
Consider the market for gasoline in Minneapolis:

Price ($/gallon) Quantity Demanded (million gallons/month) $2.00 60 $3.00 50 $4.00 40 $5.00 30 $6.00 20

Plotting price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis gives a downward-sloping demand curve.

docs.title: Movements Along vs. Shifts of the Demand Curve
docs.text:
Movement along the demand curve: Caused only by a change in the price of the good itself. This is a change in quantity demanded.

Shift of the demand curve: Caused by a change in any other factor that affects demand. The entire curve moves left (decrease) or right (increase).

Movement or Shift?

Students often say "demand increased" when a price change actually caused a movement along the curve. Before you write "shift," ask yourself: did the price of this exact good change? If yes, it's a movement, not a shift.

docs.title: Determinants of Demand (Demand Shifters)
docs.text:
Determinant Increase in Demand Decrease in Demand Income (normal good) Income rises Income falls Income (inferior good) Income falls Income rises Price of a substitute Substitute price rises Substitute price falls Price of a complement Complement price falls Complement price rises Consumer tastes Good becomes more popular Good becomes less popular Expectations (future price ↑) Buy more now Buy less now Number of buyers More buyers Fewer buyers

Substitutes and complements

  • Substitutes: Butter and margarine. If the price of butter rises, demand for margarine increases (the demand curve for margarine shifts right).
  • Complements: Cars and gasoline. If the price of gasoline rises, demand for large cars decreases (the demand curve for large cars shifts left).

Normal vs. inferior goods

  • Normal goods: As income rises, demand rises. Example: restaurant meals, new cars.
  • Inferior goods: As income rises, demand falls. Example: instant noodles, used cars. (People switch to better substitutes when they can afford it.)

docs.title: The Law of Supply
docs.text:
Supply refers to the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity that producers are willing and able to sell, holding all else equal.

The Law of Supply: When the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises (and vice versa), ceteris paribus.

The supply curve is an upward-sloping line (or curve) showing the quantity supplied at each price.

docs.title: Why Does Supply Slope Upward?
docs.text:
• Higher prices make production more profitable, inducing existing firms to expand output and attracting new firms into the market.
  • At higher prices, firms are willing to incur higher marginal costs to supply more units.

docs.title: The Supply Schedule and Curve
docs.text: Price ($/gallon) Quantity Supplied (million gallons/month) $2.00 20 $3.00 30 $4.00 40 $5.00 50 $6.00 60

docs.title: Determinants of Supply (Supply Shifters)
docs.text:
Determinant Increase in Supply Decrease in Supply Input prices (e.g., wages, materials) Input costs fall Input costs rise Technology Productivity improves Productivity falls Number of sellers More sellers enter Sellers exit Government policy Subsidy given Tax imposed Expectations (future price ↑) Withhold supply now — Prices of related goods in production Alternative good price falls Alternative good price rises

Technology and supply

The development of hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") dramatically lowered the cost of extracting natural gas. This shifted the supply curve for natural gas rightward — producers were willing to supply more at every price, driving down the market price.

Spotting Surplus vs. Shortage Fast

To tell surplus from shortage fast, compare the current price to \(P^*\): above it, picture unsold inventory piling up (surplus); below it, picture a line out the door (shortage).

docs.title: Finding Equilibrium
docs.text:
Market equilibrium occurs where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. At the equilibrium price (\(P^*\)), the market clears — there is no unsatisfied demand and no unsold surplus.

\[Q_d(P^*) = Q_s(P^*) \implies \text{market equilibrium}\]

Using our gasoline example:

Price \(Q_d\) \(Q_s\) Surplus / Shortage $2.00 60 20 Shortage of 40 $3.00 50 30 Shortage of 20 $4.00 40 40 Equilibrium $5.00 30 50 Surplus of 20 $6.00 20 60 Surplus of 40

The equilibrium is \(P^* = \$4.00\), \(Q^* = 40\) million gallons.

docs.title: Surplus and Shortage
docs.text:
Surplus (excess supply): When price is above equilibrium, \(Q_s > Q_d\). Unsold goods accumulate; sellers lower prices. The market self-corrects downward toward \(P^*\).

Shortage (excess demand): When price is below equilibrium, \(Q_d > Q_s\). Buyers compete for scarce goods; prices are bid up. The market self-corrects upward toward \(P^*\).

The market as a coordinating mechanism

Prices serve as signals. A price above equilibrium signals "too much supply — cut back." A price below equilibrium signals "too much demand — produce more." No central planner is needed.

Algebra Is Just the Table, Rewritten

Solving \(Q_d = Q_s\) algebraically feels abstract the first few times — that's normal. Work through the gasoline numbers above with a pencil before reading the worked example below; you'll find the algebra is just the table you already understand, written differently.

docs.title: Mathematical Example
docs.text:
Suppose the demand and supply equations for a good are:

\[Q_d = 100 - 2P\] \[Q_s = 10 + 3P\]

Finding equilibrium:

\[Q_d = Q_s\] \[100 - 2P = 10 + 3P\] \[90 = 5P\] \[P^* = 18\] \[Q^* = 100 - 2(18) = 64\]

The equilibrium price is $18 and equilibrium quantity is 64 units.

docs.title: 2.5 Changes in Equilibrium
docs.text:
When supply or demand shifts, the equilibrium changes. Use the following three-step method:

Step 1: Draw the initial supply and demand curves and mark the initial equilibrium. Step 2: Determine which curve shifts, and in which direction. Step 3: Find the new equilibrium and describe what happened to \(P\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Case 1: Demand Increases
docs.text:
Example: A hot summer increases demand for ice cream.

  • Demand curve shifts right.
  • At the old price, there is a shortage.
  • Price is bid up → equilibrium price rises.
  • Higher price induces more production → equilibrium quantity rises.

Result: Both P and Q rise.

docs.title: Case 2: Demand Decreases
docs.text:
Example: A health study links red meat to cancer, reducing beef demand.

  • Demand curve shifts left.
  • At the old price, there is a surplus.
  • Price falls → equilibrium price falls.
  • Lower price reduces production → equilibrium quantity falls.

Result: Both P and Q fall.

docs.title: Case 3: Supply Increases
docs.text:
Example: Better corn seed technology increases corn supply.

  • Supply curve shifts right.
  • At the old price, there is a surplus.
  • Price falls → equilibrium price falls.
  • Lower price increases quantity demanded → equilibrium quantity rises.

Result: P falls, Q rises.

docs.title: Case 4: Supply Decreases
docs.text:
Example: A drought destroys part of the wheat crop.

  • Supply curve shifts left.
  • At the old price, there is a shortage.
  • Price rises → equilibrium price rises.
  • Higher price reduces quantity demanded → equilibrium quantity falls.

Result: P rises, Q falls.

docs.title: Summary of Equilibrium Effects
docs.text:
Event Demand Supply \(\Delta P^*\) \(\Delta Q^*\) Demand increases Shifts right Unchanged ↑ ↑ Demand decreases Shifts left Unchanged ↓ ↓ Supply increases Unchanged Shifts right ↓ ↑ Supply decreases Unchanged Shifts left ↑ ↓ Both increase Shifts right Shifts right ? ↑↑ Demand ↑, Supply ↓ Shifts right Shifts left ↑↑ ?

Simultaneous shifts

When both curves shift, the effect on price or quantity may be ambiguous without knowing the relative magnitudes. For example, if demand and supply both increase, quantity definitely rises — but price could rise, fall, or stay the same depending on which shift dominates.

docs.title: Consumer Surplus
docs.text:
Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a good and what they actually pay.

\[\text{Consumer Surplus} = \text{Willingness to Pay} - \text{Price Paid}\]

Graphically, consumer surplus is the area above the price and below the demand curve.

Ticket example

Three fans value a Taylor Swift concert ticket as follows: Fan A: $300, Fan B: $200, Fan C: $100. If tickets sell for $150, only Fan A and Fan B buy. Their consumer surpluses are: - Fan A: $300 − $150 = $150 - Fan B: $200 − $150 = $50 - Total Consumer Surplus = $200

docs.title: Producer Surplus
docs.text:
Producer surplus is the difference between the price producers receive and the minimum price they would have accepted.

\[\text{Producer Surplus} = \text{Price Received} - \text{Minimum Acceptable Price}\]

Graphically, producer surplus is the area below the price and above the supply curve.

docs.title: Total Surplus and Market Efficiency
docs.text:
Total surplus = Consumer surplus + Producer surplus

A competitive market maximizes total surplus — it is allocatively efficient. No reallocation could make someone better off without making someone else worse off (this is Pareto efficiency).

The invisible hand

Adam Smith (1776) observed that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets are led by an "invisible hand" to promote the public interest. The supply-and-demand model formalizes this insight: competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Market Any arrangement facilitating exchange between buyers and sellers Demand The relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus Law of Demand As price rises, quantity demanded falls Demand Curve A downward-sloping curve showing quantity demanded at each price Quantity Demanded The specific amount buyers want at a given price Change in Demand A shift of the entire demand curve due to a non-price factor Supply The relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus Law of Supply As price rises, quantity supplied rises Supply Curve An upward-sloping curve showing quantity supplied at each price Market Equilibrium The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied Equilibrium Price The market-clearing price (\(P^*\)) Equilibrium Quantity The quantity traded at \(P^*\) Surplus Excess supply when price is above equilibrium Shortage Excess demand when price is below equilibrium Consumer Surplus Difference between willingness to pay and price paid Producer Surplus Difference between price received and minimum acceptable price Total Surplus Consumer surplus + Producer surplus; maximized at competitive equilibrium Normal Good A good for which demand rises as income rises Inferior Good A good for which demand falls as income rises Substitute A good that can replace another; their demands move together Complement A good used with another; their demands move inversely

docs.title: Problem 1 — Shifts in Demand
docs.text:
For each event, state whether demand for the good in bold increases, decreases, or is unchanged. Also state whether this is a movement along the demand curve or a shift.

a) The price of butter rises. What happens to demand for margarine (a substitute)? b) Income rises. What happens to demand for instant ramen noodles (an inferior good)? c) The price of coffee rises. What happens to demand for coffee itself? d) A new study finds that red wine reduces heart disease risk. e) The price of printers falls. What happens to demand for printer ink?

Solution

a) Demand for margarine increases (shifts right) — butter is a substitute; its higher price makes margarine relatively attractive.

b) Demand for instant ramen decreases (shifts left) — inferior good; higher income reduces demand.

c) The quantity demanded of coffee falls (movement along the demand curve) — this is a price change of the good itself, not a shift.

d) Demand for red wine increases (shifts right) — tastes change in favor of the good.

e) Demand for printer ink increases (shifts right) — printers and ink are complements; cheaper printers mean more printers sold, so more ink needed.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Market Equilibrium
docs.text:
The market for apartments in a college town has:

\[Q_d = 1200 - 3P\] \[Q_s = 300 + 2P\]

where \(Q\) is the number of apartments and \(P\) is monthly rent.

a) Find the equilibrium rent and quantity. b) At a rent of $200/month, is there a surplus or shortage? By how much? c) At a rent of $240/month, is there a surplus or shortage? By how much?

Solution

a) Set \(Q_d = Q_s\):

\[1200 - 3P = 300 + 2P$$ $$900 = 5P$$ $$P^* = \$180, \quad Q^* = 1200 - 3(180) = 660 \text{ apartments}\]

b) At P = $200: - \(Q_d = 1200 - 3(200) = 600\) - \(Q_s = 300 + 2(200) = 700\) - Surplus of 100 apartments (quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded)

c) At P = $240: - \(Q_d = 1200 - 3(240) = 480\) - \(Q_s = 300 + 2(240) = 780\) - Surplus of 300 apartments

docs.title: Problem 3 — Equilibrium Changes
docs.text:
In the market for gasoline, explain the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity of each event. State clearly which curve shifts, in which direction, and what happens to \(P^*\) and \(Q^*\).

a) The price of crude oil (a key input) rises sharply. b) Higher fuel efficiency standards cause consumers to drive less. c) A new refinery opens, and simultaneously, the price of electric vehicles falls (reducing demand for gasoline).

Solution

a) Supply decreases (shifts left) — higher input cost. - \(P^*\) rises, \(Q^*\) falls.

b) Demand decreases (shifts left) — consumers want less gasoline at every price. - \(P^*\) falls, \(Q^*\) falls.

c) Supply increases (new refinery → shifts right) AND Demand decreases (cheaper EVs reduce gas demand → shifts left). - Both shifts push \(Q^*\) down (unambiguously). - Effect on \(P^*\) is ambiguous — supply increase pushes price down, demand decrease also pushes price down, so \(P^*\) falls (in this case both effects reinforce each other).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Consumer and Producer Surplus
docs.text:
The supply and demand for a good are:

\[Q_d = 80 - P\] \[Q_s = 20 + P\]

a) Find equilibrium P* and Q*. b) Calculate consumer surplus at equilibrium. c) Calculate producer surplus at equilibrium. d) What is total surplus?

Solution

a) Set \(Q_d = Q_s\): \(80 - P = 20 + P \Rightarrow 60 = 2P \Rightarrow P^* = 30, \; Q^* = 50\)

b) Consumer surplus is the area of the triangle above the price and below the demand curve.

The demand curve hits the vertical axis when \(Q_d = 0\): \(0 = 80 - P \Rightarrow P = 80\).

\[\text{CS} = \frac{1}{2} \times (80 - 30) \times 50 = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 50 = \$1{,}250\]

c) Producer surplus is the area of the triangle below the price and above the supply curve.

The supply curve hits the vertical axis when \(Q_s = 0\): \(0 = 20 + P \Rightarrow P = -20\). Wait — the supply curve starts where \(Q_s = 0\), so: \(20 + P = 0 \Rightarrow P = -20\). But negative prices don't make sense here. The minimum supply price (the y-intercept of supply when we solve for P) is: the supply curve starts supplying when price is such that \(Q_s > 0\), i.e., when \(P > -20\). At \(P = 0\), \(Q_s = 20\).

More precisely: solving \(Q_s = 20 + P\) for P: \(P = Q_s - 20\). The supply curve (as \(P\) as a function of \(Q\)) is \(P = Q - 20\). It intercepts the horizontal axis (P=0) at Q=20, and the P-axis at P=-20. Since we can't have negative prices in this market context, the supply curve effectively starts at Q=20 when P=0.

Producer surplus = area below P* = 30 and above the supply curve, from Q=0 to Q=50. Since the supply "curve" P = Q - 20 intersects P=0 at Q=20 and P=30 at Q=50:

\[\text{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \times (30 - (-20)) \times 50 = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 50 = \$1{,}250\]

Alternatively, using the triangular area with base 50 (from Q=0 to Q=50) and height = 30 - (-20) = 50: PS = ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

d) Total surplus = CS + PS = $1,250 + $1,250 = $2,500.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Real World Application
docs.text:
In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic caused the demand for hand sanitizer to increase dramatically. At the same time, some producers switched from producing other goods to producing hand sanitizer (supply increased).

a) What happened to the equilibrium quantity of hand sanitizer? Explain. b) Is the effect on equilibrium price certain or ambiguous? Explain. c) During the pandemic, many stores ran out of hand sanitizer despite producers ramping up. Is this consistent with the supply-and-demand model? What does it suggest about prices?

Solution

a) Equilibrium quantity definitely increased — both the demand increase and the supply increase push quantity upward. The two effects reinforce each other.

b) The effect on price is ambiguous. The demand increase pushes price up; the supply increase pushes price down. The net effect depends on which shift was larger.

c) Running out of stock is a shortage — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. This is consistent with supply-and-demand theory when price is held below equilibrium. Many retailers chose not to raise prices (for ethical or reputational reasons), so prices did not rise to clear the market. This suggests that the equilibrium price for hand sanitizer rose substantially — but price controls (informal or formal) prevented prices from reaching equilibrium.

You Can Now Read a Market

You can now build a demand curve, a supply curve, find equilibrium algebraically, and measure who gains from a trade. That's the engine behind nearly every chapter still to come!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 3: Elasticity, we measure how much quantity demanded and supplied respond to price changes — a crucial tool for business and policy analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Calculate the price elasticity of demand using the percentage-change and midpoint formulas
  2. Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit-elastic, and interpret the economic meaning of each case
  3. Identify the determinants that make demand more or less elastic
  4. Use the relationship between elasticity and total revenue to predict how price changes affect firm revenue
  5. Calculate and interpret the price elasticity of supply
  6. Calculate income elasticity and cross-price elasticity of demand and classify goods using these measures
  7. Apply elasticity concepts to real-world problems in taxation, pricing strategy, and public policy

Let's Measure Responsiveness

Chapter 2 told you demand curves slope downward — but not by how much. This chapter gives you that missing number, elasticity, and it's one you'll use constantly: in pricing decisions, tax policy, and even your own grocery budget. Every choice has a trade-off, and elasticity tells you how sharply people react to one.

docs.title: 3.1 Why Elasticity Matters
docs.text:
The supply and demand model in Chapter 2 tells us the direction in which quantity responds to a price change — but not the magnitude. If a city raises the transit fare by 10%, does ridership fall by 1% or by 30%? The answer matters enormously: it determines whether the transit agency's revenue rises or falls, and it determines how much of a product tax is passed on to consumers versus absorbed by producers.

Elasticity is a general concept in economics measuring the responsiveness of one variable to a change in another, expressed in percentage terms. Because elasticity is a ratio of percentage changes, it is a unit-free number — unlike slope, which depends on the units in which price and quantity are measured. This makes elasticity ideal for comparing responsiveness across very different goods, from gasoline to shoes to higher education.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The price elasticity of demand (\(E_d\)) measures how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price:

\[E_d = \frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta P}\]

Because demand curves slope downward, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so \(E_d\) is mathematically negative. By convention, economists report the absolute value of \(E_d\) and describe demand in terms of its magnitude.

docs.title: The Percentage-Change Formula
docs.text:
\[E_d = \frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta P} = \frac{\Delta Q / Q}{\Delta P / P}\]

Simple calculation

Suppose the price of movie tickets rises from $10 to $12 (a 20% increase), and quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 900 tickets per week (a 10% decrease).

\[E_d = \frac{-10\%}{20\%} = -0.5 \implies |E_d| = 0.5\]

Demand is inelastic: quantity demanded is relatively unresponsive to the price change.

docs.title: The Midpoint (Arc Elasticity) Formula
docs.text:
The simple percentage-change formula has a flaw: the elasticity calculated for a price increase from $10 to $12 differs from the elasticity calculated for a price decrease from $12 to $10, because the base used for the percentage differs. The midpoint formula solves this by using the average of the two values as the base:

\[E_d = \frac{(Q_2 - Q_1)/\left[(Q_1+Q_2)/2\right]}{(P_2 - P_1)/\left[(P_1+P_2)/2\right]}\]

Midpoint formula applied

Using the ticket example: \(P_1 = 10, P_2 = 12, Q_1 = 1000, Q_2 = 900\).

\[\%\Delta Q = \frac{900 - 1000}{(1000+900)/2} = \frac{-100}{950} = -10.53\%\] \[\%\Delta P = \frac{12 - 10}{(10+12)/2} = \frac{2}{11} = 18.18\%\] \[E_d = \frac{-10.53\%}{18.18\%} = -0.58 \implies |E_d| = 0.58\]

This is close to, but not identical to, the simple-formula answer of 0.5 — the midpoint method gives a consistent answer regardless of the direction of the price change.

When to use which formula

Use the midpoint formula for calculations over a discrete price change (a table or a word problem giving two price-quantity pairs). When demand is given as a continuous function, economists often instead compute point elasticity using calculus: \(E_d = \frac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\frac{P}{Q}\) evaluated at a specific point.

The Number Matters More Than the Formula

Don't get lost memorizing formulas — the real insight is the classification. Whether \(|E_d|\) is exactly 0.58 or 0.6, what matters is that it's below 1: this good's buyers barely react to price.

docs.title: 3.3 Elastic, Inelastic, and Unit-Elastic Demand
docs.text:
Case Condition Interpretation Elastic \(\lvert E_d \rvert > 1\) Quantity demanded is highly responsive to price; %Δ\(Q\) > %Δ\(P\) Inelastic \(\lvert E_d \rvert < 1\) Quantity demanded is relatively unresponsive; %Δ\(Q\) < %Δ\(P\) Unit elastic \(\lvert E_d \rvert = 1\) %Δ\(Q\) exactly equals %Δ\(P\) Perfectly inelastic \(E_d = 0\) Quantity demanded does not change at all (vertical demand curve) Perfectly elastic \(E_d \to \infty\) Any price increase drives quantity demanded to zero (horizontal demand curve)

Perfectly inelastic and perfectly elastic demand

  • A patient with a life-threatening condition who needs a specific insulin dose has (approximately) perfectly inelastic demand for that dose — quantity demanded barely changes regardless of price.
  • A wheat farmer selling into a competitive world market faces (approximately) perfectly elastic demand for his own wheat — if he raises his price even slightly above the world price, buyers switch entirely to other farmers.

docs.title: 3.4 Determinants of Price Elasticity of Demand
docs.text:
Why is demand for some goods elastic and others inelastic? Four main factors determine elasticity:

  1. Availability of substitutes. The more and closer the substitutes, the more elastic demand. Demand for "Coca-Cola" is more elastic than demand for "soft drinks" in general, because a Coke drinker can switch to Pepsi.
  2. Necessity vs. luxury. Necessities (insulin, water) tend to have inelastic demand; luxuries (vacations, jewelry) tend to have elastic demand.
  3. Share of budget. Goods that take up a large share of a consumer's budget (housing, cars) tend to have more elastic demand than goods that take a tiny share (salt, matches), because a price change has a larger effect on the household budget.
  4. Time horizon. Demand is more elastic in the long run than in the short run, because consumers need time to adjust behavior, find substitutes, or change technology. When gasoline prices spike, short-run demand barely falls (people still need to commute), but over several years, people buy fuel-efficient cars, move closer to work, or switch to public transit.

Narrow vs. broad category

Narrowly defined goods (a specific brand) tend to have more elastic demand than broadly defined categories (the entire product class), because narrow categories have more substitutes available (other brands).

Four Questions, One Elasticity Estimate

Before crunching any numbers, ask yourself four quick questions: does it have substitutes, is it a necessity, does it eat a big share of the budget, and how much time do buyers have to adjust? Answering those usually tells you elastic-or-inelastic before you ever see data.

docs.title: 3.5 Total Revenue and Elasticity
docs.text: For a firm, the relationship between elasticity and total revenue (\(TR = P \times Q\)) is one of the most practically important results in microeconomics.

docs.title: The Total Revenue Test
docs.text:
Demand is... A price increase causes... A price decrease causes... Elastic (\(\lvert E_d\rvert > 1\)) Total revenue falls Total revenue rises Unit elastic (\(\lvert E_d\rvert = 1\)) Total revenue unchanged Total revenue unchanged Inelastic (\(\lvert E_d\rvert < 1\)) Total revenue rises Total revenue falls

Intuition: When demand is elastic, the percentage drop in quantity outweighs the percentage rise in price, so revenue (\(P \times Q\)) falls when price rises. When demand is inelastic, the percentage drop in quantity is small relative to the price increase, so revenue rises.

The Calculus Isn't the Hard Part

If taking a derivative here feels intimidating, remember: you already know why the answer works from the Total Revenue Test above. The calculus is just confirming, with precision, a direction you can already reason out.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Suppose a transit agency's demand curve is \(Q = 200 - 4P\), where \(Q\) is daily riders (thousands) and \(P\) is the fare in dollars.

Step 1: Write total revenue as a function of price.

\[TR(P) = P \times Q = P(200 - 4P) = 200P - 4P^2\]

Step 2: Find the revenue-maximizing price using calculus.

\[\frac{d(TR)}{dP} = 200 - 8P = 0 \implies P^* = 25\]

At \(P = 25\): \(Q = 200 - 4(25) = 100\), and \(TR = 25 \times 100 = 2{,}500\) (thousand dollars).

Step 3: Verify using elasticity. At the revenue-maximizing price, demand is unit elastic. Check:

\[E_d = \frac{dQ}{dP} \cdot \frac{P}{Q} = (-4)\cdot\frac{25}{100} = -1\]

Confirmed: \(\lvert E_d \rvert = 1\) exactly where revenue is maximized. For any price below $25, demand is inelastic (\(\lvert E_d\rvert <1\)) and raising price increases revenue; for any price above $25, demand is elastic and raising price decreases revenue.

Why airlines and concert venues care

Airlines and ticket sellers constantly estimate elasticity to set prices. If demand for a flight is inelastic (e.g., business travelers with no flexibility), raising the price increases revenue. If demand is elastic (e.g., leisure travelers who can delay or skip the trip), cutting the price increases revenue by drawing in enough new volume.

docs.title: 3.6 Price Elasticity of Supply
docs.text:
The price elasticity of supply (\(E_s\)) measures how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price:

\[E_s = \frac{\%\Delta Q_s}{\%\Delta P}\]

Because supply curves slope upward, \(E_s\) is positive. The same elastic/inelastic/unit-elastic classification applies.

docs.title: Determinants of Supply Elasticity
docs.text:
1. Availability of inputs and spare capacity. If firms have idle capacity or can easily obtain more inputs, supply is more elastic.
  2. Time horizon. Supply is more elastic in the long run, since firms can build new factories, and new firms can enter the industry.
  3. Flexibility of production. Goods that can be produced with easily reallocated resources (e.g., a farmer who can switch between crops) have more elastic supply. Goods tied to a unique, fixed resource (e.g., beachfront land, a famous painting) have highly inelastic — even perfectly inelastic — supply.

Perfectly inelastic supply

The supply of original Picasso paintings is perfectly inelastic (\(E_s = 0\)): no matter how high the price rises, no more can be produced. The entire burden of any price change falls on the demand side.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Suppose \(Q_s = -20 + 5P\). At \(P=10\), \(Q_s = 30\). If price rises to \(P=12\), \(Q_s = 40\).

Using the midpoint formula:

\[\%\Delta Q = \frac{40-30}{35} = 28.57\%, \qquad \%\Delta P = \frac{12-10}{11} = 18.18\%\] \[E_s = \frac{28.57\%}{18.18\%} = 1.57\]

Supply is elastic: producers expand quantity supplied proportionally more than the price increase.

docs.title: 3.7 Income Elasticity of Demand
docs.text:
Income elasticity of demand (\(E_I\)) measures how quantity demanded responds to a change in consumer income:

\[E_I = \frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta \text{Income}}\] Value of \(E_I\) Classification Example \(E_I > 1\) Luxury good (income elastic) Vacations, designer goods \(0 < E_I < 1\) Normal good, income inelastic Groceries, utilities \(E_I < 0\) Inferior good Instant ramen, used clothing

Income elasticity calculation

A household's income rises from $50,000 to $55,000 (a 10% increase), and their restaurant spending rises from 10 to 13 meals per month (a 30% increase using the simple formula).

\[E_I = \frac{30\%}{10\%} = 3.0\]

Restaurant meals are a strongly luxury good for this household — demand grows three times faster than income.

docs.title: 3.8 Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
docs.text:
Cross-price elasticity of demand (\(E_{xy}\)) measures how the quantity demanded of good \(X\) responds to a change in the price of good \(Y\):

\[E_{xy} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_x}{\%\Delta P_y}\] Sign of \(E_{xy}\) Relationship Example \(E_{xy} > 0\) Substitutes Coffee and tea \(E_{xy} < 0\) Complements Printers and ink \(E_{xy} = 0\) Unrelated Bananas and automobiles

Cross-price elasticity calculation

The price of Pepsi rises by 10%, and the quantity demanded of Coca-Cola rises by 4%.

\[E_{xy} = \frac{4\%}{10\%} = 0.4 > 0\]

Coke and Pepsi are substitutes, and a moderate positive cross-price elasticity suggests they are only moderately close substitutes (loyal customers of each brand do not switch readily).

docs.title: Tax Incidence
docs.text:
When a government imposes a tax on a good, elasticity determines who actually bears the burden of the tax — regardless of who physically pays it. The side of the market that is more inelastic bears a larger share of the tax burden, because that side has fewer options to avoid the tax by changing its quantity.

Cigarette taxes

Demand for cigarettes is highly inelastic (addictive good, few substitutes). When governments impose cigarette taxes, consumers continue to buy nearly the same quantity — the tax is largely passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices, and tax revenue is high and predictable. This is also why cigarette taxes are an effective tool for raising government revenue, even though they are intended to also discourage smoking.

Who Pays the Tax Isn't Who Bears It

It's easy to assume the side that legally writes the check to the government bears the tax. It doesn't — tax incidence depends entirely on relative elasticities, regardless of which side the law names as the "payer."

docs.title: Pricing Strategy and Price Discrimination
docs.text:
Firms use elasticity estimates to maximize revenue: charge a higher price to the segment of customers with inelastic demand, and a lower price to the segment with elastic demand.

Student and senior discounts

Movie theaters offer discounts to students and seniors — groups with more elastic demand (more time, less income, better substitutes like streaming) — while charging full price to working adults attending with limited scheduling flexibility, who have more inelastic demand.

docs.title: Agricultural Policy
docs.text:
Farm goods tend to have inelastic demand (necessities with few substitutes) and, in the short run, fairly inelastic supply (crops take a season to grow). A bumper harvest—a rightward shift in supply—can therefore reduce total farm revenue, because the resulting price drop is proportionally larger than the quantity increase. This is sometimes referred to as "the paradox of bumper crops," and it motivates agricultural price-support policy.

Elasticity is not fixed

A good's elasticity is not an immutable property, but depends on the price range, the time horizon, and how the good's market is defined. Always identify these conditions before applying an elasticity estimate to a new situation.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Elasticity A unit-free measure of the responsiveness of one variable to a percentage change in another Price Elasticity of Demand (\(E_d\)) % change in quantity demanded divided by % change in price Midpoint Formula Arc-elasticity formula using the average of two values as the base, giving a consistent result regardless of direction Elastic Demand \(\lvert E_d \rvert > 1\); quantity demanded is highly responsive to price Inelastic Demand \(\lvert E_d \rvert < 1\); quantity demanded is relatively unresponsive to price Unit-Elastic Demand \(\lvert E_d \rvert = 1\); % change in quantity equals % change in price Perfectly Inelastic Demand \(E_d = 0\); quantity demanded does not change at all Perfectly Elastic Demand \(E_d \to \infty\); any price increase drives quantity demanded to zero Total Revenue Test Method for inferring elasticity from how total revenue responds to a price change Price Elasticity of Supply (\(E_s\)) % change in quantity supplied divided by % change in price Income Elasticity of Demand (\(E_I\)) % change in quantity demanded divided by % change in income Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand (\(E_{xy}\)) % change in quantity demanded of good \(X\) divided by % change in price of good \(Y\) Tax Incidence The division of a tax's burden between buyers and sellers, determined by relative elasticities

docs.title: Problem 1 — Calculating Price Elasticity of Demand
docs.text:
The price of a bus pass rises from $40 to $44. Quantity demanded falls from 10,000 to 9,200 passes per month.

a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand using the midpoint formula. b) Is demand elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic? c) What will happen to the transit agency's total revenue?

Solution

a)

\[\%\Delta Q = \frac{9200-10000}{(10000+9200)/2} = \frac{-800}{9600} = -8.33\%\] \[\%\Delta P = \frac{44-40}{(40+44)/2} = \frac{4}{42} = 9.52\%\] \[E_d = \frac{-8.33\%}{9.52\%} = -0.875 \implies |E_d| = 0.875\]

b) Since \(\lvert E_d \rvert < 1\), demand is inelastic.

c) Revenue before: \(40 \times 10{,}000 = \$400{,}000\). Revenue after: \(44 \times 9{,}200 = \$404{,}800\). Revenue rises — consistent with the total revenue test: a price increase under inelastic demand raises revenue.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Determinants of Elasticity
docs.text:
For each pair, identify which good likely has more elastic demand, and explain why using the determinants of elasticity.

a) Insulin vs. a Netflix subscription b) "Honeycrisp apples" vs. "apples" (any variety) c) Gasoline demand measured over one month vs. over five years

Solution

a) Netflix subscription is more elastic — it is a discretionary entertainment good with substitutes (other streaming services, free content), while insulin is a life-necessity with no substitutes for diabetics.

b) "Honeycrisp apples" is more elastic — it is a narrowly defined good with many close substitutes (other apple varieties), while "apples" as a category has fewer substitutes (someone who wants apples can't easily substitute oranges for the same culinary purpose).

c) Demand measured over five years is more elastic — consumers have time to buy fuel-efficient vehicles, relocate, or switch to public transit; in one month, most consumption patterns are locked in.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Total Revenue and Elasticity
docs.text:
A firm's demand curve is \(Q = 300 - 5P\).

a) Derive the firm's total revenue function. b) Find the price that maximizes total revenue. c) Confirm using the elasticity formula that demand is unit elastic at that price.

Solution

a) \(TR = P \times Q = P(300-5P) = 300P - 5P^2\)

b) \(\dfrac{d(TR)}{dP} = 300 - 10P = 0 \implies P^* = 30\)

At \(P = 30\): \(Q = 300 - 5(30) = 150\), so \(TR = 30 \times 150 = \$4{,}500\).

c) \(E_d = \dfrac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\dfrac{P}{Q} = (-5)\cdot\dfrac{30}{150} = -1\). \(\lvert E_d\rvert = 1\), confirming unit elasticity at the revenue-maximizing price.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Price Elasticity of Supply
docs.text:
A supply curve is given by \(Q_s = 2P - 10\). At \(P=20\), find \(Q_s\). If price rises to \(P=25\), find the new \(Q_s\), and calculate the price elasticity of supply using the midpoint formula. Classify the result.

Solution

At \(P=20\): \(Q_s = 2(20)-10 = 30\).

At \(P=25\): \(Q_s = 2(25)-10 = 40\).

\[\%\Delta Q = \frac{40-30}{35} = 28.57\%, \qquad \%\Delta P = \frac{25-20}{22.5} = 22.22\%\] \[E_s = \frac{28.57\%}{22.22\%} = 1.29\]

Since \(E_s > 1\), supply is elastic.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Income and Cross-Price Elasticity
docs.text:
A household's income rises by 8%. As a result, their demand for public transit falls by 2%, and their demand for restaurant meals rises by 16%. Separately, when the price of butter rose by 5%, the quantity of margarine demanded by this household rose by 2%.

a) Calculate the income elasticity of demand for public transit and classify the good. b) Calculate the income elasticity of demand for restaurant meals and classify the good. c) Calculate the cross-price elasticity between butter and margarine and classify the relationship.

Solution

a) \(E_I = \dfrac{-2\%}{8\%} = -0.25\). Since \(E_I < 0\), public transit is an inferior good for this household.

b) \(E_I = \dfrac{16\%}{8\%} = 2.0\). Since \(E_I > 1\), restaurant meals are a luxury good.

c) \(E_{xy} = \dfrac{2\%}{5\%} = 0.4 > 0\). Butter and margarine are substitutes.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Tax Incidence Application
docs.text:
The government imposes a new excise tax on gasoline. Demand for gasoline is highly inelastic (\(\lvert E_d\rvert = 0.2\)) in the short run, while supply is relatively elastic (\(E_s = 1.5\)).

a) Which side of the market — consumers or producers — will bear more of the tax burden? Explain using the concept of elasticity. b) Suppose instead the government taxed a luxury good with highly elastic demand (\(\lvert E_d\rvert = 3\)) and inelastic supply (\(E_s = 0.3\)). Who bears more of the burden now?

Solution

a) Consumers bear more of the tax burden. Demand is far more inelastic than supply, meaning consumers have few alternatives and will continue buying gasoline even as the price rises to reflect the tax; producers, facing more elastic supply, can more easily adjust quantity and avoid absorbing much of the tax.

b) Producers bear more of the burden. Supply is far more inelastic than demand: producers cannot easily reduce the quantity they bring to market (perhaps due to fixed production commitments), while consumers can readily reduce quantity demanded in response to a price increase, shifting the burden back onto sellers.

You Can Now Quantify Responsiveness

You can now calculate four different elasticities, predict how a price change moves revenue, and explain who really bears a tax. That's a toolkit real firms and policymakers use every day!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 4: Consumer Theory, we go beneath the demand curve to study how individual consumers choose a utility-maximizing bundle of goods given their budget — providing the micro-foundations for the law of demand and elasticity itself.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish between total utility and marginal utility, and compute both from a utility schedule
  2. Explain and apply the law of diminishing marginal utility
  3. Use the equal marginal principle to find a consumer's utility-maximizing bundle of goods
  4. Construct and interpret a budget constraint, and explain how price and income changes affect it
  5. Read and interpret indifference curves and compute the marginal rate of substitution
  6. Find the consumer optimum using the tangency condition and explain why it maximizes utility
  7. Decompose a price change into income and substitution effects
  8. Explain how the consumer's utility-maximizing choices at different prices generate the market demand curve

Where Does Demand Really Come From?

We've been treating the demand curve as a given fact since Chapter 2 — now we build it from scratch, starting with a single consumer deciding how to spend a limited budget. By the end, you'll see the law of demand isn't an assumption; it's a conclusion. Every choice has a trade-off, and this chapter is about how people make that trade-off rationally.

docs.title: 4.1 From Market Demand to Individual Choice
docs.text: Chapter 2 introduced the demand curve as a market-level relationship between price and quantity demanded. But why does an individual consumer buy less of a good when its price rises? Consumer theory answers this question by modeling how a rational, self-interested consumer with limited income chooses among goods to make themselves as well off as possible. This chapter builds the micro-foundations of the demand curve from the ground up: first using the simpler language of utility, then using the more general and powerful tool of indifference curves.

docs.title: 4.2 Total and Marginal Utility
docs.text:
Utility is a numerical measure of the satisfaction or happiness a consumer derives from consuming goods and services. Total utility (\(TU\)) is the overall satisfaction from consuming a given quantity of a good. Marginal utility (\(MU\)) is the additional utility gained from consuming one more unit:

\[MU_n = TU_n - TU_{n-1}\]

Utility schedule for slices of pizza

Slices of Pizza Total Utility Marginal Utility 0 0 — 1 20 20 2 36 16 3 48 12 4 56 8 5 60 4 6 60 0 7 56 −4

Total utility rises with each additional slice up through slice 6, then falls — the 7th slice makes the consumer feel sick, generating negative marginal utility.

docs.title: 4.3 The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
docs.text:
The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: As a consumer consumes more units of a good within a given period, the marginal utility from each additional unit eventually decreases, holding consumption of other goods constant.

In the pizza example, marginal utility falls steadily from 20 (first slice) to 4 (fifth slice) before turning negative. This pattern — not total utility rising, but the increments getting smaller — is the single most important building block of consumer theory. It explains why consumers typically diversify their consumption across many goods rather than spending their entire income on one good: the tenth unit of anything is worth less to the consumer than the first.

Diminishing marginal utility vs. negative marginal utility

Diminishing marginal utility simply means each additional unit adds less satisfaction than the last — marginal utility is still positive, just declining. Marginal utility only becomes negative when consuming more actually makes the consumer worse off (e.g., overeating).

Why Diminishing Returns Shapes Everything

This is the single idea the rest of the chapter builds on: because each extra unit satisfies you less, you naturally spread your budget across many goods instead of binging on one. Keep this in the back of your mind as indifference curves and tangency conditions get more abstract.

docs.title: 4.4 Utility Maximization: The Equal Marginal Principle
docs.text:
A consumer with a fixed income and two goods (\(X\) and \(Y\)) maximizes total utility by allocating their budget so that the marginal utility per dollar spent is equal across all goods:

\[\frac{MU_x}{P_x} = \frac{MU_y}{P_y}\]

subject to the budget constraint \(P_x X + P_y Y = I\), where \(I\) is income.

Intuition: If \(\frac{MU_x}{P_x} > \frac{MU_y}{P_y}\), the consumer gets more "bang for the buck" from good \(X\). They should buy more \(X\) and less \(Y\) — shifting spending toward \(X\) raises total utility, until the marginal utilities per dollar are equalized.

Equal marginal principle: numerical example

A consumer has $10 to spend on candy bars (\(P_x = \$2\)) and sodas (\(P_y = \$1\)). Her marginal utility schedule:

Units \(MU_x\) (candy) \(MU_x/P_x\) \(MU_y\) (soda) \(MU_y/P_y\) 1 20 10 14 14 2 16 8 12 12 3 12 6 10 10 4 8 4 8 8 5 4 2 6 6

To maximize utility, the consumer buys units in order of highest \(MU/P\) until the $10 budget is exhausted: soda #1 (14), candy #1 (10), soda #2 (12), soda #3 (10, tie with candy #1 already bought — continue), candy #2 (8), soda #4 (8). Tracking spending: soda×4 = $4, candy×2 = $4, totaling $8 spent on 6 units... Continuing to allocate the remaining $2 to the next-highest ratios yields a bundle where \(MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y\) at the margin — in this schedule, 2 candy bars and 4 sodas spend \(2(2) + 1(4) = \$8\), and the next dollar gives equal marginal utility per dollar (4 and 6 respectively) from either additional good, with remaining funds pushing toward soda #5 and candy #3 until the ratios converge near 6.

The key takeaway is procedural: rank purchases by \(MU/P\), not by \(MU\) alone, and keep buying the next-best-value unit until the budget runs out.

docs.title: 4.5 Budget Constraints
docs.text:
The budget constraint shows all combinations of two goods a consumer can afford given their income and the goods' prices:

\[P_x X + P_y Y = I\]

Solving for \(Y\) gives the equation of the budget line:

\[Y = \frac{I}{P_y} - \frac{P_x}{P_y}X\]

The vertical intercept (\(I/P_y\)) is the maximum amount of \(Y\) affordable (if all income is spent on \(Y\)); the horizontal intercept (\(I/P_x\)) is the maximum amount of \(X\) affordable. The slope, \(-P_x/P_y\), is the opportunity cost of \(X\) in terms of \(Y\) — how much \(Y\) must be given up to buy one more unit of \(X\).

Budget line example

Income \(I = \$100\), \(P_x = \$5\) (movies), \(P_y = \$2\) (snacks).

\[Y = \frac{100}{2} - \frac{5}{2}X = 50 - 2.5X\]

If the consumer buys 0 movies, they can afford 50 snacks. If they buy 20 movies, they can afford 0 snacks. The slope is \(-2.5\): each additional movie costs 2.5 snacks in forgone consumption.

docs.title: Shifts of the Budget Line
docs.text:
• Income increases: The budget line shifts outward (parallel shift), since both intercepts increase proportionally.
  • Income decreases: The budget line shifts inward (parallel shift).
  • Price of \(X\) falls: The horizontal intercept (\(I/P_x\)) increases; the line rotates outward around the vertical intercept, becoming flatter.
  • Price of \(X\) rises: The horizontal intercept decreases; the line rotates inward, becoming steeper.

docs.title: 4.6 Indifference Curves and the Marginal Rate of Substitution
docs.text: An indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of total utility. The consumer is, by definition, indifferent between any two bundles on the same curve.

docs.title: Properties of Indifference Curves
docs.text:
1. Downward sloping: To keep utility constant while consuming more of one good, the consumer must give up some of the other.
  2. Convex to the origin (bowed inward): This reflects a diminishing willingness to trade one good for another as more of it is consumed.
  3. Higher curves represent higher utility: A consumer prefers any bundle on a curve farther from the origin.
  4. Curves do not intersect: If they did, it would imply inconsistent preferences.

docs.title: The Marginal Rate of Substitution
docs.text:
The marginal rate of substitution (\(MRS\)) is the rate at which a consumer is willing to trade one good for another while remaining equally satisfied — it is the (absolute value of the) slope of the indifference curve:

\[MRS_{xy} = -\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\bigg|_{\text{along indifference curve}} = \frac{MU_x}{MU_y}\]

Because of diminishing marginal utility, \(MRS\) diminishes as the consumer moves down an indifference curve (substituting more \(X\) for \(Y\)) — this is the law of diminishing marginal rate of substitution, and it is what gives indifference curves their characteristic convex (bowed-in) shape.

Diminishing MRS

Starting with 1 movie and 20 snacks, a consumer might willingly give up 8 snacks for a 2nd movie (\(MRS = 8\)). But starting with 4 movies and 4 snacks, she might only give up 1 snack for a 5th movie (\(MRS = 1\)) — movies have become relatively abundant, snacks relatively scarce, so she is far less willing to sacrifice additional snacks.

MRS Is Just a Ratio

No graph needed to find MRS — it's just \(MU_x/MU_y\). If a problem hands you marginal utilities, you already have the slope of the indifference curve at that point.

docs.title: 4.7 Consumer Optimum: The Tangency Condition
docs.text:
The consumer optimum is the bundle of goods that maximizes utility subject to the budget constraint. Graphically, it occurs where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve — the point where the budget line just touches, but does not cross, an indifference curve.

At this tangency point, the slope of the indifference curve equals the slope of the budget line:

\[MRS_{xy} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{MU_x}{P_x} = \frac{MU_y}{P_y}\]

This confirms that the tangency condition is mathematically identical to the equal marginal principle from Section 4.4 — two different ways of describing the same utility-maximizing condition.

Why not buy more of the good with higher MRS relative to price ratio?

If \(MRS_{xy} > P_x/P_y\), the consumer values an extra unit of \(X\) (in terms of \(Y\)) more than the market requires her to sacrifice. She should buy more \(X\) and less \(Y\), increasing utility, until the two ratios are equalized at the tangency point.

Partial Derivatives, One Variable at a Time

Taking \(MU_x\) and \(MU_y\) from a utility function like \(U=XY\) looks intimidating, but it's just ordinary differentiation treating the other variable as a constant. Work through the steps below slowly the first time — it gets mechanical fast.

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Consumer Optimum
docs.text:
Suppose a consumer's utility function is \(U(X,Y) = XY\), income is \(I = \$120\), \(P_x = \$4\), and \(P_y = \$6\).

Step 1: Compute marginal utilities: \(MU_x = Y\), \(MU_y = X\) (partial derivatives of \(U = XY\)).

Step 2: Apply the tangency condition:

\[\frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{P_x}{P_y} \implies \frac{Y}{X} = \frac{4}{6} \implies Y = \frac{2}{3}X\]

Step 3: Substitute into the budget constraint:

\[4X + 6Y = 120 \implies 4X + 6\left(\frac{2}{3}X\right) = 120 \implies 4X + 4X = 120 \implies X^* = 15\] \[Y^* = \frac{2}{3}(15) = 10\]

Check: \(4(15) + 6(10) = 60 + 60 = 120\). ✓ The optimal bundle is 15 units of \(X\) and 10 units of \(Y\).

docs.title: 4.8 Income and Substitution Effects
docs.text:
When the price of a good changes, the total change in quantity demanded can be decomposed into two distinct effects:

Effect Definition Substitution effect The change in quantity demanded due only to the change in relative prices, holding the consumer's utility (satisfaction) constant Income effect The change in quantity demanded due to the change in real purchasing power caused by the price change, holding relative prices constant

Total effect = Substitution effect + Income effect

Don't Assume the Income Effect Always Shrinks Demand

It's tempting to think the income effect always works against the substitution effect, but that's only true for inferior goods. For a normal good, both effects push quantity demanded in the same direction.

When the price of a good falls:

  • Substitution effect: The good becomes relatively cheaper compared to other goods, so the consumer substitutes toward it. This effect is always in the direction of buying more of the good whose price fell.
  • Income effect: The price decrease increases the consumer's real purchasing power (effectively like a raise in income). For a normal good, higher real income increases quantity demanded (reinforcing the substitution effect). For an inferior good, higher real income decreases quantity demanded (working against the substitution effect).
Good Type Substitution Effect (price ↓) Income Effect (price ↓) Net Effect Normal good Quantity ↑ Quantity ↑ Quantity ↑ (law of demand holds) Inferior good Quantity ↑ Quantity ↓ (but smaller) Quantity ↑ overall (law of demand still holds) Giffen good (rare) Quantity ↑ Quantity ↓ (dominates) Quantity ↓ overall (law of demand violated)

Giffen goods are a theoretical curiosity

A Giffen good is an extreme case of an inferior good where the negative income effect is so strong it overwhelms the substitution effect, causing quantity demanded to fall when price falls — violating the law of demand. Documented Giffen goods are exceedingly rare (some studies point to staple foods like rice or bread among very poor households); nearly all real-world goods obey the law of demand.

Graphical decomposition (verbal walkthrough)

Suppose the price of bus fare falls. Graphically: 1. The budget line rotates outward (pivoting on the \(Y\)-axis intercept, since only \(P_x\) changed). 2. Draw a hypothetical budget line parallel to the new budget line, but tangent to the original indifference curve — this isolates the substitution effect (same utility, new relative prices). The movement from the original optimum to this hypothetical point is the substitution effect. 3. The movement from this hypothetical point to the final optimum on the new, higher indifference curve is the income effect.

docs.title: 4.9 Deriving the Demand Curve from Consumer Theory
docs.text:
Consumer theory lets us derive the market demand curve directly from utility maximization. Holding income and the price of \(Y\) fixed, we can trace out the consumer's optimal quantity of \(X\) at each possible price of \(X\):

  1. Start at the consumer optimum for a given \(P_x\).
  2. Lower \(P_x\) — the budget line rotates outward, generating a new tangency point with a higher indifference curve, and (for a normal good) a higher optimal quantity of \(X\).
  3. Repeat for several prices and plot each price against the corresponding optimal quantity.
  4. The resulting locus of points is the individual's demand curve for \(X\).

This is why the demand curve slopes downward for ordinary (non-Giffen) goods: at every price, the consumer re-optimizes using the tangency condition, and for normal and most inferior goods, a lower price leads to a higher quantity demanded via the combined substitution and income effects.

From individual to market demand

The market demand curve is the horizontal summation of all individual consumers' demand curves — at each price, add up the quantity demanded by every consumer in the market.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Utility A numerical measure of satisfaction a consumer derives from consumption Total Utility The overall satisfaction from a given quantity of consumption Marginal Utility The additional utility from consuming one more unit of a good Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility Marginal utility decreases as more units of a good are consumed, holding other consumption constant Equal Marginal Principle Utility is maximized when marginal utility per dollar is equal across all goods Budget Constraint The set of all bundles of goods a consumer can afford given income and prices Indifference Curve A curve showing all bundles of goods that yield the same total utility Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS) The rate at which a consumer will trade one good for another while holding utility constant; equals \(MU_x/MU_y\) Consumer Optimum The utility-maximizing bundle, found where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve Tangency Condition \(MRS_{xy} = P_x/P_y\); the condition defining the consumer optimum Substitution Effect The change in quantity demanded from a price change, holding utility constant Income Effect The change in quantity demanded from the change in real purchasing power caused by a price change Giffen Good A good for which quantity demanded falls when price falls, violating the law of demand

docs.title: Problem 1 — Total and Marginal Utility
docs.text:
A consumer's total utility from consuming cups of coffee is given below:

Cups 0 1 2 3 4 5 Total Utility 0 30 54 72 84 90

a) Calculate the marginal utility of each cup. b) Does this schedule display diminishing marginal utility? Explain. c) At what point (if shown) would marginal utility become negative, based on the pattern?

Solution

a) \(MU_1 = 30, MU_2 = 24, MU_3 = 18, MU_4 = 12, MU_5 = 6\).

b) Yes — marginal utility falls steadily from 30 to 6 with each additional cup, which is the definition of diminishing marginal utility.

c) The marginal utilities are falling by 6 each time (30, 24, 18, 12, 6), so the 6th cup would have \(MU_6 = 0\), and the 7th cup would have \(MU_7 = -6\) (negative) if the pattern continues.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Equal Marginal Principle
docs.text:
A consumer has $18 to spend on apples (\(P = \$2\)) and oranges (\(P = \$3\)). Marginal utility schedules:

Units \(MU\) apples \(MU\) oranges 1 24 27 2 20 21 3 16 15 4 12 9 5 8 6 6 4 3

Find the utility-maximizing combination of apples and oranges that exhausts the $18 budget.

Solution

Compute \(MU/P\) for each unit:

Units \(MU_a/P_a\) (÷2) \(MU_o/P_o\) (÷3) 1 12 9 2 10 7 3 8 5 4 6 3 5 4 2 6 2 1

Rank and purchase in order of highest \(MU/P\) until $18 is spent: apple#1 (12, $2), apple#2 (10, $2), orange#1 (9, $3), apple#3 (8, $2), orange#2 (7, $3), apple#4 (6, $2) — running total: 2+2+3+2+3+2 = $14. Next highest is orange#3 (5, $3) → total $17. Next highest remaining is apple#5 (4) but only $1 left, not enough for apple ($2) or another orange ($3).

Final bundle: 4 apples and 3 oranges, spending \(4(2) + 3(3) = 8 + 9 = \$17\) (the remaining $1 cannot buy another unit of either good, so it is unspent or saved).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Budget Constraint
docs.text:
Income is $200, \(P_x = \$10\) (concert tickets), \(P_y = \$4\) (books).

a) Write the equation for the budget line (solve for \(Y\) in terms of \(X\)). b) Find both intercepts. c) If the price of concert tickets falls to $8, how does the budget line change?

Solution

a) \(10X + 4Y = 200 \implies Y = 50 - 2.5X\)

b) Vertical intercept (\(X=0\)): \(Y = 50\) books. Horizontal intercept (\(Y=0\)): \(0 = 50-2.5X \implies X = 20\) tickets.

c) New line: \(8X + 4Y = 200 \implies Y = 50 - 2X\). The vertical intercept stays at 50 (books unaffected), but the horizontal intercept rises to \(X = 25\). The budget line rotates outward around the vertical intercept, becoming flatter (opportunity cost of tickets in terms of books falls from 2.5 to 2).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Consumer Optimum (Tangency Condition)
docs.text:
A consumer's utility function is \(U(X,Y) = X^2Y\), giving \(MU_x = 2XY\) and \(MU_y = X^2\). Income is \(I = \$300\), \(P_x = \$10\), \(P_y = \$5\).

a) Set up the tangency condition. b) Solve for the optimal bundle \((X^*, Y^*)\).

Solution

a) Tangency condition: \(\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \dfrac{P_x}{P_y} \implies \dfrac{2XY}{X^2} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 \implies \dfrac{2Y}{X} = 2 \implies Y = X\)

b) Substitute into budget constraint: \(10X + 5Y = 300\). Since \(Y = X\): \(10X + 5X = 300 \implies 15X = 300 \implies X^* = 20\), and \(Y^* = 20\).

Check: \(10(20) + 5(20) = 200 + 100 = 300\). ✓ Optimal bundle: \(X^*=20, Y^*=20\).

docs.title: Problem 5 — Income and Substitution Effects
docs.text:
Classify each scenario by good type and describe the direction of the substitution and income effects.

a) The price of name-brand cereal falls, and a normal-good consumer buys more of it. b) The price of store-brand macaroni (an inferior good) falls, and the consumer buys more of it, but less than the substitution effect alone would predict. c) A hypothetical Giffen good's price falls, and the consumer buys less of it overall.

Solution
