a) Normal good: substitution effect (quantity ↑, cheaper relative price) and income effect (quantity ↑, higher real income raises demand for normal good) both point in the same direction — quantity demanded rises, consistent with the law of demand.

b) Inferior good: substitution effect (quantity ↑) and income effect (quantity ↓, since higher real income reduces demand for an inferior good) work in opposite directions, but the substitution effect dominates, so quantity demanded still rises overall — the law of demand still holds.

c) Giffen good: substitution effect (quantity ↑) and income effect (quantity ↓) work in opposite directions, but here the income effect dominates, causing quantity demanded to fall when price falls — a violation of the law of demand, confirming this good is a (rare) Giffen good.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Deriving Demand from Consumer Theory
docs.text:
A consumer's utility function is \(U(X,Y)=XY\), income is $100, and \(P_y = \$5\). Using the tangency condition and budget constraint (following the method of Section 4.7), find the optimal quantity of \(X\) when \(P_x = \$5\), and again when \(P_x = \$2\). What does this reveal about the shape of the individual's demand curve for \(X\)?

Solution

For \(U=XY\): \(MU_x = Y\), \(MU_y = X\). Tangency: \(\dfrac{Y}{X} = \dfrac{P_x}{P_y} \implies Y = \dfrac{P_x}{P_y}X\).

At \(P_x = 5\): \(Y = \dfrac{5}{5}X = X\). Budget: \(5X + 5Y = 100 \implies 5X+5X=100 \implies X^*=10\).

At \(P_x = 2\): \(Y = \dfrac{2}{5}X\). Budget: \(2X + 5\left(\dfrac{2}{5}X\right) = 100 \implies 2X+2X=100 \implies X^*=25\).

As \(P_x\) fell from $5 to $2, the optimal quantity of \(X\) rose from 10 to 25. Plotting these price-quantity pairs \((5,10)\) and \((2,25)\) traces out points on a downward-sloping demand curve for \(X\) — exactly the relationship predicted by the law of demand, now derived rigorously from utility maximization rather than simply assumed.

You've Built the Demand Curve From Scratch

You just derived the law of demand from first principles — utility, a budget, and a tangency condition — instead of simply assuming it. That's real theoretical grounding, and it's what separates an economist from someone who just memorized a downward-sloping line.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 5: Production and Costs, we turn from the consumer's side of the market to the producer's side, studying how firms transform inputs into output and how their cost structures shape the supply decisions introduced in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Describe a production function and distinguish between fixed and variable inputs
  2. Calculate and interpret total, marginal, and average product
  3. Distinguish between the short run and the long run in production decisions
  4. Explain and apply the law of diminishing marginal returns
  5. Distinguish fixed costs, variable costs, and total costs, and graph each
  6. Calculate average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost
  7. Calculate marginal cost and explain its relationship to average costs
  8. Explain economies and diseconomies of scale and identify the minimum efficient scale

From Costs to Curves

We've studied how consumers choose what to buy — now we flip to the other side of the market and ask how firms decide what to produce. Everything here sets up the shutdown and supply decisions coming in Chapter 6, so pay close attention to how marginal cost behaves. Every choice has a trade-off, and for a firm, that trade-off is written into its cost curves.

docs.title: 5.1 The Production Function
docs.text:
A production function describes the maximum quantity of output a firm can produce from a given combination of inputs, given the current state of technology:

\[Q = f(L, K)\]

where \(Q\) is output, \(L\) is labor, and \(K\) is capital (the two most common inputs in simplified models). A production function is a purely technological relationship — it says nothing yet about costs or prices, only about what is physically possible.

Inputs across industries

  • A bakery: labor (bakers), capital (ovens, mixers), and raw materials (flour, sugar)
  • A software firm: labor (engineers), capital (servers, computers)
  • A farm: labor, capital (tractors), and land

docs.title: 5.2 Total, Marginal, and Average Product
docs.text:
Economists track three related measures of a firm's output as it varies one input (typically labor) while holding others fixed:

Measure Definition Formula Total Product (TP) Total output produced by a given quantity of the variable input \(TP = Q\) Marginal Product (MP) The additional output from one more unit of the variable input \(MP_L = \dfrac{\Delta TP}{\Delta L}\) Average Product (AP) Output per unit of the variable input \(AP_L = \dfrac{TP}{L}\)

Production schedule for a food truck

Workers (\(L\)) Total Product (\(TP\)) Marginal Product (\(MP_L\)) Average Product (\(AP_L\)) 0 0 — — 1 10 10 10.0 2 22 12 11.0 3 33 11 11.0 4 40 7 10.0 5 44 4 8.8 6 44 0 7.3 7 40 −4 5.7

Marginal product rises at first (workers 1–2, benefiting from specialization in a small kitchen), then falls (diminishing returns as the truck's limited grill space becomes crowded), reaches zero at worker 6 (the truck is at capacity), and turns negative at worker 7 (too many cooks literally get in each other's way, lowering total output).

docs.title: The Relationship Between MP and AP
docs.text:
• When \(MP_L > AP_L\), average product is rising (an above-average worker pulls the average up).
  • When \(MP_L < AP_L\), average product is falling (a below-average worker pulls the average down).
  • When \(MP_L = AP_L\), average product is at its maximum.

This is the same mathematical relationship that governs marginal and average cost later in this chapter — marginal always "pulls" average toward it.

Marginal Always Pulls the Average

Hold onto this pattern — it reappears constantly: whenever a marginal value sits above an average, it pulls that average up; below, it pulls it down. You'll see this exact logic again with marginal and average cost in a few sections.

docs.title: 5.3 Short Run vs. Long Run
docs.text:
Short Run Long Run Definition A period in which at least one input (typically capital/plant size) is fixed A period long enough that all inputs, including plant size, are variable Firm's decision How much of the variable input (e.g., labor) to use with a fixed plant What size of plant to build, and how much of every input to use Flexibility Limited — some costs are fixed no matter what output level is chosen Full — the firm can choose any point on its production function, including exiting entirely

The short run is a planning horizon, not a fixed calendar length

"Short run" does not mean "a few weeks." It means before the firm can adjust its fixed inputs. For a nuclear power plant, the short run might be a decade (construction time for a new plant); for a food truck, the short run might be a few months (time to buy a second truck).

docs.title: 5.4 The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns
docs.text:
The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns: As more units of a variable input are added to a fixed amount of other inputs, the marginal product of the variable input eventually declines.

This law does not say that marginal product is always falling — it explicitly allows for marginal product to rise initially, as in the food truck example (workers 1 and 2 benefit from specialization). The law only requires that, eventually, each additional unit of the variable input adds less output than the previous one, because the input is being combined with a progressively smaller share of the fixed input.

Why diminishing returns set in

One cook in a kitchen with ten burners is understaffed — adding a second cook roughly doubles output. But once ten cooks are using ten burners, an eleventh cook has no burner to use and can only marginally help (fetching ingredients, cleaning), with the twelfth and beyond contributing almost nothing, or even getting in the way.

This law is the production-side mirror of the law of diminishing marginal utility from Chapter 4, and it is the fundamental reason why short-run marginal cost curves eventually slope upward, as the next sections show.

docs.title: 5.5 Fixed, Variable, and Total Costs
docs.text:
Cost Type Definition Behavior as Output Rises Fixed Cost (FC) Costs that do not vary with the quantity of output produced Constant Variable Cost (VC) Costs that change with the quantity of output produced Rises with output Total Cost (TC) The sum of fixed and variable costs \(TC = FC + VC\)

Fixed and variable costs for a food truck

  • Fixed costs: Truck lease ($2,000/month), permit fees — paid regardless of how many tacos are sold.
  • Variable costs: Ingredients, hourly wages, propane — rise directly with the number of tacos made.

Fixed Cost Is Not the Same as Sunk Cost

A fixed cost (like the truck lease) still has to be paid going forward and can sometimes be avoided by shutting down entirely — a true sunk cost, from Chapter 1, is money already spent that no decision can get back.

docs.title: Cost Schedule Example
docs.text:
Output (\(Q\)) \(FC\) \(VC\) \(TC\) 0 $100 $0 $100 1 $100 $50 $150 2 $100 $90 $190 3 $100 $120 $220 4 $100 $160 $260 5 $100 $220 $320

Notice that \(FC\) stays at $100 throughout, while \(VC\) and therefore \(TC\) rise with output.

docs.title: 5.6 Average Costs
docs.text:
Measure Formula Interpretation Average Fixed Cost (AFC) \(AFC = FC/Q\) Fixed cost per unit; always falling as \(Q\) rises ("spreading the overhead") Average Variable Cost (AVC) \(AVC = VC/Q\) Variable cost per unit; typically U-shaped Average Total Cost (ATC) \(ATC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC\) Total cost per unit; U-shaped

Using the schedule from Section 5.5:

\(Q\) \(AFC\) \(AVC\) \(ATC\) 1 $100.00 $50.00 $150.00 2 $50.00 $45.00 $95.00 3 $33.33 $40.00 $73.33 4 $25.00 $40.00 $65.00 5 $20.00 $44.00 $64.00

\(AFC\) falls continuously ($100.00 → $20.00) as fixed costs are spread over more units. \(AVC\) falls, then rises, as the firm first benefits from and then suffers from diminishing marginal returns. \(ATC\) follows a U-shape, reaching its lowest point (around \(Q=5\) here) where the two forces balance.

AFC Always Falls — No Exceptions

You can always sanity-check an AFC column: it should shrink every single time output rises, since a fixed dollar amount is being divided by a growing number. If your AFC ever rises, recheck your arithmetic.

docs.title: 5.7 Marginal Cost
docs.text:
Marginal cost (MC) is the additional cost of producing one more unit of output:

\[MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q}\]

(Since fixed costs don't change with output, the change in total cost equals the change in variable cost.)

\(Q\) \(TC\) \(MC\) 0 $100 — 1 $150 $50 2 $190 $40 3 $220 $30 4 $260 $40 5 $320 $60

Marginal cost falls initially (as the firm benefits from increasing marginal returns to its variable input), reaches a minimum, and then rises (as diminishing marginal returns set in) — the same U-shape, driven by the same underlying production relationship, as marginal product's inverse.

docs.title: The MC-ATC and MC-AVC Relationship
docs.text:
Just as marginal product "pulls" average product (Section 5.2), marginal cost "pulls" the average cost curves:

  • When \(MC < ATC\) (or \(AVC\)), the average is falling.
  • When \(MC > ATC\) (or \(AVC\)), the average is rising.
  • \(MC\) crosses \(ATC\) and \(AVC\) at their respective minimum points.

Why MC always crosses ATC at ATC's minimum

This is a purely mathematical property of averages and margins: if the next unit costs less than the current average, it pulls the average down; if it costs more, it pulls the average up. The average can only be at a minimum (neither rising nor falling) when the marginal value exactly equals it.

Derivatives Make This Faster, Not Harder

Deriving MC and ATC from a cost function can feel like a lot of new notation at once. Take it one step at a time: differentiate TC for MC, divide TC by Q for ATC, then set them equal — the algebra below walks through exactly that.

docs.title: Worked Example: Deriving Costs from a Cost Function
docs.text:
Suppose a firm's total cost function is \(TC(Q) = 200 + 10Q + 2Q^2\).

Step 1: Identify fixed and variable cost.

\[FC = 200 \qquad VC(Q) = 10Q + 2Q^2\]

Step 2: Derive marginal cost.

\[MC(Q) = \frac{d(TC)}{dQ} = 10 + 4Q\]

Step 3: Derive average total cost.

\[ATC(Q) = \frac{TC}{Q} = \frac{200}{Q} + 10 + 2Q\]

Step 4: Find the output that minimizes ATC, by setting \(MC = ATC\):

\[10 + 4Q = \frac{200}{Q} + 10 + 2Q\] \[2Q = \frac{200}{Q}\] \[2Q^2 = 200 \implies Q^2 = 100 \implies Q^* = 10\]

At \(Q=10\): \(ATC = \dfrac{200}{10} + 10 + 2(10) = 20+10+20 = \$50\), and \(MC = 10+4(10) = \$50\). The curves intersect exactly at \(ATC\)'s minimum, confirming the relationship above.

docs.title: 5.8 Long-Run Average Cost and Economies of Scale
docs.text:
In the long run, a firm can choose its plant size. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is the envelope of all the short-run average total cost curves available to the firm at different plant sizes — at each output level, it shows the lowest possible average cost achievable by choosing the best plant size for that output.

Region of LRAC Name Cause Downward-sloping Economies of scale Average cost falls as output rises — specialization of labor, bulk-purchasing discounts, more efficient large-scale equipment, spreading fixed costs (like R&D) over more units Flat (bottom) Constant returns to scale Average cost is roughly unchanged as output rises over this range Upward-sloping Diseconomies of scale Average cost rises as output rises — coordination and communication problems, bureaucracy, and management difficulties in very large organizations

Economies of scale in practice

Amazon's enormous distribution network allows it to negotiate better shipping rates and spread the cost of its technology infrastructure across billions of transactions, lowering its average cost per package far below what a small retailer could achieve.

Diseconomies of scale in practice

A restaurant chain that grows too quickly may struggle to maintain food quality and consistent management across hundreds of new locations, with layers of corporate bureaucracy slowing decisions and raising average costs per location.

docs.title: 5.9 Minimum Efficient Scale
docs.text:
The minimum efficient scale (MES) is the lowest level of output at which a firm achieves all available economies of scale — that is, the smallest output level at which the LRAC curve reaches its minimum point (or the start of its flat region).

The size of the minimum efficient scale relative to the size of the overall market helps determine the structure of an industry:

  • If MES is small relative to market demand, many firms can operate efficiently — the industry tends toward many competitors (e.g., restaurants, hair salons).
  • If MES is large relative to market demand, only a few firms can operate at an efficient scale — the industry tends toward few large firms or even a natural monopoly (e.g., electric utilities, semiconductor fabrication).

Preview: market structure

Minimum efficient scale is one of the key concepts that will reappear in Chapters 6 through 9 when we study how the number and size of firms in an industry — perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly — depend partly on the shape of the long-run average cost curve.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Production Function The relationship showing the maximum output obtainable from given quantities of inputs Total Product (TP) Total output produced by a given quantity of the variable input Marginal Product (MP) The additional output from one more unit of a variable input Average Product (AP) Output per unit of the variable input Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns Marginal product of a variable input eventually declines as more of it is added to a fixed input Fixed Cost (FC) Costs that do not vary with the quantity of output Variable Cost (VC) Costs that vary with the quantity of output Total Cost (TC) \(FC + VC\) Average Fixed Cost (AFC) \(FC/Q\) Average Variable Cost (AVC) \(VC/Q\) Average Total Cost (ATC) \(TC/Q\) Marginal Cost (MC) The additional cost of producing one more unit of output Long-Run Average Cost (LRAC) The lowest average cost achievable at each output level when plant size is variable Economies of Scale Average cost falls as output rises Diseconomies of Scale Average cost rises as output rises Minimum Efficient Scale (MES) The smallest output level at which all available economies of scale are achieved

docs.title: Problem 1 — Total, Marginal, and Average Product
docs.text:
A firm's production schedule is:

Labor (\(L\)) 0 1 2 3 4 5 Total Product 0 15 34 48 58 63

a) Calculate the marginal product of each worker. b) Calculate the average product of each quantity of labor. c) At what point does marginal product start declining? Is this consistent with the law of diminishing marginal returns?

Solution

a) \(MP_1=15, MP_2=19, MP_3=14, MP_4=10, MP_5=5\).

b) \(AP_1=15.0, AP_2=17.0, AP_3=16.0, AP_4=14.5, AP_5=12.6\).

c) Marginal product rises from worker 1 to worker 2 (15→19), then declines continuously from worker 2 onward (19→14→10→5). This is consistent with diminishing marginal returns: increasing returns initially (specialization benefits), then diminishing returns as more labor is combined with the fixed capital.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Fixed, Variable, and Total Cost
docs.text:
A firm has fixed costs of $500. Its variable costs are given below:

\(Q\) 0 1 2 3 4 \(VC\) $0 $200 $360 $480 $640

a) Calculate total cost at each output level. b) Calculate marginal cost at each output level. c) Calculate average total cost at \(Q=4\).

Solution

a) \(TC = FC+VC\): \(TC_0=\$500, TC_1=\$700, TC_2=\$860, TC_3=\$980, TC_4=\$1{,}140\).

b) \(MC_1 = 700-500=\$200\); \(MC_2=860-700=\$160\); \(MC_3=980-860=\$120\); \(MC_4=1140-980=\$160\).

c) \(ATC_4 = TC_4/Q = 1140/4 = \$285\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Deriving Costs Algebraically
docs.text:
A firm's total cost function is \(TC(Q) = 300 + 20Q + Q^2\).

a) Identify fixed cost and derive the variable cost function. b) Derive the marginal cost function. c) Derive the average total cost function. d) Find the output level that minimizes ATC.

Solution

a) \(FC = 300\); \(VC(Q) = 20Q + Q^2\).

b) \(MC(Q) = \dfrac{d(TC)}{dQ} = 20 + 2Q\).

c) \(ATC(Q) = \dfrac{300}{Q} + 20 + Q\).

d) Set \(MC = ATC\): \(20+2Q = \dfrac{300}{Q}+20+Q \implies Q = \dfrac{300}{Q} \implies Q^2 = 300 \implies Q^* \approx 17.3\).

At \(Q^* \approx 17.3\): \(ATC = \dfrac{300}{17.3} + 20 + 17.3 \approx 17.3+20+17.3 = \$54.6\), matching \(MC = 20+2(17.3) \approx \$54.6\). ✓

docs.title: Problem 4 — Short Run vs. Long Run
docs.text:
For each scenario, state whether the firm is operating in the short run or the long run, and explain.

a) An airline adds two extra flights per day using its existing fleet of planes. b) A chip manufacturer breaks ground on a new $10 billion fabrication plant. c) A coffee shop hires one additional barista for the morning rush.

Solution

a) Short run — the airline is adjusting a variable input (flight schedules/crew usage) while its fixed input (the fleet of planes/number of planes owned) is unchanged.

b) Long run — building an entirely new plant is a change in the firm's fixed input (capital/plant size itself), which by definition only happens in the long run.

c) Short run — the coffee shop is adjusting its variable input (labor) while its fixed input (the shop's physical space and equipment) remains the same.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Economies of Scale
docs.text:
A firm observes the following long-run average costs at different plant sizes:

Output (units/day) 100 500 1,000 2,000 3,000 LRAC ($/unit) $40 $25 $18 $18 $22

a) Over what range of output does the firm experience economies of scale? b) Over what range does it experience constant returns to scale? c) Over what range does it experience diseconomies of scale? d) What is the approximate minimum efficient scale?

Solution

a) Economies of scale from 100 to 1,000 units/day — LRAC falls continuously ($40 → $25 → $18).

b) Constant returns to scale from 1,000 to 2,000 units/day — LRAC stays flat at $18.

c) Diseconomies of scale from 2,000 to 3,000 units/day — LRAC rises ($18 → $22).

d) The minimum efficient scale is approximately 1,000 units/day — the smallest output level at which LRAC first reaches its minimum ($18).

docs.title: Problem 6 — MC and ATC Relationship
docs.text:
A firm's marginal cost and average total cost at various output levels are given:

\(Q\) 10 20 30 40 \(MC\) $15 $20 $25 $35 \(ATC\) $25 $22 $22 $24

a) Between \(Q=10\) and \(Q=20\), is ATC rising or falling? Explain using the MC-ATC relationship. b) Between \(Q=30\) and \(Q=40\), is ATC rising or falling? Explain. c) Approximately where does ATC reach its minimum?

Solution

a) Between \(Q=10\) and \(Q=20\), \(MC\) ($15–$20) is below \(ATC\) ($25–$22), so \(ATC\) is falling — a below-average marginal cost pulls the average down.

b) Between \(Q=30\) and \(Q=40\), \(MC\) ($25–$35) is above \(ATC\) ($22–$24), so \(ATC\) is rising — an above-average marginal cost pulls the average up.

c) \(ATC\) reaches its minimum around \(Q=30\), where \(MC\) ($25) is closest to equaling \(ATC\) ($22), the transition point between \(ATC\) falling and rising.

You Can Now Read Any Cost Curve

From a bare production schedule, you can now build every cost curve a firm has — fixed, variable, average, and marginal — and explain exactly why each one bends the way it does. That's the foundation for everything about firm behavior still to come!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 6: Perfect Competition, we combine the cost curves developed here with market price-taking behavior to derive a firm's profit-maximizing output and the industry supply curve first introduced in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Identify the four characteristics that define a perfectly competitive market
  2. Explain why a competitive firm is a "price taker" and graph its demand and marginal revenue curves
  3. Apply the MR = MC rule to find a competitive firm's profit-maximizing output
  4. Apply the shutdown rule to determine a firm's short-run supply decision
  5. Derive the short-run industry supply curve from individual firms' marginal cost curves
  6. Distinguish short-run and long-run equilibrium in a competitive industry
  7. Explain why economic profit is driven to zero in long-run competitive equilibrium
  8. Use consumer and producer surplus to show that competitive equilibrium is allocatively efficient

The Benchmark Market

Perfect competition is the model every other market structure in this book gets compared against. Learn its MR = MC logic well here, in its simplest form, and Chapters 7 through 9 will feel like variations on a theme rather than brand-new material. Every choice has a trade-off, and here you'll see firms make that trade-off with zero power over price.

docs.title: 6.1 Characteristics of Perfectly Competitive Markets
docs.text:
Perfect competition is a market structure characterized by four conditions:

  1. Many buyers and many sellers, each too small to individually influence the market price.
  2. A standardized (homogeneous) product — consumers view every seller's output as identical, so there is no reason to prefer one seller over another based on the product itself.
  3. Free entry and exit — firms can enter the industry when profits are attractive and exit when losses persist, with no significant barriers.
  4. Perfect information — buyers and sellers have full knowledge of prices and product quality.

Approximations to perfect competition

No real-world market perfectly satisfies all four conditions, but several come close: commodity agricultural markets (wheat, corn), foreign exchange markets, and many online markets for standardized goods. Even if imperfect, the competitive model is a powerful benchmark against which to measure other market structures (studied in Chapters 7–9).

docs.title: 6.2 The Competitive Firm as a Price Taker
docs.text:
Because a competitive firm is one of many sellers of an identical product, it has no ability to influence the market price — it is a price taker. If a wheat farmer tried to charge above the market price, buyers would simply purchase from any of thousands of other farmers selling identical wheat. If the farmer charged below market price, they would needlessly sacrifice revenue, since they can already sell as much as they want at the market price.

This means the individual competitive firm faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve at the market price \(P^*\), even though the market demand curve is downward sloping (recall from Chapter 3 that \(E_d \to \infty\) at the firm level).

docs.title: Marginal Revenue for a Price Taker
docs.text:
Since the firm can sell every unit at the same price \(P^*\), each additional unit sold adds exactly \(P^*\) to total revenue:

\[MR = \frac{\Delta TR}{\Delta Q} = P^*\]

For a perfectly competitive firm: \(P^* = MR\). This is a special simplification that will not hold for the imperfectly competitive firms studied in Chapters 7–9.

Price-Taking Is the Special Case

\(MR = P\) only holds because a competitive firm can sell unlimited units at one fixed price. Remember this carefully — starting next chapter, firms with market power face falling marginal revenue, and this simplification disappears.

docs.title: 6.3 Profit Maximization: The MR = MC Rule
docs.text:
Every firm, regardless of market structure, maximizes profit by producing the quantity at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost:

\[MR = MC\]

Intuition: If \(MR > MC\), producing one more unit adds more to revenue than to cost — profit rises, so the firm should produce more. If \(MR < MC\), the last unit cost more to produce than it earned — profit falls, so the firm should produce less. Only where \(MR = MC\) is profit maximized (with the second-order condition that \(MC\) is rising at that point).

For a competitive firm, since \(MR = P^*\), the rule becomes:

\[P^* = MC\]

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A competitive firm faces a market price of \(P^* = \$40\). Its cost schedule is:

\(Q\) \(TC\) \(MC\) \(TR\) (\(=40Q\)) Profit 0 $50 — $0 −$50 1 $80 $30 $40 −$40 2 $105 $25 $80 −$25 3 $135 $30 $120 −$15 4 $170 $35 $160 −$10 5 $210 $40 $200 −$10 6 $255 $45 $240 −$15

At \(Q=5\), \(MC=\$40\) exactly equals \(P^*=MR=\$40\) — profit is maximized (tied with \(Q=4\) at −$10, but \(Q=5\) is the last unit where \(MC \leq MR\); producing the 6th unit would reduce profit since \(MC=\$45 > MR=\$40\)). The firm maximizes profit (minimizes loss) at \(Q^*=5\), earning profit of −$10.

docs.title: 6.4 Short-Run Supply Decision and the Shutdown Rule
docs.text:
In the short run, a firm has already incurred its fixed costs regardless of whether it produces. The question the firm faces is not "should I exist?" but "should I produce at all, or shut down (produce zero) this period?"

The Shutdown Rule: A firm should continue to produce in the short run as long as the price it receives covers average variable cost:

\[P^* \geq AVC_{\min} \implies \text{produce } Q \text{ where } P^*=MC\] \[P^* < AVC_{\min} \implies \text{shut down (produce } Q=0\text{)}\]

Shutting Down Isn't Going Out of Business

"Shut down" here means producing zero this period while still paying fixed costs — not permanently closing. A firm can shut down in a slow month and reopen once price recovers.

Intuition: If \(P^* \geq AVC\), the firm covers all its variable costs and contributes at least something toward fixed costs — producing is better than shutting down, even if the firm is making an overall loss (since fixed costs must be paid either way in the short run). If \(P^* < AVC\), the firm cannot even cover the variable cost of production — every unit sold loses money beyond its direct cost, so it is better to produce nothing and lose only the fixed cost.

Why 'losing money while producing' can be the right call

A restaurant with a $5,000/month lease (a sunk fixed cost in the short run) finds that at the going price, revenue covers all ingredient and labor costs (variable costs) plus $2,000 toward the lease. Shutting down would mean losing the full $5,000 lease payment with zero revenue; staying open loses only $3,000 (the $5,000 lease minus the $2,000 contribution). The restaurant should stay open, even though it is losing money overall.

docs.title: The Short-Run Supply Curve of a Firm
docs.text:
The competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its marginal cost curve that lies at or above the minimum point of AVC. For any price below that threshold, the firm supplies zero.

\[\text{Firm's short-run supply curve} = MC \text{ curve, for all } P \geq AVC_{\min}\]

One Number Decides Everything

Facing a shutdown question? You only need two numbers: price and minimum AVC. Skip the full profit calculation — just compare those two and the decision falls out immediately.

docs.title: 6.5 Short-Run Industry Supply Curve
docs.text:
The short-run industry (market) supply curve is obtained by horizontally summing the supply curves (the relevant portions of \(MC\) above \(AVC_{\min}\)) of every individual firm in the industry, at each price.

Horizontal summation

Suppose an industry has 1,000 identical firms, and at a price of $40, each individual firm supplies 5 units (as in the Section 6.3 example). The industry quantity supplied at \(P=\$40\) is \(1{,}000 \times 5 = 5{,}000\) units. Repeating this calculation at every price generates the industry supply curve.

Price Quantity Supplied per Firm Number of Firms Industry Quantity Supplied $30 3 1,000 3,000 $35 4 1,000 4,000 $40 5 1,000 5,000 $45 6 1,000 6,000

This is exactly the market supply curve introduced in Chapter 2, now derived rigorously from firms' marginal cost curves and profit-maximizing behavior.

docs.title: Short-Run Equilibrium
docs.text:
In the short run, the number of firms in the industry is fixed (entry/exit takes time). The market price is determined by the intersection of the (fixed-number-of-firms) short-run industry supply curve and market demand. At this price, individual firms may earn:

  • Positive economic profit (price exceeds average total cost)
  • Zero economic profit (price equals average total cost — "normal profit")
  • A loss (price is below average total cost, but above \(AVC_{\min}\), so the firm still produces)

Economic profit vs. accounting profit

Economic profit subtracts all costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's time and capital (implicit costs), from revenue. Accounting profit subtracts only explicit (out-of-pocket) costs. A firm can show positive accounting profit while earning zero or negative economic profit — meaning its resources could have earned more being used elsewhere.

docs.title: Long-Run Equilibrium
docs.text:
In the long run, firms can enter or exit the industry freely (one of the four defining conditions from Section 6.1):

  • If firms are earning positive economic profit, new firms are attracted into the industry. Entry increases industry supply, shifting the supply curve right, which lowers the market price until profit is driven to zero.
  • If firms are earning negative economic profit (losses), existing firms exit the industry. Exit decreases industry supply, shifting the supply curve left, which raises the market price until the remaining firms earn zero economic profit.

This entry-and-exit process continues until price settles exactly at the minimum point of each firm's long-run average cost curve, where economic profit is exactly zero.

docs.title: 6.7 Zero Economic Profit in the Long Run
docs.text:
Long-run competitive equilibrium occurs where:

\[P^* = MR = MC = ATC_{\min}\]

At this point, each firm earns exactly zero economic profit — meaning it earns a "normal" return just sufficient to keep its resources employed in this industry (no better use of those resources exists elsewhere), but no excess return that would attract further entry.

Zero economic profit is not the same as going broke

Zero economic profit means the firm is earning exactly the market rate of return on its invested resources — comparable to what the owner could earn in their next-best alternative. It is a perfectly sustainable, "break-even" outcome in the economic sense, not a sign of business failure.

docs.title: Worked Example: Long-Run Adjustment
docs.text:
Dividing Market by Firm Size, Step by Step

Finding the long-run number of firms looks like a lot of moving parts at once — demand, ATC minimum, firm output — but it's really just one division at the end. Follow the three steps below in order and it resolves quickly.

Suppose the long-run average cost curve of every (identical) firm in a competitive industry has its minimum at \(ATC_{\min} = \$20\) per unit, occurring at an output of 100 units per firm.

Step 1: In long-run equilibrium, price must equal $20 (otherwise entry or exit would still be occurring).

Step 2: Suppose market demand at \(P=\$20\) is \(Q_D = 50{,}000\) units.

Step 3: The number of firms in long-run equilibrium is:

\[\text{Number of firms} = \frac{Q_D}{q_{\text{firm}}} = \frac{50{,}000}{100} = 500 \text{ firms}\]

If demand increased, price would temporarily rise above $20 in the short run (attracting entry), and the number of firms would increase until price returned to $20 in the new long-run equilibrium.

docs.title: 6.8 Consumer and Producer Surplus; Allocative Efficiency
docs.text: Recall from Chapter 2: consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price; producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price. Competitive equilibrium (where \(S=D\)) maximizes total surplus (CS + PS).

docs.title: Why Competitive Equilibrium Is Allocatively Efficient
docs.text:
Allocative efficiency occurs when resources are allocated to produce the combination of goods that society values most, given its resources — formally, when price equals marginal cost (\(P = MC\)) for every good, so that the value society places on the last unit produced (captured by price, which reflects consumers' willingness to pay) exactly equals the cost of producing it.

In long-run competitive equilibrium, we have shown:

\[P^* = MC = ATC_{\min}\]

Because \(P = MC\) at every competitive firm, no reallocation of resources — producing more or less of this good, or shifting resources to another industry — can increase total surplus. This is the formal justification for the informal notion, introduced in Chapter 2, of the "invisible hand": competitive markets, driven purely by self-interested price-taking behavior, achieve the surplus-maximizing, allocatively efficient outcome without any central coordination.

Two distinct efficiency results, now connected

Chapter 2 showed that competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus. This chapter shows why, by deriving the supply curve from cost-minimizing, profit-maximizing firms. The \(P=MC\) condition is the single thread connecting individual firm behavior to market-wide efficiency.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Perfect Competition A market structure with many buyers/sellers, a standardized product, free entry/exit, and perfect information Price Taker A firm that must accept the market price because it cannot influence it Marginal Revenue (MR) The additional revenue from selling one more unit; equals price for a competitive firm MR = MC Rule The profit-maximizing condition for any firm: produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost Shutdown Rule A firm should produce in the short run if \(P \geq AVC_{\min}\); otherwise it should shut down Short-Run Industry Supply Curve The horizontal sum of all firms' short-run supply curves (their \(MC\) above \(AVC_{\min}\)) Economic Profit Revenue minus all costs, including implicit opportunity costs Accounting Profit Revenue minus only explicit (out-of-pocket) costs Long-Run Equilibrium The state reached after free entry/exit drives economic profit to zero across the industry Allocative Efficiency The condition where price equals marginal cost, so resources are allocated to their highest-valued use Consumer Surplus The area below the demand curve and above the price Producer Surplus The area above the supply curve and below the price

docs.title: Problem 1 — Price Taking and Marginal Revenue
docs.text:
A competitive wheat farmer sells wheat at the market price of $8 per bushel.

a) What is the farmer's marginal revenue for the 1st bushel? The 100th bushel? b) What does the farmer's individual demand curve look like, and why? c) If the farmer tried to charge $9 per bushel, what would happen to sales?

Solution

a) Marginal revenue is $8 for every bushel, including the 1st and the 100th — as a price taker, every unit sold earns exactly the market price.

b) The farmer's individual demand curve is horizontal (perfectly elastic) at \(P=\$8\) — the farmer can sell any quantity at this price, but nothing at a higher price, since buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere.

c) Sales would fall to zero — buyers would simply purchase wheat from any of the many other farmers selling an identical product at the $8 market price.

docs.title: Problem 2 — MR = MC Rule
docs.text:
A competitive firm faces a market price of $25. Its marginal cost schedule is:

\(Q\) 1 2 3 4 5 6 \(MC\) $10 $15 $20 $25 $30 $36

a) What quantity maximizes the firm's profit? b) Explain why producing one unit less, or one unit more, would reduce profit.

Solution

a) The firm should produce where \(P=MR=MC\). At \(Q=4\), \(MC=\$25=P\). \(Q^*=4\).

b) Producing the 3rd unit instead of stopping at 4 (i.e., only producing 3) would mean forgoing a unit where \(MR(\$25) > MC(\$25\), the 4th unit\()\) — wait, more precisely: at \(Q=3\), the next (4th) unit has \(MC=\$25=MR\), so producing it adds exactly as much to revenue as to cost (zero net effect, but included since \(MC \leq MR\)). Producing a 5th unit would cost \(MC=\$30 > MR=\$25\) — this unit reduces profit by $5, so the firm should not produce it. Thus \(Q=4\) is optimal: every unit up to 4 has \(MC \leq MR\), and the 5th unit would have \(MC > MR\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Shutdown Rule
docs.text:
A competitive firm has the following short-run cost data at its profit-maximizing output of 10 units: \(ATC = \$18\), \(AVC=\$12\), \(AFC=\$6\).

a) If the market price is $15, should the firm produce or shut down in the short run? Explain. b) If the market price is $10, should the firm produce or shut down? Explain. c) In case (a), is the firm earning a profit or a loss? How much per unit?

Solution

a) Produce. Since \(P=\$15 > AVC=\$12\), the firm covers all variable costs and contributes $3 per unit toward fixed costs. Even though \(P < ATC\) (a loss), producing is better than shutting down.

b) Shut down. Since \(P=\$10 < AVC=\$12\), the firm cannot even cover its variable costs; every unit produced loses money beyond the fixed cost it must pay regardless. Producing zero minimizes losses to just the fixed cost.

c) At \(P=\$15\) and \(ATC=\$18\), the firm earns a loss of $3 per unit (×10 units = $30 total loss), but this is still better than shutting down, which would mean losing the full fixed cost of \(AFC \times Q = \$6 \times 10 = \$60\).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Industry Supply Curve
docs.text:
An industry has 200 identical competitive firms. Each individual firm's supply schedule (quantity supplied at each price, from its \(MC\) curve above \(AVC_{\min}\)) is:

Price Quantity Supplied per Firm $10 0 (below shutdown price) $15 20 $20 30 $25 40

a) Construct the short-run industry supply curve. b) If market demand at \(P=\$20\) is 5,000 units, is the market in equilibrium? Explain.

Solution

a) Multiply each firm's quantity by 200 firms:

Price Industry Quantity Supplied $10 0 $15 4,000 $20 6,000 $25 8,000

b) At \(P=\$20\), industry supply is 6,000 units, but demand is only 5,000 units — this means there is a surplus of 1,000 units at \(P=\$20\). The market is not in equilibrium; price must fall until quantity demanded rises (and quantity supplied falls) to meet at a lower equilibrium price.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Long-Run Equilibrium
docs.text:
Every firm in a competitive industry has identical long-run average costs, with \(ATC_{\min} = \$12\) at an output of 50 units per firm. Currently, the market price is $18, and each firm is producing 60 units.

a) Is the industry in long-run equilibrium? Explain. b) What will happen to the number of firms in the industry over time, and why? c) What price will prevail once the long run is reached?

Solution

a) No, the industry is not in long-run equilibrium. Since \(P=\$18 > ATC_{\min}=\$12\), firms are earning positive economic profit, which will attract entry.

b) New firms will enter the industry, attracted by the positive economic profit. As more firms enter, industry supply shifts right, pushing the market price down.

c) Entry will continue until economic profit is driven to zero, i.e., until price falls to \(P = ATC_{\min} = \mathbf{\$12}\).

docs.title: Problem 6 — Allocative Efficiency
docs.text:
A competitive market is in long-run equilibrium with \(P^* = MC = ATC_{\min} = \$30\).

a) Explain why this outcome is allocatively efficient. b) Suppose a policy forced price down to $25 (below marginal cost at the equilibrium quantity). Using the concept of consumer and producer surplus, explain why this would reduce total surplus (create a deadweight loss), even though consumers pay a lower price.

Solution

a) The outcome is allocatively efficient because \(P=MC\): the price consumers are willing to pay for the last unit (reflecting its value to them) exactly equals the marginal cost of producing it (reflecting the value of resources used elsewhere). No reallocation of resources toward or away from this good could increase total surplus.

b) At a forced price of $25, quantity supplied would fall below the equilibrium quantity (since \(P < MC\) at the original equilibrium quantity means producers are no longer willing to supply that much). The reduction in quantity traded means some units that consumers valued more than their cost of production (units where willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost) are no longer produced and exchanged — this lost surplus from forgone mutually beneficial trades is a deadweight loss. Even though remaining consumers benefit from a lower price, this transfer is outweighed by the surplus lost from the reduction in quantity traded, so total surplus falls.

You've Derived Market Efficiency From Scratch

You just connected firm-level profit maximization all the way to market-wide allocative efficiency — the same invisible-hand result from Chapter 2, now proven rather than asserted. That's one of the deepest ideas in all of economics!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 7: Monopoly, we remove the price-taking assumption entirely and study the opposite extreme — a single seller with market power — to see how the MR = MC rule, pricing, and efficiency outcomes change when a firm can influence price.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Identify the sources of monopoly power and the barriers that sustain it
  2. Derive a monopolist's marginal revenue curve from its demand curve
  3. Find the profit-maximizing price and quantity for a monopolist
  4. Compare monopoly outcomes to perfect competition and quantify the deadweight loss
  5. Distinguish first-, second-, and third-degree price discrimination and their welfare effects
  6. Explain why natural monopoly arises and how regulators respond to it
  7. Describe the goals and tools of antitrust policy

Meet the Opposite Extreme

Chapter 6 gave you a firm with zero pricing power. This chapter flips that completely: one seller, full control over price, and a very different set of trade-offs. Every choice has a trade-off, and here you'll see how a monopolist's own pricing choice creates a cost society actually bears.

docs.title: 7.1 Sources of Monopoly Power
docs.text:
A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a good that has no close substitutes. Unlike the price-taking firms of Chapter 6, a monopolist is a price maker — it chooses a point on the market demand curve rather than accepting a price set by the market.

Monopoly power persists only if barriers to entry prevent other firms from competing it away. The major sources are:

Barrier Description Example Economies of scale Average cost falls over the entire relevant range of output, so one large firm can produce more cheaply than several small ones Local water utility Control of a key input A firm owns or controls an essential resource De Beers' historical control of diamond mines Legal restrictions Government grants exclusive rights Patents, copyrights, broadcast licenses Network effects The good becomes more valuable as more people use it, locking in the largest network Early social media platforms Government franchise The government designates a single provider U.S. Postal Service for first-class mail

Patents as a deliberate monopoly

A pharmaceutical patent grants the developer the exclusive right to sell a drug for a fixed period (typically 20 years from filing). This is monopoly power created on purpose — society trades higher short-run drug prices for the incentive to innovate in the first place.

A firm with the largest market share is not necessarily a monopolist in the economic sense; what matters is the absence of close substitutes and the durability of the barriers protecting its position.

docs.title: 7.2 The Monopolist's Demand and Marginal Revenue
docs.text:
Because the monopolist is the only seller, the market demand curve is the firm's demand curve. This is the single most important fact distinguishing monopoly from perfect competition: a competitive firm faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve at the market price, but a monopolist faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve.

This has a crucial consequence: to sell more output, the monopolist must lower its price on all units sold, not just the marginal unit. Marginal revenue therefore falls faster than price.

docs.title: Deriving Marginal Revenue
docs.text:
Let the monopolist face a linear demand curve:

\[P = a - bQ\]

Total revenue is:

\[TR = P \times Q = (a - bQ)Q = aQ - bQ^2\]

Marginal revenue is the derivative of total revenue with respect to quantity:

\[MR = \frac{d(TR)}{dQ} = a - 2bQ\]

Key result: For a linear demand curve \(P = a - bQ\), the marginal revenue curve is also linear, has the same vertical intercept \(a\), but is twice as steep as demand. The \(MR\) curve lies below the demand curve at every quantity greater than zero.

docs.title: Numerical Example
docs.text:
Suppose demand is \(P = 100 - 2Q\), so \(MR = 100 - 4Q\).

\(Q\) \(P\) \(TR = P \times Q\) \(MR\) (next unit) 0 100 0 96 10 80 800 60 20 60 1,200 20 25 50 1,250 0 30 40 1,200 −20 40 20 800 −60

Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as price and reaches zero at \(Q = 25\) — exactly where total revenue is maximized. Beyond \(Q = 25\), marginal revenue is negative: selling additional units reduces total revenue because the price cut needed to sell them outweighs the extra units sold.

MR and the elasticity of demand

Marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic (\(|\varepsilon_d| > 1\)), zero where demand is unit-elastic, and negative where demand is inelastic (\(|\varepsilon_d| < 1\)). A profit-maximizing monopolist never knowingly operates in the inelastic region of demand, since it could raise price, sell less, and still earn more revenue while incurring lower cost.

Why a Monopolist Avoids the Inelastic Region

If MR is negative, raising price actually increases revenue while cutting output — and lowering output also cuts cost. No rational monopolist would ever knowingly sit where demand is inelastic; it's strictly better to raise price and sell less.

docs.title: 7.3 Profit Maximization for a Monopolist
docs.text:
Like any firm, a monopolist maximizes profit by choosing the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost:

\[MR = MC\]

The key difference from perfect competition is that the monopolist then charges the price given by the demand curve at that quantity — not the (lower) marginal cost.

docs.title: Steps to Solve
docs.text:
1. Find the demand curve \(P(Q)\) and derive \(MR(Q)\).
  2. Find \(MC(Q)\) from the cost function.
  3. Set \(MR = MC\) and solve for \(Q^M\) (the monopoly quantity).
  4. Plug \(Q^M\) into the demand curve to find \(P^M\) (the monopoly price).
  5. Compute profit: \(\pi = (P^M - ATC(Q^M)) \times Q^M\).

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A monopolist faces demand \(P = 100 - 2Q\) and has constant marginal cost \(MC = 20\) (so \(TC = 20Q\), with no fixed costs in this simplified example).

From Section 7.2, \(MR = 100 - 4Q\). Set \(MR = MC\):

\[100 - 4Q = 20\] \[80 = 4Q\] \[Q^M = 20\]

Price from the demand curve:

\[P^M = 100 - 2(20) = \$60\]

Profit (since \(ATC = MC = 20\) at every quantity here):

\[\pi = (P^M - ATC) \times Q^M = (60 - 20) \times 20 = \$800\]

Common mistake

Students often set \(P = MC\) (the competitive rule) instead of \(MR = MC\). A monopolist that set \(P = MC\) would be ignoring the fact that producing more requires cutting the price on all units, not just the last one. Always find \(MR\) first, then read price off the demand curve.

docs.title: Monopoly Does Not Guarantee Profit
docs.text: A monopolist earns economic profit only if \(P^M > ATC(Q^M)\). If demand is weak relative to costs, a monopolist can still suffer a loss — monopoly power guarantees the absence of competitors, not profitability.

docs.title: 7.4 Monopoly vs. Competitive Pricing
docs.text:
Compare the monopoly outcome to what would happen if this same market were perfectly competitive, with many small firms whose combined marginal cost curve equals the monopolist's \(MC\) curve (i.e., supply is \(MC\)).

Using the numbers from Section 7.3: under perfect competition, price equals marginal cost along the demand curve:

\[100 - 2Q = 20 \implies Q^C = 40, \quad P^C = \$20\] Perfect Competition Monopoly Price $20 $60 Quantity 40 20 Outcome \(P = MC\) (efficient) \(P > MC\) (inefficient)

Relative to the competitive outcome, the monopolist restricts output and raises price. This is the defining inefficiency of monopoly: the monopolist refuses to sell units for which willingness to pay exceeds the marginal cost of production, because selling them would require lowering the price on units already sold.

docs.title: 7.5 Deadweight Loss and Inefficiency
docs.text: Because the monopolist produces less than the efficient (competitive) quantity, some mutually beneficial trades never happen. The lost total surplus is the deadweight loss (DWL) of monopoly.

docs.title: Graphical Logic
docs.text:
• Consumer surplus shrinks because price is higher and quantity is lower than under competition.
  • Producer surplus (profit) may rise — the monopolist gains from the higher price on units it does sell, but loses the surplus from units it no longer sells.
  • Part of what was consumer surplus under competition is transferred to the monopolist as higher profit (this is a transfer, not a loss to society).
  • The surplus on units between \(Q^M\) and \(Q^C\) that are no longer traded is lost entirely — this is the deadweight loss.

docs.title: Numerical Example (continuing Sections 7.3–7.4)
docs.text:
With \(P = 100 - 2Q\) and \(MC = 20\): \(Q^C = 40\), \(Q^M = 20\), \(P^M = 60\).

The deadweight loss is the triangle between the demand curve and the \(MC\) curve, over the quantity range from \(Q^M = 20\) to \(Q^C = 40\):

\[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (P^M - MC) \times (Q^C - Q^M) = \frac{1}{2} \times (60 - 20) \times (40 - 20)\] \[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 20 = \$400\]

Interpreting the deadweight loss

This $400 represents the total surplus that would have been created by trading units 21 through 40 — surplus that simply vanishes because the monopolist won't produce them. No one captures this value; it is a pure loss to society, which is why monopoly is called allocatively inefficient.

docs.title: 7.6 Price Discrimination
docs.text:
Price discrimination is charging different prices to different customers (or for different units) for reasons unrelated to cost differences. It is a strategy for capturing some of the consumer surplus that uniform pricing leaves on the table — and, counterintuitively, it can reduce deadweight loss by expanding output toward the efficient level.

Three conditions must hold for price discrimination to be possible and profitable: (1) the firm must have market power, (2) it must be able to identify or sort customers by willingness to pay, and (3) it must be able to prevent resale (arbitrage) between low-price and high-price customers.

docs.title: First-Degree (Personalized) Price Discrimination
docs.text:
The firm charges each customer exactly their willingness to pay. This is the theoretical extreme: the firm captures all consumer surplus as profit, and because every unit for which willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost gets sold, output expands to \(Q^C\) and the deadweight loss falls to zero. All surplus becomes producer surplus — efficient, but with no consumer surplus at all.

Real-world approximations

Perfect first-degree discrimination is rare, but a car salesperson haggling individually with each buyer, or a university's financial-aid office setting each student's net tuition based on need and merit, approximates it.

docs.title: Second-Degree Price Discrimination
docs.text:
The firm offers a menu of price-quantity (or price-quality) bundles, and customers self-select the bundle that suits them. The firm doesn't observe willingness to pay directly but infers it from customers' choices.

Second-degree discrimination in practice

  • Quantity discounts: Costco's bulk packaging; buy-one-get-one offers.
  • Versioning: Airlines selling Basic Economy, Economy, and Business Class seats on the same flight at very different markups over cost.
  • Software tiers: "Home," "Pro," and "Enterprise" versions of the same software, with the Pro version artificially limited to be less useful than Enterprise.

docs.title: Third-Degree Price Discrimination
docs.text:
The firm sorts customers into groups based on an observable characteristic correlated with willingness to pay (age, student status, location, time of purchase) and charges each group a different price.

Rule for third-degree discrimination: The firm sets \(MR_1 = MR_2 = MC\) across the two (or more) markets. The group with the less elastic demand is charged the higher price.

Two Markets, Same Rule, Twice

Don't let two demand curves at once feel like double the difficulty — you're just applying MR = MC separately in each market. Solve one market fully before even glancing at the other.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A monopolist sells to two markets with demand curves:

\[P_1 = 50 - Q_1 \quad \text{(Market 1: adults)}\] \[P_2 = 30 - Q_2 \quad \text{(Market 2: students)}\]

Marginal cost is constant at \(MC = 10\) in both markets, and resale between markets is impossible.

Marginal revenue in each market: \(MR_1 = 50 - 2Q_1\), \(MR_2 = 30 - 2Q_2\).

Set each equal to \(MC = 10\):

\[50 - 2Q_1 = 10 \implies Q_1 = 20, \quad P_1 = 50 - 20 = \$30\] \[30 - 2Q_2 = 10 \implies Q_2 = 10, \quad P_2 = 30 - 10 = \$20\] Market Price Quantity Adults (less elastic at any common price) $30 20 Students (more elastic) $20 10

Students — typically more price-sensitive — pay the lower price, consistent with the rule that the more elastic group gets the discount.

Why 'student discounts' and 'senior discounts' exist

Movie theaters and software companies offer discounts to students and seniors not out of charity, but because these groups tend to have more elastic demand (lower income, more substitutes, more free time to shop around). Charging them less while charging full price to less price-sensitive adults raises total profit.

docs.title: Welfare Effects of Price Discrimination
docs.text:
Degree Consumer Surplus Producer Surplus Deadweight Loss None (uniform price) Positive Positive Positive (as in 7.5) First-degree Zero Maximum (= old CS + old DWL) Zero Second/Third-degree Reduced, but not zero Increased Reduced relative to uniform pricing (generally)

Price discrimination is therefore ambiguous for consumers as a whole — some pay more, some pay less — but it typically increases total surplus relative to uniform monopoly pricing, because it induces the monopolist to serve customers (like price-sensitive students) it would otherwise exclude.

Three Degrees, One Pattern

Remember them by how much the firm knows: first-degree knows each customer's exact value, second-degree lets customers sort themselves with a menu, third-degree sorts customers by an observable group trait. More information always means more surplus captured.

docs.title: 7.7 Natural Monopoly and Regulation
docs.text:
A natural monopoly arises when a single firm can supply the entire market at lower cost than two or more firms could — typically because very large fixed costs and economies of scale cause average total cost (\(ATC\)) to decline throughout the relevant range of market demand.

Classic natural monopolies

  • Electricity transmission and distribution
  • Water and sewer utilities
  • Natural gas pipelines

Because duplicating the fixed infrastructure (power lines, pipes) would be wasteful, society typically allows a single regulated firm to operate rather than forcing competition.

docs.title: The Regulator's Dilemma
docs.text:
For a natural monopoly, the efficient price (\(P = MC\)) typically lies below average total cost, because large fixed costs pull \(ATC\) above \(MC\) at every relevant quantity. Setting \(P = MC\) (marginal-cost pricing) is efficient but forces the firm into a loss, which is unsustainable without a subsidy.

Efficient Doesn't Mean Sustainable

It's tempting to say regulators should always set \(P = MC\) since it's efficient. But for a natural monopoly, that price doesn't cover fixed costs — without a subsidy, the firm goes bankrupt and stops providing the service at all.

Regulatory Rule Price Effect Marginal-cost pricing (\(P = MC\)) Lowest, efficient Firm earns a loss equal to its fixed cost — needs a subsidy to survive Average-cost pricing (\(P = ATC\)) Higher than MC pricing Firm breaks even (zero economic profit); some deadweight loss remains, but far less than unregulated monopoly Rate-of-return regulation Set to allow a "fair" return on invested capital Common in practice; can blunt incentives to cut costs

Most real-world utility regulation uses average-cost pricing as a practical compromise: it lets the firm cover its costs (including a normal return on capital) while keeping price well below the unregulated monopoly price.

docs.title: 7.8 Antitrust Policy
docs.text: Antitrust policy (called "competition policy" outside the U.S.) refers to laws and government actions aimed at preventing firms from acquiring or abusing monopoly power in ways that harm consumers.

docs.title: Key U.S. Antitrust Laws
docs.text: Law Year Main Provision Sherman Antitrust Act 1890 Outlaws contracts, combinations, and conspiracies that restrain trade; outlaws monopolization Clayton Act 1914 Prohibits specific practices: price discrimination that harms competition, exclusive dealing, mergers that substantially lessen competition Federal Trade Commission Act 1914 Created the FTC to enforce antitrust and consumer-protection law

docs.title: Enforcement Tools
docs.text:
• Blocking mergers that would substantially reduce competition (reviewed by the FTC and Department of Justice).
  • Breaking up firms found to be illegally monopolizing a market (e.g., Standard Oil, 1911).
  • Prohibiting price-fixing and collusion among competitors (a per se violation — illegal regardless of its effect on price).
  • Prohibiting predatory pricing — deliberately pricing below cost to drive out rivals, intending to raise prices later.

Monopoly is not illegal; monopolizing is

U.S. antitrust law does not punish a firm simply for becoming a monopoly through superior products, lower costs, or business acumen. It targets firms that acquire or maintain monopoly power through anticompetitive conduct — exclusionary contracts, predatory pricing, or illegal mergers — rather than through competing on the merits.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Monopoly A market with a single seller of a good with no close substitutes Barrier to Entry A factor that prevents new firms from entering a market Natural Monopoly A market where one firm can supply the entire market at lower cost than multiple firms Price Maker A firm whose own output decisions affect the market price Marginal Revenue (MR) The change in total revenue from selling one more unit Monopoly Price/Quantity The price and quantity where \(MR = MC\) and price is read off the demand curve Deadweight Loss The lost total surplus from producing less than the efficient quantity Price Discrimination Charging different prices to different customers for reasons unrelated to cost First-Degree Price Discrimination Charging each customer exactly their willingness to pay Second-Degree Price Discrimination Offering a menu of price-quantity bundles that customers self-select Third-Degree Price Discrimination Charging different groups of customers different prices based on an observable trait Arbitrage Reselling a good from low-price buyers to high-price buyers, which undermines price discrimination Marginal-Cost Pricing Regulatory rule setting price equal to marginal cost; efficient but may cause losses for a natural monopoly Average-Cost Pricing Regulatory rule setting price equal to average total cost; allows the firm to break even Antitrust Policy Laws and enforcement actions aimed at preventing anticompetitive monopoly power Sherman Antitrust Act 1890 law outlawing restraint of trade and monopolization

docs.title: Problem 1 — Marginal Revenue
docs.text:
A monopolist faces demand \(P = 60 - Q\).

a) Write the total revenue function and derive the marginal revenue function. b) At what quantity does \(MR = 0\)? c) Over what range of quantity is demand elastic?

Solution

a) \(TR = PQ = (60-Q)Q = 60Q - Q^2\). \(MR = \dfrac{d(TR)}{dQ} = 60 - 2Q\).

b) \(MR = 0 \Rightarrow 60 - 2Q = 0 \Rightarrow Q = 30\).

c) Demand is elastic wherever \(MR > 0\), i.e., for \(Q < 30\). (Demand is unit-elastic at \(Q=30\) and inelastic for \(Q > 30\).)

docs.title: Problem 2 — Profit Maximization
docs.text:
A monopolist faces demand \(P = 120 - 2Q\) and has total cost \(TC = 10Q + 200\) (so \(MC = 10\)).

a) Find the profit-maximizing quantity and price. b) Calculate the monopolist's profit. c) Is this monopolist earning an economic profit, breaking even, or earning a loss?

Solution

a) \(MR = 120 - 4Q\). Set \(MR = MC\): \(120 - 4Q = 10 \Rightarrow Q^M = 27.5\). Then \(P^M = 120 - 2(27.5) = \$65\).

b) \(TR = 65 \times 27.5 = \$1{,}787.50\). \(TC = 10(27.5) + 200 = 275 + 200 = \$475\). Profit \(= 1{,}787.50 - 475 = \$1{,}312.50\).

c) The firm earns a positive economic profit of $1,312.50, since \(TR > TC\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Deadweight Loss
docs.text:
Demand is \(P = 200 - Q\) and marginal cost is constant at \(MC = 40\) (no fixed costs).

a) Find the competitive price and quantity. b) Find the monopoly price and quantity. c) Calculate the deadweight loss from monopoly.

Solution

a) Competitive: \(P = MC \Rightarrow 200 - Q = 40 \Rightarrow Q^C = 160\), \(P^C = 40\).

b) Monopoly: \(MR = 200 - 2Q\). Set \(MR = MC\): \(200 - 2Q = 40 \Rightarrow Q^M = 80\). \(P^M = 200 - 80 = \$120\).

c) \(DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (P^M - MC) \times (Q^C - Q^M) = \frac{1}{2} \times (120-40) \times (160-80) = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 80 = \$3{,}200\).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Third-Degree Price Discrimination
docs.text:
An airline sells tickets to business travelers and leisure travelers on the same flight. Demand curves are:

\[P_B = 800 - 2Q_B \quad \text{(business)}\] \[P_L = 400 - 2Q_L \quad \text{(leisure)}\]

Marginal cost per seat is constant at \(MC = 100\), and the airline can prevent resale (tickets are non-transferable).

a) Find the profit-maximizing price and quantity in each segment. b) Which group pays more, and why does this make economic sense?

Solution

a) Business: \(MR_B = 800 - 4Q_B\). Set equal to \(MC\): \(800 - 4Q_B = 100 \Rightarrow Q_B = 175\), \(P_B = 800 - 2(175) = \$450\).

Leisure: \(MR_L = 400 - 4Q_L\). Set equal to \(MC\): \(400 - 4Q_L = 100 \Rightarrow Q_L = 75\), \(P_L = 400 - 2(75) = \$250\).

b) Business travelers pay more ($450 vs. $250). Business demand is less elastic — business travelers typically have inflexible schedules and employer-paid tickets, so they are less price-sensitive. The airline exploits this by charging them a higher markup over marginal cost.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Natural Monopoly Regulation
docs.text:
A water utility faces market demand \(P = 22 - Q\) and has total cost \(TC = 35 + 10Q\) (so \(MC = 10\) and fixed cost is $35).

a) Find the price and quantity under unregulated monopoly. b) Find the price and quantity under marginal-cost-pricing regulation (\(P = MC\)). What is the utility's profit at this price? c) Find the price and quantity under average-cost-pricing regulation (\(P = ATC\)), choosing the solution with the larger quantity. Confirm the firm earns zero economic profit there.

Solution

a) \(MR = 22 - 2Q\). Set \(MR = MC\): \(22 - 2Q = 10 \Rightarrow Q^M = 6\), \(P^M = 22 - 6 = \$16\).

b) Marginal-cost pricing: \(P = MC = \$10\). From demand, \(10 = 22 - Q \Rightarrow Q = 12\). Profit \(= TR - TC = (10)(12) - [35 + 10(12)] = 120 - 155 = -\$35\) — a loss exactly equal to the fixed cost, since price covers only marginal cost and nothing toward fixed cost.

c) Average-cost pricing requires \(P = ATC = \dfrac{35}{Q} + 10\). Set this equal to the demand price \(22 - Q\):

\[22 - Q = \frac{35}{Q} + 10$$ $$12Q - Q^2 = 35$$ $$Q^2 - 12Q + 35 = 0$$ $$(Q-5)(Q-7) = 0 \implies Q = 5 \text{ or } Q = 7\]

Taking the larger root, \(Q = 7\): \(P = 22 - 7 = \$15\). Check: \(ATC = 35/7 + 10 = 5 + 10 = \$15 = P\). ✓ Profit \(= (15)(7) - [35 + 10(7)] = 105 - 105 = \$0\) — the firm exactly breaks even.

Comparing all three regimes: price rises from $10 (marginal-cost) to $15 (average-cost) to $16 (unregulated monopoly), while quantity falls from 12 to 7 to 6. Average-cost regulation lands between the efficient outcome and the unregulated monopoly outcome — it sacrifices some efficiency to keep the utility financially viable without a subsidy.

You Understand Market Power

You can now find a monopolist's price and quantity, measure the deadweight loss it creates, and explain why price discrimination can actually make a market more efficient. That's a genuinely sophisticated set of tools!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 8: Monopolistic Competition, we study markets that blend elements of both competition and monopoly — many firms, but each with a slightly differentiated product and some pricing power of its own.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. List the characteristics that define monopolistic competition
  2. Explain how product differentiation and brand loyalty give firms some pricing power
  3. Find a monopolistically competitive firm's short-run profit-maximizing price and quantity
  4. Explain why economic profit is driven to zero in the long run and show this graphically
  5. Explain excess capacity and why monopolistically competitive firms price above marginal cost
  6. Analyze the economic role of advertising and other non-price competition
  7. Weigh the efficiency costs of monopolistic competition against the benefits of product variety

The Blend of Both Worlds

This chapter sits right between the last two: many firms like perfect competition, but each with a sliver of pricing power like a monopolist. Think about your own favorite coffee shop as you read — every choice has a trade-off, and here the trade-off is between efficiency and the variety you actually enjoy.

docs.title: 8.1 Characteristics of Monopolistic Competition
docs.text:
Monopolistic competition describes a market structure that combines features of both perfect competition and monopoly:

Feature Perfect Competition Monopolistic Competition Monopoly Number of firms Many Many One Product Identical Differentiated Unique (no substitutes) Entry/exit Free Free Blocked Price-setting power None (price taker) Some Full (price maker) Long-run economic profit Zero Zero Can be positive

Think of restaurants, hair salons, clothing brands, coffee shops, or gas stations in a city: there are many firms, entry is relatively easy, but each firm's product is slightly different from its rivals' — a Chipotle burrito is not identical to a Qdoba burrito, even though both compete in the "fast casual Mexican food" market.

Monopolistically competitive industries

  • Restaurants and coffee shops
  • Clothing and shoe brands
  • Hair salons and barbershops
  • Smartphone apps in a given category (e.g., note-taking apps)

docs.title: 8.2 Product Differentiation and Brand Loyalty
docs.text:
Product differentiation means firms make their product distinct from competitors' in the eyes of consumers — through physical features, location, service quality, branding, or perceived quality.

Differentiation matters because it gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve (unlike the horizontal demand curve of a perfectly competitive firm). If a monopolistically competitive firm raises its price slightly, it loses some customers to rivals, but not all of them — because its product isn't a perfect substitute for theirs.

Brand loyalty is the tendency of some consumers to keep buying a firm's product even when a rival offers a lower price or a seemingly identical product. Loyalty is built through advertising, consistent quality, and habit, and it is what allows firms to charge a price above marginal cost without losing every customer.

Why the firm's demand curve is downward-sloping but highly elastic

Because many competitors offer close (though not perfect) substitutes, a monopolistically competitive firm's demand curve, while downward-sloping, is typically much flatter (more elastic) than a true monopolist's. Raising price loses a lot of customers to rivals — just not literally all of them, as it would for a perfectly competitive firm.

A Flatter Monopoly, Not a Weaker Competitor

It helps to think of each monopolistically competitive firm as a tiny monopolist over its own small slice of brand loyalty — just one facing unusually flat, elastic demand because so many close substitutes exist nearby.

docs.title: 8.3 Short-Run Profit Maximization
docs.text:
In the short run, a monopolistically competitive firm behaves exactly like a monopolist: it faces a downward-sloping demand curve \(D\) (and corresponding marginal revenue curve \(MR\), which lies below \(D\)), and it maximizes profit where:

\[MR = MC\]

It then charges the price given by the demand curve at that quantity.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
A local coffee shop faces demand \(P = 8 - 0.02Q\) (price in dollars, \(Q\) in cups per week) and has marginal cost \(MC = 2\) with fixed cost \(FC = 400\) per week (so \(TC = 400 + 2Q\)).

Marginal revenue: \(TR = PQ = 8Q - 0.02Q^2 \Rightarrow MR = 8 - 0.04Q\).

Set \(MR = MC\):

\[8 - 0.04Q = 2\] \[6 = 0.04Q\] \[Q = 150\]

Price: \(P = 8 - 0.02(150) = 8 - 3 = \$5\).

\(ATC\) at \(Q=150\): \(ATC = \dfrac{400 + 2(150)}{150} = \dfrac{700}{150} \approx \$4.67\).

Since \(P = \$5.00 > ATC \approx \$4.67\), the shop earns a short-run economic profit of approximately \((5.00 - 4.67) \times 150 \approx \$50\) per week.

Value Profit-maximizing quantity 150 cups/week Price $5.00 \(ATC\) $4.67 Economic profit ≈ $50/week

docs.title: 8.4 Long-Run Equilibrium: Zero Economic Profit
docs.text: Short-run profits like the one above are a signal. Because entry is free in monopolistic competition, the coffee shop's success attracts new competitors — new coffee shops, cafés, and even non-coffee alternatives that split the market.

docs.title: The Entry Mechanism
docs.text:
1. Existing firms earn positive economic profit in the short run.
  2. New firms enter, offering their own differentiated versions of the product.
  3. Entry shifts each incumbent firm's demand curve to the left (and makes it more elastic/flatter) — the same total market demand is now shared among more sellers, and each firm's product has more close substitutes than before.
  4. Entry continues until demand has shifted left enough that price equals average total cost everywhere along the firm's residual demand curve at its profit-maximizing quantity — economic profit falls to zero.
  5. If firms were suffering losses, the reverse happens: exit shifts remaining firms' demand curves right until losses disappear.

docs.title: The Long-Run Equilibrium Condition
docs.text:
In long-run equilibrium, two conditions hold simultaneously:

\[MR = MC \quad \text{(profit-maximizing quantity)}\] \[P = ATC \quad \text{(zero economic profit)}\]

Graphically, this means the firm's downward-sloping demand curve is tangent to its \(ATC\) curve at the profit-maximizing quantity — the demand curve touches \(ATC\) at exactly one point, from above, without crossing it. If demand sat above \(ATC\) at the best quantity, profit would still be positive and more entry would occur; if it sat entirely below, firms would be exiting.

Tangency, step by step

Starting from the coffee shop's short-run profit in Section 8.3, new cafés enter the neighborhood. Demand for our shop's coffee shrinks and becomes more elastic. This process continues — shifting demand left — until the best price the shop can charge exactly covers its average total cost. At that point, there is no longer an incentive for further entry.

Watch the Demand Curve Walk Left

Three snapshots of a shifting demand curve can feel like a lot to track at once. Focus on just one thing per row: as demand shifts left, find the new \(MR=MC\) quantity, then check whether \(P\) still beats \(ATC\).

docs.title: Tracking the Coffee Shop Through Entry
docs.text:
Continuing the example from Section 8.3, suppose entry gradually shifts the coffee shop's demand curve inward. The table below illustrates three snapshots of this adjustment process (illustrative, not derived from a single equation) as new shops open nearby:

Stage Demand Curve \(Q^*\) (where \(MR=MC\)) \(P^*\) \(ATC\) at \(Q^*\) Economic Profit Short run (Section 8.3) \(P = 8 - 0.02Q\) 150 $5.00 $4.67 ≈ +$50/week After some entry \(P = 7 - 0.02Q\) 125 $4.50 $4.40 ≈ +$12.50/week Long-run equilibrium \(P = 6.4 - 0.02Q\) 110 $4.20 $4.20 $0/week

As rival cafés open, the demand curve shifts down and to the left, the profit-maximizing quantity falls, and profit shrinks toward zero. Entry stops exactly when price just equals \(ATC\) at the firm's best quantity.

docs.title: 8.5 Excess Capacity and the Markup
docs.text: Even though long-run economic profit is zero, monopolistic competition does not replicate the perfectly competitive outcome. Two differences remain:

docs.title: Price Above Marginal Cost (the Markup)
docs.text:
Because the firm's demand curve is downward-sloping (not horizontal), the tangency condition \(P = ATC\) occurs where \(MR = MC\), and since \(MR < P\) for a downward-sloping demand curve, it must be that:

\[P > MC\]

even in long-run equilibrium. The firm retains a small markup over marginal cost, unlike a perfectly competitive firm, which drives \(P = MC\).

Spot the Markup Fast

Any time a firm's demand curve slopes downward, \(MR\) sits below it — so setting \(MR = MC\) automatically leaves \(P > MC\). You don't need to recompute this each time; it's baked into any downward-sloping demand curve.

docs.title: Excess Capacity
docs.text:
The tangency between demand and \(ATC\) must occur at a quantity to the left of the minimum point of the \(ATC\) curve (where \(ATC\) is still declining). This is because a downward-sloping demand curve can only be tangent to a U-shaped \(ATC\) curve on its declining portion.

This means each firm in long-run equilibrium produces less than the output that would minimize its average total cost. The gap between the firm's actual output and the output at minimum \(ATC\) is called excess capacity:

\[\text{Excess Capacity} = Q_{\min ATC} - Q^*\]

Interpreting excess capacity

If the coffee shop merely served more cups at the same quality, its average cost per cup would fall. It doesn't, because demand for any single shop isn't large enough at a profitable price. This is why monopolistically competitive markets tend to have "too many" firms, each operating below their efficient scale — think of how many lightly-patronized coffee shops and nail salons can coexist on a few blocks of a city.

Perfect Competition (long run) Monopolistic Competition (long run) Economic profit Zero Zero \(P\) vs. \(MC\) \(P = MC\) \(P > MC\) Output relative to minimum \(ATC\) At minimum \(ATC\) (efficient scale) Below minimum \(ATC\) (excess capacity) Product variety None (identical goods) Significant

Zero Profit Doesn't Mean 'Just Like Competition'

Long-run economic profit hits zero in both market structures, but don't stop there — monopolistic competition still leaves \(P > MC\) and excess capacity behind, two inefficiencies a truly competitive market never has.

docs.title: 8.6 Advertising and Non-Price Competition
docs.text: Because price competition alone cannot fully differentiate a monopolistically competitive firm's product, firms frequently rely on non-price competition — advertising, packaging, location, customer service, and other means of making their product seem different (or better) without changing its price.

docs.title: Economic Effects of Advertising
docs.text:
Advertising has two competing economic interpretations:

View Argument Informative view Advertising provides useful information about product existence, price, and quality, helping consumers make better choices and lowering their search costs Persuasive view Advertising manipulates preferences, creates artificial brand loyalty, and raises barriers to entry (new firms must spend heavily to build a comparable brand), without adding real value

Both effects are present in practice. Advertising can raise a firm's fixed costs (another reason output may remain below the cost-minimizing scale) but can also expand the firm's customer base enough to lower average costs by spreading large fixed costs over more sales — the net effect on prices is ambiguous and depends on the specific market.

Advertising and generic drugs

Advertising intensity correlates with brand loyalty: heavily advertised brand-name drugs often sell at a large premium over chemically identical generics, even after the patent expires and legal barriers to entry disappear. This illustrates the persuasive view — advertising alone sustains a price gap unrelated to any real product difference.

docs.title: 8.7 Welfare Analysis: Efficiency vs. Variety
docs.text:
Monopolistic competition is not allocatively efficient in the strict sense used for perfect competition: price exceeds marginal cost, and firms operate with excess capacity rather than at their efficient scale.
