In isolation, this looks like a cost to society, similar to (though usually smaller than) the deadweight loss created by a monopolist.

However, a purely efficiency-focused comparison misses something perfectly competitive markets cannot provide: product variety. Consumers place real value on having many distinct options — different cuisines, different store locations, different brands with different features — rather than one standardized product sold at minimum cost.

docs.title: The Trade-off
docs.text:
Benefit Cost Fewer, larger, more standardized firms Lower average cost per unit (closer to efficient scale) Less product variety; less convenient locations; fewer choices Many smaller, differentiated firms Greater product variety and convenience Higher average cost per unit; price above marginal cost; some deadweight loss

Whether monopolistic competition is "good" or "bad" for society, therefore, depends on how much consumers value variety relative to the efficiency loss from excess capacity and markups. Most economists view monopolistic competition as a reasonably efficient compromise: it delivers substantial variety at a modest efficiency cost, which is why it describes so much of the real-world retail and service economy.

A note on 'wasteful' competition

It is tempting to call duplicated storefronts, overlapping product lines, and advertising "wasteful." But in a world where consumers demonstrably value choice — different flavors, different neighborhoods, different aesthetics — some of this apparent waste is actually consumers paying (via slightly higher prices) for variety they want.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Monopolistic Competition A market structure with many firms, free entry and exit, and differentiated products Product Differentiation Making a firm's product distinct from competitors' in consumers' eyes Brand Loyalty Consumers' tendency to keep buying a firm's product despite lower-priced alternatives Short-Run Equilibrium The price and quantity where \(MR = MC\) for a monopolistically competitive firm Long-Run Equilibrium The zero-economic-profit outcome where the demand curve is tangent to \(ATC\) Markup The amount by which price exceeds marginal cost Excess Capacity The gap between a firm's actual output and the output that minimizes average total cost Non-Price Competition Competing through advertising, quality, service, or location rather than price Informative Advertising Advertising that reduces consumer search costs by conveying real product information Persuasive Advertising Advertising that shapes preferences and builds brand loyalty unrelated to real product differences Product Variety The range of differentiated options available to consumers in a market Tangency Condition The long-run condition where the firm's demand curve just touches its \(ATC\) curve

docs.title: Problem 1 — Characteristics
docs.text:
For each market, identify whether it is best described as perfect competition, monopolistic competition, or monopoly, and justify your answer briefly.

a) Wheat farming b) Nail salons in a large city c) The local electric utility d) Smartphone photo-editing apps

Solution

a) Perfect competition — identical product (wheat is a commodity), many sellers, price takers.

b) Monopolistic competition — many salons, free entry, but each differentiated by location, staff, ambiance, and service quality.

c) Monopoly — a single firm supplies the entire local market; high fixed-cost barriers to entry (natural monopoly).

d) Monopolistic competition — many apps compete, entry is relatively easy (low cost to publish an app), but each app differentiates through features, design, and branding.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Short-Run Profit Maximization
docs.text:
A boutique clothing store faces demand \(P = 60 - 0.5Q\) and has \(MC = 10\) with fixed costs of \(FC = 200\) (so \(TC = 200 + 10Q\)).

a) Find the profit-maximizing price and quantity. b) Calculate \(ATC\) at that quantity. c) Is the store earning a short-run economic profit, a loss, or breaking even? By how much?

Solution

a) \(TR = 60Q - 0.5Q^2 \Rightarrow MR = 60 - Q\). Set \(MR = MC\): \(60 - Q = 10 \Rightarrow Q = 50\). \(P = 60 - 0.5(50) = \$35\).

b) \(ATC = \dfrac{200 + 10(50)}{50} = \dfrac{700}{50} = \$14\).

c) \(P = \$35 > ATC = \$14\), so the store earns a short-run economic profit of \((35-14) \times 50 = \$1{,}050\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Long-Run Adjustment
docs.text:
Using the boutique from Problem 2, suppose the $1,050 short-run profit attracts new clothing boutiques into the neighborhood.

a) What happens to the original boutique's demand curve as new competitors enter? b) What happens to its profit over time? c) What condition characterizes the new long-run equilibrium?

Solution

a) The demand curve shifts left (fewer customers per firm at any price) and becomes more elastic (flatter), since more close substitutes are now available nearby.

b) Profit shrinks toward zero as entry continues, because the demand curve keeps shifting left (and becoming more elastic) until no further profit is available to attract entry.

c) Long-run equilibrium occurs where \(MR = MC\) and \(P = ATC\) simultaneously — the (now-shifted) demand curve is tangent to the \(ATC\) curve at the firm's profit-maximizing quantity.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Excess Capacity
docs.text:
In long-run equilibrium, a bakery's \(ATC\) curve reaches its minimum value of $3.00 per loaf at \(Q = 300\) loaves per week. In its actual long-run equilibrium, the bakery produces 220 loaves per week at a price of $3.40, which equals its \(ATC\) at that quantity.

a) What is the bakery's excess capacity? b) Is price above or below marginal cost at the equilibrium quantity? Explain why this must be true given the tangency condition. c) Does this bakery earn positive, zero, or negative economic profit in the long run? Explain.

Solution

a) Excess capacity \(= Q_{\min ATC} - Q^* = 300 - 220 = 80\) loaves per week.

b) Price is above marginal cost. Because the firm's demand curve slopes downward, \(MR < P\) at every quantity. Since the firm sets \(MR = MC\), and \(MR < P\), it follows that \(MC < P\) — the markup is a direct consequence of facing a downward-sloping (not horizontal) demand curve.

c) Economic profit is zero, because price equals \(ATC\) ($3.40 = $3.40) exactly at the equilibrium quantity — this is the defining feature of long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Advertising and Welfare
docs.text:
A regional airline begins a major advertising campaign emphasizing its loyalty rewards program, successfully increasing brand loyalty among business travelers.

a) How would you expect this to affect the airline's demand curve (shape and position)? b) How would you expect it to affect the airline's markup over marginal cost? c) Does this advertising represent the "informative" or "persuasive" view, and does it necessarily reduce consumer welfare? Explain both sides.

Solution

a) The demand curve should shift right (more customers at every price) and become less elastic / steeper (more loyal customers are less willing to switch to a rival even if price rises).

b) A less elastic demand curve allows a larger markup over marginal cost — the airline can raise price further above \(MC\) without losing as many customers.

c) This is closer to the persuasive view, since loyalty programs are explicitly designed to make switching costly rather than to convey new information about the product itself. However, it is not purely wasteful: loyalty programs can also provide real value (discounts, perks, convenience) that consumers genuinely appreciate, so some of the brand loyalty built reflects real, not manufactured, value — the welfare effect is ambiguous and depends on how much of the loyalty reflects real benefits versus pure habit or switching costs.

You Can Explain Your Own Neighborhood

You can now explain why there are five coffee shops within walking distance, none of them huge, all charging slightly different prices — and why that's a real trade-off between efficiency and the variety you get to choose from!

Next Chapter

In Chapter 9: Oligopoly, we turn to markets with only a few large sellers, where each firm's pricing and output decisions directly affect its rivals — introducing the strategic interdependence that sets the stage for game theory.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Identify the characteristics that distinguish oligopoly from the other market structures
  2. Solve for the Cournot (quantity-setting) equilibrium in a duopoly
  3. Solve for the Bertrand (price-setting) equilibrium and explain the Bertrand paradox
  4. Explain why collusion is profitable but unstable, using the OPEC cartel as an example
  5. Use the kinked demand curve model to explain price rigidity in oligopoly
  6. Calculate and interpret concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)
  7. Describe the goals of antitrust law and competition policy

A Few Big Players, All Watching Each Other

Welcome to the market structure where rivals can't ignore each other! In perfect competition and monopoly, a firm could set its price or quantity without a second thought about what anyone else was doing — not here. Every choice has a trade-off, and in oligopoly your trade-offs are tangled up with your rivals' trade-offs too. Get ready to think like a strategist, not just a profit-maximizer.

docs.title: 9.1 Characteristics of Oligopoly
docs.text:
An oligopoly is a market structure with a small number of large sellers, each of whom has market power and is aware that its own pricing and output decisions affect — and are affected by — the decisions of its rivals.

Real-world oligopolies

  • Commercial aircraft manufacturing (Boeing, Airbus)
  • U.S. wireless carriers (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile)
  • Breakfast cereal (Kellogg's, General Mills, Post)
  • Crude oil production (OPEC member states and a handful of non-OPEC producers)

The defining feature of oligopoly is strategic interdependence: unlike a perfectly competitive firm (which ignores its rivals because each is too small to matter) or a monopolist (which has no rivals), an oligopolist must explicitly anticipate how its competitors will react to its choices. This is why oligopoly is the market structure in which game theory (Chapter 10) becomes indispensable.

Feature Perfect Competition Monopoly Oligopoly Number of sellers Many One Few Market power None Substantial Significant, but checked by rivals Awareness of rivals None needed No rivals Essential Barriers to entry None High Usually high Price-setting Price taker Price maker Strategic — depends on rivals

Entry barriers in oligopoly resemble those in monopoly: economies of scale, high capital requirements, patents, and network effects. What makes oligopoly analytically distinct is not the barrier itself but the fact that a few firms, not one, clear the market and interact repeatedly.

The Mental Shift: You Can't Optimize Alone Anymore

Notice what just changed. In every market structure so far, a firm could maximize profit by looking only at its own costs and demand. Here, the right choice depends on a guess about what rivals will do — and their choice depends on a guess about you. That circular reasoning is exactly what game theory, coming up in Chapter 10, was invented to resolve.

docs.title: 9.2 The Cournot Model: Competing in Quantities
docs.text:
The Cournot model (named for French economist Antoine Augustin Cournot, 1838) assumes that firms simultaneously and independently choose quantities to produce, each firm correctly anticipating the other's output choice in equilibrium.

Consider a duopoly (two firms, Firm 1 and Firm 2) producing an identical good with inverse market demand:

\[P = a - b(Q_1 + Q_2)\]

Yes, There's Calculus Ahead — You're Ready for It

If a derivative-based equilibrium makes your stomach drop a little, that's a completely normal reaction — this is genuinely one of the more demanding derivations in the course. Take it one line at a time: write the profit function, take one derivative, set it to zero. You've already made this exact move in the monopoly chapter; the only new wrinkle is that your rival's quantity sits in the equation as a fixed number you don't control.

Each firm has constant marginal cost \(c\). Firm 1's profit is:

\[\pi_1 = [a - b(Q_1 + Q_2)]Q_1 - cQ_1\]

Taking the derivative with respect to \(Q_1\) (treating \(Q_2\) as given) and setting it to zero gives Firm 1's best-response function:

\[Q_1 = \frac{a - c - bQ_2}{2b}\]

By symmetry, Firm 2's best response is \(Q_2 = \dfrac{a - c - bQ_1}{2b}\).

Numerical Cournot equilibrium

Let \(P = 100 - (Q_1 + Q_2)\) and \(c = 10\) for both firms (so \(a = 100\), \(b = 1\)).

Firm 1's best response: \(Q_1 = \dfrac{90 - Q_2}{2}\). By symmetry, \(Q_2 = \dfrac{90 - Q_1}{2}\).

Substituting the symmetric condition \(Q_1 = Q_2 = Q^*\):

\[Q^* = \frac{90 - Q^*}{2} \implies 2Q^* = 90 - Q^* \implies Q^* = 30\]

Each firm produces 30 units; total quantity \(Q = 60\); market price \(P = 100 - 60 = \$40\).

Compare this to the competitive outcome (\(P = MC = 10 \implies Q = 90\)) and the monopoly (collusive) outcome (a single firm maximizing joint profit produces \(Q_m = 45\), \(P = \$55\)). Cournot duopoly output (60) lies between the competitive output (90) and the monopoly output (45) — more sellers push output up and price down toward the competitive level.

Solving the two best-response equations simultaneously and plotting them on a graph with \(Q_1\) on one axis and \(Q_2\) on the other produces two downward-sloping lines; their intersection is the Cournot-Nash equilibrium, the point where each firm's output is a best response to the other's.

More firms, more competition

With \(n\) symmetric Cournot firms, it can be shown that equilibrium industry output converges toward the competitive level as \(n \to \infty\), and price converges toward marginal cost. Cournot competition with a large number of firms behaves increasingly like perfect competition — a useful bridge between the two models.

docs.title: 9.3 The Bertrand Model: Competing in Prices
docs.text:
The Bertrand model (Joseph Bertrand, 1883) assumes firms compete by simultaneously choosing prices rather than quantities, with consumers buying entirely from whichever firm charges the lower price (splitting demand if prices are tied).

With identical products and constant marginal cost \(c\), consider what happens if Firm 1 sets \(P_1 > c\). Firm 2 can capture the entire market by setting \(P_2\) just below \(P_1\), as long as \(P_2 > c\) still yields a profit. Each firm has an incentive to undercut the other — a race that stops only when price equals marginal cost.

\[P_1 = P_2 = MC\]

This is the Bertrand paradox: with only two identical firms, price competition alone (no capacity limits, homogeneous goods) drives price all the way down to the competitive, zero-economic-profit level — the same outcome as perfect competition, even though only two firms exist.

Why the Bertrand paradox rarely holds exactly

Real-world duopolies rarely show marginal-cost pricing. The paradox weakens once we introduce:

  • Product differentiation (firms are not perfect substitutes, so undercutting doesn't capture 100% of rivals' sales)
  • Capacity constraints (a firm cannot always serve the whole market even at the lowest price)
  • Repeated interaction (firms can sustain higher prices through implicit cooperation — see Section 9.4 and Chapter 10)

The contrast between Cournot and Bertrand illustrates an important lesson: the strategic variable firms compete on (quantity vs. price) changes the predicted outcome, even holding the number of firms and cost structure fixed.

Same Firms, Same Costs, Totally Different Outcomes

Step back and compare the two models: Cournot firms competing on quantity land on a price above marginal cost, but Bertrand firms competing on price crash all the way down to marginal cost — same two firms, same costs, same demand curve, wildly different results. Carry that forward as your mental model: in oligopoly, how firms compete matters just as much as how many firms there are.

docs.title: 9.4 Collusion and Cartels
docs.text:
Collusion occurs when oligopolists coordinate their pricing or output decisions to behave jointly like a monopolist, raising price above the competitive (or Cournot) level and increasing joint profit. A formal, explicit collusive agreement among firms is called a cartel.

OPEC: the world's most visible cartel

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) coordinates crude-oil production quotas among member nations to influence the world price of oil. When members comply with assigned quotas, world output falls below the competitive level and price rises — exactly as the cartel model predicts. OPEC's history, however, also illustrates the model's central weakness.

Why collusion is profitable: Joint profit is maximized by restricting output to the monopoly level and dividing it (and the associated economic profit) among members — strictly more profit than any member could earn acting alone at the competitive or Cournot output.

Why collusion is unstable: Each cartel member faces a powerful incentive to cheat — secretly producing more than its assigned quota. If a quota holds price at the monopoly level \(P_m\) while a member's marginal cost is well below \(P_m\), that member earns extra profit on every unit it sneaks past its quota, as long as other members don't retaliate. Because every member faces this same temptation simultaneously, the gains from mutual restriction — the cartel — tend to unravel. This instability is formally a prisoner's dilemma, developed fully in Chapter 10.

  • In most countries, cartels among domestic firms are illegal under antitrust law (Section 9.6) — this is precisely why OPEC, a cartel among sovereign nations, can operate openly, while a cartel among U.S. airlines could not.
  • Price-fixing conspiracies prosecuted under U.S. antitrust law include historical cases in lysine, vitamins, and electrical equipment manufacturing.

docs.title: 9.5 The Kinked Demand Curve Model
docs.text:
The kinked demand curve model (Paul Sweezy, 1939) explains a puzzling empirical regularity: oligopoly prices often stay unchanged for long stretches even as costs fluctuate modestly — a phenomenon called price rigidity.

The model assumes an asymmetric belief about rival behavior:

  • If a firm raises its price above the current level, rivals will not follow — they are happy to keep their own price low and capture the firm's customers. Demand for the price-raising firm is therefore highly elastic above the current price.
  • If a firm lowers its price below the current level, rivals will match the cut to avoid losing market share. Demand for the price-cutting firm is therefore much less elastic below the current price.

This creates a demand curve with a kink at the current price \(P^*\) — relatively flat above \(P^*\), steeper below it. Because marginal revenue has a discontinuous (vertical) jump at the output level corresponding to the kink, a range of marginal costs can all intersect that vertical segment at the same quantity, leaving the firm's profit-maximizing price unchanged even though its costs shifted.

The intuition in one sentence

A firm that believes "rivals will match my price cuts but ignore my price increases" has every reason to leave price alone — any price change in either direction loses relative to the status quo.

The kinked demand curve describes behavior that sustains a price, not how that price was originally set — it explains rigidity around an existing equilibrium rather than predicting what that equilibrium will be.

docs.title: 9.6 Measuring Market Concentration
docs.text:
Economists and antitrust regulators quantify how "oligopolistic" an industry is using concentration measures computed from each firm's market share.

Concentration ratio (CR\(_n\)): the combined market share of the largest \(n\) firms.

\[CR_4 = s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + s_4\]

where \(s_i\) is firm \(i\)'s market share (ranked largest to smallest).

Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI): the sum of squared market shares (shares expressed as whole-number percentages, e.g., 25 for 25%), giving more weight to large firms than CR\(_n\) does.

\[HHI = \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i^2\] Market Structure Example \(s_i\) HHI Perfect competition (many tiny firms) 100 firms at 1% each \(100 \times 1^2 = 100\) Duopoly, equal shares Two firms at 50% each \(50^2 + 50^2 = 5{,}000\) Pure monopoly One firm at 100% \(100^2 = 10{,}000\)

A Quick Way to Sanity-Check Any HHI

Want to catch an arithmetic slip before you report a wrong HHI? The market shares should sum to roughly 100, so the squared terms can never add up anywhere near 10,000 unless one firm is close to a true monopoly. And remember, it's the squaring that punishes a handful of giants — equal shares split among more firms always pulls HHI down.

The U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission use HHI thresholds to screen proposed mergers:

  • HHI below 1,500: unconcentrated market — mergers rarely challenged
  • HHI between 1,500 and 2,500: moderately concentrated — mergers scrutinized, especially large HHI increases
  • HHI above 2,500: highly concentrated — mergers face the greatest scrutiny

Computing HHI

An industry has five firms with market shares of 30%, 25%, 20%, 15%, and 10%.

\[HHI = 30^2 + 25^2 + 20^2 + 15^2 + 10^2 = 900 + 625 + 400 + 225 + 100 = 2{,}250\]

An HHI of 2,250 falls in the "moderately concentrated" range — a proposed merger between the two largest firms (which would push HHI well above 2,500) would likely draw regulatory scrutiny.

docs.title: 9.7 Antitrust Law and Competition Policy
docs.text:
Antitrust law (called competition law outside the United States) is the body of government policy aimed at preventing monopolization, collusion, and anticompetitive mergers in order to protect consumers and preserve market efficiency.

Key pillars of U.S. antitrust policy:

  • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies in restraint of trade (Section 1 — targets price-fixing and cartels) and monopolization (Section 2)
  • Clayton Act (1914): prohibits mergers and acquisitions that would substantially lessen competition, along with specific practices like price discrimination that harms competition
  • Federal Trade Commission Act (1914): created the FTC and prohibits "unfair methods of competition"

What antitrust enforcement targets

  • Horizontal price-fixing — direct agreements among competitors to set prices or output (per se illegal; no defense is accepted)
  • Anticompetitive mergers — combinations that would push concentration and market power too high (evaluated partly using HHI, Section 9.6)
  • Predatory and exclusionary conduct — e.g., a dominant firm pricing below cost specifically to drive out rivals, then raising prices once competitors exit

Bigness Isn't the Crime — Conduct Is

A common trap: assuming a large market share is itself illegal. It isn't. Antitrust law targets conduct — price-fixing agreements, exclusionary tactics, mergers that would substantially lessen competition — not the mere fact that a firm is big or dominant. A monopolist that earned its position through a better product has broken no law; a cartel of modest-sized firms that agreed to fix prices has.

Competition policy reflects the same core trade-off this chapter has developed: a few large firms can achieve scale efficiencies unavailable to many small ones, but without a competitive check, they can also exercise the market power this chapter's models all describe — raising prices above, and restricting output below, the competitive levels that maximize total surplus.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Oligopoly A market with a small number of large, interdependent sellers Strategic interdependence Each firm's optimal decision depends on rivals' decisions Cournot model Firms simultaneously choose quantities, each anticipating the other's output Best-response function A firm's optimal choice given a specific (fixed) choice by its rival Cournot-Nash equilibrium The quantity pair at which each firm's output is a best response to the other's Bertrand model Firms simultaneously choose prices; lowest price captures the market Bertrand paradox Price competition between just two identical firms drives price to marginal cost Collusion Coordination among firms to raise joint profit above the non-cooperative level Cartel A formal, explicit collusive agreement among firms Kinked demand curve A demand curve with a kink at the current price, explaining price rigidity Concentration ratio (CR\(_n\)) Combined market share of the largest \(n\) firms Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) Sum of squared market shares; used to screen mergers Antitrust law Government policy preventing monopolization, collusion, and anticompetitive mergers

docs.title: Problem 1 — Cournot Equilibrium
docs.text:
Two firms compete in a Cournot duopoly with market demand \(P = 120 - (Q_1 + Q_2)\) and identical marginal cost \(c = 20\).

a) Find each firm's best-response function. b) Solve for the Cournot-Nash equilibrium quantities and price. c) Compare total output to the competitive output (\(P = MC\)) and the monopoly output.

Solution

a) Firm 1 maximizes \(\pi_1 = [120 - Q_1 - Q_2]Q_1 - 20Q_1\). Taking \(\partial \pi_1/\partial Q_1 = 0\):

\[120 - 2Q_1 - Q_2 - 20 = 0 \implies Q_1 = \frac{100 - Q_2}{2}\]

By symmetry, \(Q_2 = \dfrac{100 - Q_1}{2}\).

b) Imposing symmetry \(Q_1 = Q_2 = Q^*\): \(Q^* = \dfrac{100 - Q^*}{2} \implies 2Q^* = 100 - Q^* \implies Q^* = 33.33\).

Total output \(Q = 66.67\); price \(P = 120 - 66.67 = \$53.33\).

c) Competitive output: \(P = MC \implies 120 - Q = 20 \implies Q = 100\). Monopoly output: maximize \([120-Q]Q - 20Q \implies Q_m = 50\). Cournot output (66.67) lies between monopoly (50) and competitive (100), as expected.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Bertrand Competition
docs.text:
Two firms sell an identical product with marginal cost \(c = \$15\). Under Bertrand competition, what price will prevail in equilibrium? Explain why neither firm can profitably deviate.

Solution

Equilibrium price \(P_1 = P_2 = \$15 = MC\). If either firm priced above $15, the other could undercut it by a cent, capture the entire market, and still earn a positive margin — so prices above $15 cannot be an equilibrium. Neither firm will price below $15 because that guarantees a loss on every unit sold. The only price from which neither firm wants to deviate is \(P = MC = \$15\), the same outcome as perfect competition.

docs.title: Problem 3 — HHI and Merger Review
docs.text:
An industry has four firms with market shares 40%, 30%, 20%, and 10%.

a) Calculate the industry's HHI. b) The two smallest firms (20% and 10%) propose to merge. Calculate the post-merger HHI. c) Would this merger likely draw antitrust scrutiny? Explain using the DOJ/FTC thresholds.

Solution

a) \(HHI = 40^2 + 30^2 + 20^2 + 10^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3{,}000\).

b) Post-merger, the combined firm has \(20 + 10 = 30\%\) share, alongside the 40% and 30% firms: \(HHI = 40^2 + 30^2 + 30^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 900 = 3{,}400\). The HHI increase is \(3{,}400 - 3{,}000 = 400\).

c) The market was already "highly concentrated" (HHI > 2,500) before the merger, and the merger increases HHI further (by 400 points). Under DOJ/FTC guidelines, mergers in already highly concentrated markets that increase HHI by more than 100 points are presumed likely to enhance market power — this merger would very likely draw significant antitrust scrutiny.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Cartel Instability
docs.text:
Two firms in a cartel agree to split the market and each charge the monopoly price of $60, with marginal cost of $20 for each. Secretly, Firm A considers cutting its price to $55 while Firm B keeps its price at $60, capturing all of the market's 100 units.

a) What does Firm A earn if it cheats and Firm B does not retaliate? b) What would Firm A earn if it honored the agreement and received half of the market at $60? c) Why is this an unstable arrangement even though both firms are better off than under competition?

Solution

a) Cheating profit: \((55 - 20) \times 100 = \$3{,}500\).

b) Honoring the agreement: assume the cartel's total quantity at \(P=\$60\) is 50 units; Firm A's half-share profit: \((60-20) \times 25 = \$1{,}000\) (using a 50-unit total split evenly).

c) Even though both arrangements beat the competitive outcome, each firm individually gains far more by secretly undercutting the agreed price while the other complies — exactly the logic of a prisoner's dilemma (Chapter 10). Because both firms recognize this incentive, the cartel tends to break down unless firms can detect and punish cheating (e.g., through repeated interaction).

docs.title: Problem 5 — Kinked Demand
docs.text:
A firm believes that if it raises its price, no rival will follow, but if it cuts its price, every rival will match the cut. Using this belief, explain why the firm might leave its price unchanged even after a 10% increase in its marginal cost.

Solution

Above the current price, demand is highly elastic (rivals don't follow a price increase, so the firm loses most of its customers to competitors) — raising price loses more in volume than it gains in margin. Below the current price, demand is much less elastic (rivals match the cut, so the firm doesn't gain market share, it just earns less per unit on the same customers) — cutting price loses margin without gaining volume. Because marginal revenue jumps discontinuously at the kink, a range of marginal costs — including the cost both before and after a moderate 10% increase — can all still point to the same profit-maximizing output and price. The firm rationally leaves its price unchanged.

You Just Tamed Four of the Toughest Models in the Course

Cournot, Bertrand, cartel instability, and kinked demand — you worked through all four, and you can now calculate equilibria, spot a doomed cartel, and explain why prices sometimes just don't move. That's strategic thinking, and it's exactly what Chapter 10 builds on next.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 10: Game Theory, we formalize the strategic reasoning this chapter relied on informally — dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, and the prisoner's dilemma — giving us the tools to fully explain why cartels break down and how firms sustain cooperation when they interact repeatedly.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Define a game in terms of players, strategies, and payoffs, and represent it as a payoff matrix
  2. Identify dominant and dominated strategies
  3. Find the Nash equilibrium (or equilibria) of a simultaneous game
  4. Explain the prisoner's dilemma and why mutually beneficial cooperation can fail
  5. Distinguish coordination games from games of pure conflict
  6. Explain how repeated interaction can sustain cooperation
  7. Solve sequential games using backward induction
  8. Apply game theory to oligopoly, auctions, and bargaining

Finally — The Tools to Read Your Rivals' Minds

Every choice has a trade-off, and this chapter is about trade-offs that get tangled up with someone else's choices too. We spent all of Chapter 9 reasoning informally about rivals anticipating each other — now you get the actual toolkit: payoff matrices, dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, and backward induction. By the end, you'll be able to predict how strategic situations resolve, from boardrooms to auction houses to a police interrogation room.

docs.title: 10.1 What Is a Game?
docs.text:
A game is any strategic situation in which the outcome for each participant depends not only on that participant's own choice but on the choices of others. Formally, a game has three elements:

  • Players — the decision-makers (e.g., two firms, two bidders, two countries)
  • Strategies — the complete set of actions available to each player
  • Payoffs — the outcome (typically profit, utility, or some numerical score) each player receives for every possible combination of strategies chosen

We summarize a simple two-player, two-strategy game in a payoff matrix: a table whose rows are one player's strategies, whose columns are the other player's strategies, and whose cells list the payoff to each player (Row player's payoff, Column player's payoff) under that combination.

Reading a payoff matrix

Firm B: Low Price Firm B: High Price Firm A: Low Price (10, 10) (50, 5) Firm A: High Price (5, 50) (30, 30)

If Firm A charges a Low Price and Firm B charges a High Price, Firm A earns 50 and Firm B earns 5 — the first number in each cell always belongs to the row player (Firm A), the second to the column player (Firm B).

Game theory formalizes the strategic reasoning this textbook has used informally since oligopoly (Chapter 9): every oligopoly pricing decision, cartel agreement, and antitrust case is, at its core, a game.

The Shift: Solving for a Combination, Not a Single Choice

Here's the mental shift for this whole chapter: instead of solving for one person's optimal choice, you're solving for a combination of choices — one per player — that are each other's best responses at the same time. Every tool coming up, dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, backward induction, is just a different technique for finding that self-consistent combination.

docs.title: 10.2 Dominant Strategies
docs.text:
A dominant strategy is a strategy that gives a player a higher payoff than any other strategy available, no matter what the other player does. A strategy that is always worse than some alternative, regardless of the opponent's choice, is called a dominated strategy — a rational player never plays one.

Finding a dominant strategy

B: Confess B: Stay Silent A: Confess (−5, −5) (0, −10) A: Stay Silent (−10, 0) (−1, −1)

Check Player A's options: if B Confesses, A's best response is Confess (−5 beats −10). If B Stays Silent, A's best response is still Confess (0 beats −1). Since Confess is A's best response regardless of what B does, Confess is A's dominant strategy. By the matrix's symmetry, Confess is also B's dominant strategy.

Not every game has a dominant strategy for every player — many games require a more general equilibrium concept, introduced next.

docs.title: 10.3 Nash Equilibrium
docs.text:
A Nash equilibrium (John Nash, 1950) is a combination of strategies, one for each player, such that no player can improve their own payoff by unilaterally changing their own strategy, given the strategies chosen by everyone else. It is a mutual best response: each player's strategy is optimal given what the others are doing.

Finding a Nash equilibrium by inspection: underline or circle each player's best response to each of the other player's strategies; any cell where both players' payoffs are marked as best responses is a Nash equilibrium.

Stay Organized on a Bigger Matrix

Here's a shortcut for keeping track on a matrix bigger than 2x2: go column by column and underline Player A's best payoff in each column, then go row by row and circle Player B's best payoff in each row. Any cell with both an underline and a circle is a Nash equilibrium — no mental juggling required.

Finding the Nash equilibrium

B: Left B: Right A: Up (8, 3) (2, 2) A: Down (5, 5) (4, 8)

Check A's best response to each of B's choices: if B plays Left, A's best response is Up (8 > 5). If B plays Right, A's best response is Down (4 > 2).

Check B's best response to each of A's choices: if A plays Up, B's best response is Left (3 > 2). If A plays Down, B's best response is Right (8 > 5).

(Up, Left) is a Nash equilibrium: A's best response to Left is Up, and B's best response to Up is Left — both conditions hold simultaneously. Checking (Down, Right): A's best response to Right is Down, and B's best response to Down is Right — both conditions hold here too. This game has two Nash equilibria: (Up, Left) and (Down, Right).

Every dominant-strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium (if Confess is dominant for both players in Section 10.2's example, (Confess, Confess) is trivially a mutual best response), but not every Nash equilibrium involves dominant strategies — many games (like the one above) have Nash equilibria without any dominant strategy at all.

docs.title: 10.4 The Prisoner's Dilemma
docs.text:
The prisoner's dilemma is the most famous game in economics: a game in which each player has a dominant strategy, but the resulting equilibrium leaves both players worse off than if they had cooperated.

The classic prisoner's dilemma

Two suspects are held separately. Each can Confess (implicating the other) or Stay Silent. Payoffs are years of prison avoided (higher is better):

B: Confess B: Stay Silent A: Confess (−5, −5) (0, −10) A: Stay Silent (−10, 0) (−1, −1)

As shown in Section 10.2, Confess is the dominant strategy for both players, so the Nash equilibrium is (Confess, Confess), giving each player −5. Yet (Silent, Silent) would have given each player −1 — strictly better for both. Rational, self-interested behavior by each individual player produces a worse outcome for both than mutual cooperation would have.

The Single Most Important Insight in This Chapter

Sit with that result for a second. Each player reasoned perfectly in their own self-interest, and the two of them together still landed somewhere worse than if they'd both just cooperated. Individually rational behavior and a collectively good outcome are not the same thing — and a huge share of economics lives in exactly that gap.

The prisoner's dilemma structure explains the cartel instability from Chapter 9: each cartel member's dominant strategy is to "cheat" (produce more than its quota) regardless of what the other does, yet mutual cheating leaves both firms worse off than if both had honored the cartel agreement.

Oligopoly Cartel Prisoner's Dilemma Equivalent Honor the quota Stay Silent Cheat on the quota Confess Mutual cheating (Nash equilibrium) Mutual confession Mutual cartel compliance (better for both, but not an equilibrium) Mutual silence

docs.title: 10.5 Coordination Games
docs.text:
Not every game is a prisoner's dilemma. In a coordination game, players benefit from matching each other's choice, and there is no built-in conflict of interest pulling them toward a worse joint outcome.

Pure coordination: choosing a technology standard

B: Format X B: Format Y A: Format X (10, 10) (0, 0) A: Format Y (0, 0) (10, 10)

Both (Format X, Format X) and (Format Y, Format Y) are Nash equilibria — each player is happy as long as they match the other. The challenge is not conflicting interests but agreeing on which equilibrium to coordinate on.

A variant, the battle of the sexes, adds a mild conflict of interest on top of the coordination problem: both players prefer to be together over being apart, but each has a different preferred activity.

Battle of the sexes

B: Opera B: Game A: Opera (3, 2) (0, 0) A: Game (0, 0) (2, 3)

(Opera, Opera) and (Game, Game) are both Nash equilibria. A prefers the first, B prefers the second — unlike the prisoner's dilemma, both equilibria are individually rational outcomes; the difficulty is purely about which equilibrium the two players land on, not whether to cooperate at all.

docs.title: 10.6 Repeated Games and Cooperation
docs.text:
The one-shot prisoner's dilemma predicts that players never cooperate. But in a repeated game — the same players interacting over and over — cooperation can emerge as an equilibrium, because players can reward cooperation and punish defection in future rounds.

The best-known cooperative strategy in a repeated prisoner's dilemma is tit-for-tat: cooperate on the first round, then on every subsequent round do whatever the opponent did in the previous round.

Why repetition changes the outcome

In a one-shot game, cheating has no future cost. In a repeated game (with no fixed, known end date, or an indefinite/infinite horizon), cheating today can trigger retaliation tomorrow, reducing all future payoffs. If players value the future enough (a high enough discount factor), the threat of future punishment can make "honor the cartel quota" (or "stay silent") a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game — even though "cheat" remains the dominant strategy in any single round viewed in isolation.

This is precisely how real-world cartels (Chapter 9) sometimes sustain cooperation for years: firms interact repeatedly, can observe (with a lag) whether rivals are cheating on output quotas, and can credibly threaten a price war in response — converting a one-shot incentive to cheat into a repeated-game equilibrium of sustained cooperation.

Finite, known-end games unravel

If both players know the game will be played a fixed, known number of rounds, the logic of repeated cooperation can fail: in the last round there is no future to protect, so both players defect (as in the one-shot game); knowing this, both defect in the second-to-last round too (since the last round's cooperation incentive is already gone); this reasoning unravels all the way back to the first round. Sustained cooperation is most robust when the game's end is uncertain or indefinitely distant.

docs.title: 10.7 Sequential Games and Backward Induction
docs.text:
In a sequential game, players move one after another (rather than simultaneously), and later movers can observe earlier moves before choosing their own. Sequential games are typically represented with a game tree, and solved using backward induction: start at the final decision nodes and work backward, at each step assuming every player will choose the best available action given what will happen afterward.

Working Backward Feels Backward — That's Normal

If "start at the end and work backward" feels disorienting at first, you're not alone — most people need to trace through one full example before it clicks. Just hold onto the rule: solve the last decision first, treat that solved decision as a known fact, then solve the decision one step earlier, and repeat until you're back at move one.

A simple market-entry game, solved by backward induction

An entrant firm decides whether to Enter a market or Stay Out. If it Enters, the incumbent firm decides whether to Fight (start a price war) or Accommodate (share the market peacefully).

Payoffs (Entrant, Incumbent):

  • Stay Out: (0, 50)
  • Enter, then Incumbent Fights: (−10, 10)
  • Enter, then Incumbent Accommodates: (20, 20)

Backward induction, step 1 (last mover first): if the entrant has already entered, what does the incumbent do? Fight gives the incumbent 10; Accommodate gives the incumbent 20. The incumbent's best response to entry is Accommodate.

Backward induction, step 2 (work back to the first mover): knowing the incumbent will Accommodate (not Fight) if it enters, the entrant compares Enter-then-Accommodate (20) to Stay Out (0). The entrant's best choice is Enter.

Solution: Entrant enters; Incumbent accommodates. Note that a threat to "Fight" announced before the entrant decides would not be credible — once entry has actually occurred, fighting (10) is worse for the incumbent than accommodating (20), so a rational entrant should ignore the threat. This is the concept of a non-credible threat.

Backward induction is the sequential-game counterpart to Nash equilibrium: it rules out strategies (like "I'll fight if you enter") that are not actually optimal when the moment to carry them out arrives.

docs.title: 10.8 Applications: Oligopoly, Auctions, and Bargaining
docs.text:
Game theory's tools recur across economics:

  • Oligopoly (Chapter 9): The Cournot and Bertrand models are simultaneous games solved for Nash equilibrium; cartel instability is a repeated prisoner's dilemma; entry deterrence and predatory pricing are sequential games solved by backward induction.
  • Auctions: In a sealed-bid, second-price auction (the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own), a bidder's dominant strategy is to bid exactly their true value for the item — bidding higher risks overpaying if you win, and bidding lower only risks losing an auction you'd have profited from, with no offsetting benefit, since the price you pay is set by the other bidder either way.
  • Bargaining: Sequential bargaining (e.g., alternating-offer negotiations over a fixed sum of money) is solved by backward induction from an assumed final deadline, showing that the party with more patience (or a credible threat to walk away) secures a larger share — a formal foundation for real-world negotiation strategy.

Don't Import First-Price Instincts Into a Second-Price Auction

A common mix-up: carrying over the instinct to "shade your bid below your value," which is smart advice for a first-price auction, into a second-price auction, where it's exactly wrong. Because the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own, shading down only risks losing a profitable auction for no benefit. Bid your true value, every time.

The common thread

Every application above shares the same discipline: write down who moves, what they can do, and what they get — then find the strategy combination from which no one wants to unilaterally deviate (Nash equilibrium for simultaneous games; backward induction for sequential ones). This same discipline, applied to firms rather than individuals, is exactly what powered the oligopoly models of Chapter 9.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Game A strategic situation defined by players, strategies, and payoffs Payoff matrix A table showing each player's payoff for every combination of strategies Dominant strategy A strategy that is a player's best choice regardless of what others do Dominated strategy A strategy that is always worse than some alternative, regardless of others' choices Nash equilibrium A strategy combination in which no player can gain by unilaterally changing strategy Prisoner's dilemma A game where dominant strategies lead to an outcome worse for both players than mutual cooperation Coordination game A game where players benefit from matching each other's choice Battle of the sexes A coordination game with a mild conflict over which equilibrium is reached Repeated game A game played multiple times by the same players, enabling reward/punishment strategies Tit-for-tat A repeated-game strategy: cooperate first, then mirror the opponent's previous move Sequential game A game in which players move in turns, observing earlier moves Backward induction Solving a sequential game by reasoning from the last move backward to the first Non-credible threat An announced future action that would not actually be optimal to carry out

docs.title: Problem 1 — Dominant Strategy
docs.text:
B: Advertise B: Don't Advertise A: Advertise (4, 4) (8, 2) A: Don't Advertise (2, 8) (6, 6)

a) Does Firm A have a dominant strategy? Find it. b) Does Firm B have a dominant strategy? c) What is the Nash equilibrium? Is it the best joint outcome for both firms?

Solution

a) If B Advertises, A's best response is Advertise (4 > 2). If B Doesn't Advertise, A's best response is Advertise (8 > 6). Advertise is A's dominant strategy.

b) By the matrix's symmetry, Advertise is also B's dominant strategy.

c) The Nash equilibrium is (Advertise, Advertise), giving each firm a payoff of 4. This is not the best joint outcome — (Don't Advertise, Don't Advertise) gives each firm 6. This is a prisoner's dilemma: both firms would be better off if neither advertised, but each firm's dominant strategy leads them to advertise anyway.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Finding Nash Equilibria
docs.text:
B: Left B: Right A: Up (6, 6) (0, 5) A: Down (5, 0) (4, 4)

Find all Nash equilibria of this game.

Solution

Check A's best responses: if B plays Left, A's best response is Up (6 > 5). If B plays Right, A's best response is Down (4 > 0).

Check B's best responses: if A plays Up, B's best response is Left (6 > 5). If A plays Down, B's best response is Right (4 > 0).

(Up, Left): A's best response to Left is Up ✓, and B's best response to Up is Left ✓ — this is a Nash equilibrium.

(Down, Right): A's best response to Right is Down ✓, and B's best response to Down is Right ✓ — this is also a Nash equilibrium.

There are two Nash equilibria: (Up, Left) with payoffs (6,6), and (Down, Right) with payoffs (4,4). Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, players here have aligned interests — both prefer (Up, Left) — but must still coordinate on it.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Repeated Games
docs.text:
Two firms play the cartel game from Chapter 9 repeatedly, with no fixed end date. Firm A proposes a tit-for-tat strategy: "I will honor the quota as long as you do; if you ever cheat, I will cheat in every round after that."

a) Explain intuitively why this threat can sustain cooperation when a one-shot game cannot. b) What condition on how much firms value future profits (relative to today's profits) is needed for this to work?

Solution

a) In a one-shot game, cheating has no consequence — there is no "tomorrow" in which to be punished. In a repeated game, cheating today triggers retaliation (mutual cheating) in all future rounds, reducing every future period's profit. If the loss from future retaliation outweighs the one-time gain from cheating today, honoring the quota becomes individually rational.

b) Firms must value future profits highly enough (a sufficiently high discount factor/low impatience) that the discounted sum of lower profits from permanent future retaliation exceeds the one-time gain from cheating now. If firms are very impatient (heavily discount the future), the one-time gain from cheating dominates, and cooperation unravels even in a repeated game.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Backward Induction
docs.text:
A government decides whether to Subsidize a new industry or Not Subsidize. If subsidized, a firm then decides whether to Invest or Not Invest. Payoffs (Government, Firm):

  • Not Subsidize: (0, 0)
  • Subsidize, then firm Invests: (10, 15)
  • Subsidize, then firm Does Not Invest: (−5, 5)

a) Using backward induction, what does the firm do if subsidized? b) What does the government do, anticipating the firm's response? c) Is there any risk of a non-credible element in this game, and if so, where?

Solution

a) If subsidized, the firm compares Invest (15) to Not Invest (5). The firm's best response is to Invest.

b) Anticipating that the firm will Invest if subsidized, the government compares Subsidize-then-Invest (10) to Not Subsidize (0). The government's best choice is to Subsidize.

c) The risk runs the other way: if the firm could credibly threaten "I won't invest even if subsidized" before the government decides, the government would compare Subsidize-then-No-Invest (−5) to Not Subsidize (0) and choose Not Subsidize. But once the subsidy is actually granted, the firm's best response is to Invest (15 > 5) — so a pre-subsidy threat not to invest would not be credible, and backward induction correctly predicts the firm invests once the subsidy is in place.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Second-Price Auctions
docs.text:
In a sealed-bid, second-price auction, explain why bidding exactly your true value for the item is a dominant strategy, using the logic of "what happens if I bid higher" and "what happens if I bid lower."

Solution

If you bid above your true value and win, you might end up paying a price (the second-highest bid) that exceeds your own value — a loss you would have avoided by bidding your true value, since in a second-price auction your own bid never sets the price you pay, only whether you win. If you bid below your true value, you risk losing the auction to a bid between your lowered bid and your true value — an auction you would have won (and profited from) had you bid your true value. In neither direction does bidding anything other than your true value ever help, and in both directions it can hurt — so bidding your true value is a dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do.

You Can Now Formally Out-Think the Room

From payoff matrices to Nash equilibrium to backward induction through a full game tree — you just learned to formally predict how strategic situations resolve, not just guess at them. That's the exact toolkit behind cartel breakdowns, technology-standard wars, and why second-price auctions are designed the way they are.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 11: Factor Markets, we turn from the markets for goods and services to the markets for the inputs that produce them — labor, capital, and land — where firms are no longer sellers but buyers, hiring workers and renting capital according to the same marginal principles developed throughout this unit.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain why the demand for labor and other inputs is a derived demand
  2. Calculate marginal revenue product (MRP) and use it to find a firm's profit-maximizing hiring level
  3. Derive a firm's labor demand curve and explain what shifts it
  4. Analyze the labor supply decision as a work-leisure trade-off
  5. Determine the equilibrium wage and employment level in a competitive labor market
  6. Contrast competitive labor markets with monopsony and explain why monopsony depresses wages and employment
  7. Explain how interest rates allocate capital, and distinguish economic rent from other factor payments

Same Marginal Logic, Brand New Markets

Every choice has a trade-off — and up to now, you've mostly analyzed that trade-off from the seller's side of an output market. This chapter flips the lens: firms become buyers, hiring workers and renting capital, and the same marginal reasoning you already mastered — set marginal benefit equal to marginal cost — explains wages, interest rates, and rents too. You already know more of this chapter than you think.

docs.title: 11.1 Input Markets and Derived Demand
docs.text:
So far we have studied markets for output — the goods and services firms sell to consumers. This chapter turns to markets for the inputs, or factors of production, that firms use to produce that output: labor, capital, land, and entrepreneurship. The prices of these factors — wages, interest rates, rents, and profits — determine how income is distributed across the economy.

Input markets differ from output markets in one crucial way: nobody wants an input for its own sake. A firm does not hire a worker because it enjoys having workers around; it hires a worker because that worker helps produce a good the firm can sell. This gives rise to the concept of derived demand: the demand for an input is derived from the demand for the output it helps produce.

Derived demand in practice

When consumer demand for new housing rises, the demand for construction workers, lumber, and land for development all rise with it — not because anyone values carpenters or two-by-fours intrinsically, but because they are necessary to produce houses. When housing demand collapses (as in 2008), derived demand for construction labor collapses too.

This linkage means every input market is connected to some output market. To understand the labor market for software engineers, you must understand the demand for software; to understand the market for farmland, you must understand the demand for food.

Every Input Curve Has an Output Market Hiding Inside It

Here's the mental model to carry through this whole chapter: nobody ever demands an input for its own sake. Every curve you draw for labor, capital, or land secretly has an output market baked into it — shift the demand for houses, and you've just shifted the demand for construction workers, lumber, and land, whether or not you drew that connection explicitly.

docs.title: Defining MRP
docs.text:
How many workers should a profit-maximizing firm hire? The key concept is marginal revenue product (MRP): the additional revenue a firm earns from employing one more unit of an input.

\[MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\]

where \(MP_L\) is the marginal product of labor (the extra output produced by one more worker) and \(MR\) is the marginal revenue the firm earns from selling one more unit of output. In a perfectly competitive output market, \(MR = P\), so:

\[MRP_L = MP_L \times P\]

MRP tells the firm exactly what an additional worker is worth to it in dollar terms.

docs.title: A Worked Numerical Example
docs.text:
Consider a competitive bakery selling bread at \(P = \$4\) per loaf. The table below shows how output responds as the bakery adds workers, holding its ovens (capital) fixed.

Workers (\(L\)) Total Product (loaves/day) Marginal Product (\(MP_L\)) MRP (\(MP_L \times \$4\)) 0 0 — — 1 20 20 $80 2 36 16 $64 3 48 12 $48 4 56 8 $32 5 60 4 $16 6 60 0 $0

Notice that marginal product falls as more workers are added — this is diminishing marginal returns (Chapter 5), which arises because the fixed number of ovens means each additional worker has less capital to work with.

docs.title: The Hiring Rule
docs.text:
A profit-maximizing firm keeps hiring workers as long as each additional worker adds more to revenue than to cost. The firm hires up to the point where:

\[MRP_L = w\]

where \(w\) is the wage rate. If \(MRP_L > w\), the worker generates more revenue than they cost — hire them. If \(MRP_L < w\), the worker costs more than they generate — do not hire them (or lay them off).

Applying the hiring rule

Suppose the market wage for bakery workers is \(w = \$50\)/day. Using the table above:

  • Hiring the 3rd worker: \(MRP_L = \$48 < \$50\). Not worth it — stop before the 3rd worker.
  • Hiring the 2nd worker: \(MRP_L = \$64 > \$50\). Worth it — hire the 2nd worker.

The bakery hires 2 workers, since that is the largest \(L\) for which \(MRP_L \geq w\). At \(w = \$32\), the bakery would hire 4 workers instead (\(MRP_L = \$32\) at \(L=4\)).

This is the same logic as the MR = MC rule from Chapter 6, applied to an input rather than an output: hire inputs up to the point where the marginal benefit (MRP) equals the marginal cost (the wage).

docs.title: The Labor Demand Curve
docs.text:
Because the hiring rule says "hire until \(MRP_L = w\)," the MRP curve is the firm's labor demand curve. It is downward-sloping because \(MP_L\) diminishes as more labor is added (holding capital fixed).

\[Q_L^d = f(w), \quad \frac{\partial Q_L^d}{\partial w} < 0\]

A market labor demand curve is the horizontal sum of all firms' individual MRP curves in that labor market.

docs.title: What Shifts Labor Demand?
docs.text:
Determinant Effect on Labor Demand Increase in output price (\(P\)) Demand increases (MRP = \(MP_L \times P\) rises) Increase in productivity (\(MP_L\)), e.g., better technology or training Demand increases More capital (complementary input) Demand increases, if capital and labor are complements Automation that substitutes for labor Demand decreases Increase in demand for the final good Demand increases (derived demand)

Technology and labor demand: two directions

A new software tool that lets each accountant process twice as many tax returns raises each accountant's \(MP_L\), shifting labor demand for accountants to the right (more accountants demanded at every wage, assuming the firm cannot shrink too much). But self-checkout kiosks are a direct substitute for cashiers, shifting labor demand for cashiers to the left.

docs.title: The Individual's Decision
docs.text:
Workers must decide how to divide their 24 hours between labor (which earns income to buy goods) and leisure (unpaid time, which they also value). The wage rate \(w\) is the opportunity cost of leisure — every hour not worked is an hour of wages foregone.

A higher wage has two competing effects on how many hours a person chooses to work:

  1. Substitution effect: A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, inducing people to work more hours (substitute away from leisure toward labor).
  2. Income effect: A higher wage raises income at any given number of hours, making people feel richer and want more leisure (assuming leisure is a normal good), inducing them to work fewer hours.

docs.title: The Backward-Bending Labor Supply Curve
docs.text:
At low wages, the substitution effect typically dominates — as wages rise, people work more. But past some wage level, the income effect can dominate — people are rich enough that they "buy back" leisure time by working less even as wages continue to rise. This produces a labor supply curve that slopes upward at first, then bends backward.

Backward-bending supply in practice

A surgeon earning $500/hour may choose to work fewer hours than one earning $300/hour, if at the higher wage she can meet her desired income target more quickly and prefers additional leisure. Many lottery winners also reduce hours worked, consistent with a pure income effect with no change in the wage at all.

Don't Confuse the Individual Curve With the Market Curve

A common mix-up: assuming every worker's supply curve bends backward, and then confusing that backward-bending individual curve with the upward-sloping market curve covered next. Most workers, most of the time, sit on the ordinary upward-sloping portion — the backward bend is a high-wage phenomenon that shows up for only some workers at some wage levels.

docs.title: Market Labor Supply
docs.text: While an individual's supply curve may bend backward, the market labor supply curve is typically upward-sloping: a higher wage draws new workers into the labor force (increasing labor force participation) even if some existing workers choose to work fewer hours.

docs.title: Finding the Equilibrium Wage
docs.text:
In a competitive labor market — many buyers (firms) and many sellers (workers), none with market power — the equilibrium wage \(w^*\) and employment level \(L^*\) are found just as in Chapter 2, by setting labor demand equal to labor supply:

\[L^d(w) = L^s(w)\]

Solving for equilibrium

Suppose the labor market for baristas in a city has:

\[L^d = 2000 - 100w \qquad L^s = -400 + 150w\]

Setting \(L^d = L^s\):

\[2000 - 100w = -400 + 150w$$ $$2400 = 250w$$ $$w^* = \$9.60/\text{hour}, \qquad L^* = 2000 - 100(9.60) = 1040 \text{ workers}\]

A Ten-Second Check on Any Labor-Market Equilibrium

After solving for \(w^*\), plug it back into the demand equation and the supply equation separately. If they don't land on the same \(L^*\), you made an algebra error somewhere upstream — this quick check catches most mistakes before they cost you the whole problem.

docs.title: Why Wages Differ Across Markets
docs.text:
Competitive labor markets predict a single wage for a homogeneous type of labor. In reality, wages differ enormously across occupations because:

  • Differences in MRP: workers with higher skill or productivity command higher MRP and thus higher wages.
  • Human capital (Section 11.9): education and training raise \(MP_L\).
  • Compensating differentials: unpleasant, dangerous, or inconvenient jobs (night-shift work, offshore oil rigs) must pay more to attract workers, compensating for the non-wage disadvantages.
  • Labor market frictions and discrimination: barriers to entry, imperfect information, and discrimination can prevent wages from equalizing even for similarly productive workers.

docs.title: 11.6 Monopsony: A Single Buyer of Labor
What Is Monopsony?
docs.text:
A monopsony is a market with only one (or a dominant) buyer of an input — the mirror image of a monopoly, which has only one seller of output. Classic examples include a single large factory or hospital that is the overwhelmingly dominant employer in an isolated town, or historically, company towns where one firm owned the mine, the housing, and the store.

Because a monopsonist is the only buyer, it faces the entire upward-sloping market labor supply curve, not a flat wage set by the market. To hire one more worker, it must raise the wage for all its workers, not just the marginal hire. This means the monopsonist's marginal cost of labor (MCL) exceeds the wage:

\[MCL > w\]

Monopsony Is Monopoly's Mirror Image

Notice the symmetry: a monopolist's marginal revenue falls below price because selling one more unit forces the price down on all units sold. A monopsonist's marginal cost of labor rises above the wage because hiring one more worker forces the wage up for all workers already employed. Same underlying mechanic, opposite side of the market.

docs.title: The Monopsony Hiring Rule
docs.text:
A profit-maximizing monopsonist hires where \(MRP_L = MCL\) (marginal benefit equals true marginal cost) — but then pays only the wage on the labor supply curve at that quantity, which is less than \(MRP_L\).

Market Structure Hiring Rule Wage Paid Competitive labor market \(MRP_L = w\) \(w = MRP_L\) Monopsony \(MRP_L = MCL\) \(w < MRP_L\), read off the supply curve

Monopsony depresses both wages and employment

Relative to a competitive labor market, a monopsonist hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage than the competitive outcome. Just as monopoly creates deadweight loss in output markets by restricting output, monopsony creates deadweight loss in input markets by restricting employment.

docs.title: Numerical Example
docs.text:
Suppose a monopsonist faces labor supply \(w = 10 + 0.02L\) (so the wage it must pay rises as it hires more).

Three Small Moves, Not One Big One

If deriving MCL from total labor cost feels like a lot at once, break it into three small moves: multiply wage by \(L\) to get total cost, take one derivative, then set the result equal to \(MRP_L\). It's the same three-move pattern as the Cournot derivation back in Chapter 9 — you've already done this.

Its total labor cost is \(TLC = wL = (10 + 0.02L)L = 10L + 0.02L^2\), so:

\[MCL = \frac{d(TLC)}{dL} = 10 + 0.04L\]

Suppose \(MRP_L = 100 - 0.04L\). Setting \(MRP_L = MCL\):

\[100 - 0.04L = 10 + 0.04L\] \[90 = 0.08L\] \[L^* = 1125\]

The wage paid is read off the supply curve at \(L = 1125\):

\[w^* = 10 + 0.02(1125) = \$32.50\]

But the value of the marginal worker is \(MRP_L = 100 - 0.04(1125) = \$55\). The gap between \(MRP_L = \$55\) and \(w^* = \$32.50\) is the hallmark of monopsony power — the firm pays workers less than the value they create. Had this been a competitive market (hiring where \(MRP_L = w\) directly), employment and wages would both have been higher.

docs.title: Policy Responses
docs.text: A minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can, in a pure monopsony model (unlike in a competitive market), increase both the wage and employment simultaneously, because it forces the monopsonist closer to the competitive outcome rather than creating a surplus of unhired workers. This is one reason labor economists' views on minimum-wage effects depend heavily on how competitive they believe local labor markets actually are.

docs.title: Capital as a Factor
docs.text: Capital refers to produced inputs used to make other goods — machinery, buildings, and equipment. Firms "rent" capital in the sense of paying for its use, whether they lease it or purchase it with borrowed funds. The interest rate (\(r\)) is the price of capital — more precisely, the price of loanable funds used to finance capital investment.

docs.title: The Investment Decision
docs.text:
A firm invests in a piece of capital if the expected return exceeds the cost of financing it. Formally, a firm should invest in a project as long as:

\[\text{Expected Marginal Rate of Return} \geq r\]

This means capital, like labor, has its own downward-sloping demand curve — the lower the interest rate, the more investment projects become profitable, so the quantity of capital demanded rises as \(r\) falls.

docs.title: Present Value
docs.text:
Because capital investments pay off over time, firms must compare a dollar today with a dollar in the future. The present value (PV) of a future payment \(FV\) received in \(t\) years, discounted at rate \(r\), is:

\[PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^t}\]

Should the firm buy the machine?

A firm can buy a machine today for $10,000. The machine will generate $11,500 in revenue one year from now, and then be worthless. The market interest rate is 10%.

\[PV = \frac{\$11{,}500}{(1+0.10)^1} = \frac{\$11{,}500}{1.10} = \$10{,}454.55\]

Since the present value of the machine's payoff ($10,454.55) exceeds its $10,000 cost, the firm should buy the machine — the net present value is positive (\(\$454.55\)).

docs.title: Loanable Funds Market
docs.text: The equilibrium interest rate is determined by the supply of loanable funds (household saving) and the demand for loanable funds (firm investment and government borrowing), exactly analogous to the supply-and-demand framework of Chapter 2, with \(r\) playing the role of price.

docs.title: Land Supply Is (Nearly) Fixed
docs.text: Land, in the economic sense, refers to natural resources whose total supply cannot be increased by human effort — most importantly, the physical land itself. Because the aggregate supply of land is essentially fixed regardless of price, the supply curve for land is vertical (perfectly inelastic).

docs.title: Economic Rent
docs.text:
Economic rent is the payment to any factor of production whose supply is fixed (or nearly fixed) — a payment determined entirely by demand, since supply cannot respond. Because supply is vertical, any payment above the bare minimum needed to keep the resource in its current use is pure economic rent; the entire price paid for the use of the land is, in effect, rent.

\[\text{Rent} = \text{entire market-clearing payment, since } Q_s \text{ is fixed}\]

Economic rent for prime farmland

Prime farmland near a growing city has a fixed supply. As the city's population grows, demand for that land rises (both for farming and for development), pushing up the rental price — but no more of this specific land can ever be created. The entire increase in rental price is economic rent: it rewards owning a scarce, fixed resource, not any new cost of production.

The concept of economic rent generalizes beyond literal land: any payment to a resource in excess of what is needed to keep it in its current use — a star athlete's salary beyond what would keep them playing, a uniquely located retail storefront — is also called economic rent.

docs.title: Education and Training as Investment
docs.text:
Human capital is the stock of skills, education, training, and experience embodied in workers that raises their productivity (\(MP_L\)) and therefore their MRP and wages. Human capital theory treats education and training as an investment decision, analogous to a firm's capital investment decision in Section 11.7: incur a cost now (tuition, foregone wages while studying) in exchange for higher earnings later.

A rational worker invests in education as long as the present value of the additional future earnings exceeds the cost of acquiring the education:

\[PV(\text{additional lifetime earnings}) > \text{Cost of education (tuition + foregone wages)}\]

The college decision as human capital investment

A student forgoes four years of full-time wages (say $35,000/year = $140,000 total opportunity cost) and pays tuition (say $40,000) to earn a college degree, for a total cost of $180,000. If the degree raises her expected lifetime earnings by a present value of $500,000, human capital theory predicts she should make the investment — the returns substantially exceed the costs.

docs.title: Why Does Education Raise Wages?
docs.text:
Two leading explanations exist, and they are not mutually exclusive:

  1. Human capital (productivity) view: Education directly raises a worker's skills and productivity (\(MP_L\)), raising MRP and therefore wages.
  2. Signaling view: Education may not raise productivity much directly, but completing a rigorous degree signals to employers that a worker is capable, disciplined, and intelligent — traits employers cannot observe directly but value highly.

Both views predict that educated workers earn more; they differ on why, with important policy implications for how much a given investment in education will raise economy-wide productivity versus merely reshuffling who gets which job.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Derived Demand Demand for an input that arises from demand for the output it helps produce Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) The additional revenue from employing one more unit of an input; \(MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\) Marginal Product of Labor (\(MP_L\)) The additional output produced by one more unit of labor Hiring Rule A firm hires an input up to the point where $MRP = $ input price Labor Demand Curve Equivalent to the MRP curve; shows quantity of labor demanded at each wage Work-Leisure Trade-off The decision of how to divide time between paid labor and unpaid leisure Substitution Effect (labor supply) A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, inducing more work Income Effect (labor supply) A higher wage raises income, inducing more leisure (fewer hours worked) Backward-Bending Labor Supply An individual supply curve that slopes up then bends backward at high wages Monopsony A market with a single (or dominant) buyer of an input Marginal Cost of Labor (MCL) The monopsonist's true marginal cost of hiring one more worker, exceeding the wage Interest Rate (\(r\)) The price of loanable funds; the cost of financing capital investment Present Value (PV) The value today of a future payment, discounted at the interest rate Economic Rent Payment to a factor in fixed supply, determined purely by demand Human Capital The stock of skills, education, and experience that raises worker productivity

docs.title: Problem 1 — Marginal Revenue Product
docs.text:
A furniture shop sells chairs at a competitive price of \(P = \$60\). Labor is the only variable input.

Workers Total Chairs/Week \(MP_L\) \(MRP_L\) 1 10 — — 2 18 — — 3 24 — — 4 28 — —

a) Fill in the \(MP_L\) and \(MRP_L\) columns. b) If the wage is $360/week, how many workers should the shop hire? c) If the wage falls to $240/week, how many workers should the shop hire?

Solution

a)

Workers Total Chairs \(MP_L\) \(MRP_L\) 1 10 10 $600 2 18 8 $480 3 24 6 $360 4 28 4 $240

b) At \(w = \$360\): hire up to where \(MRP_L \geq w\). \(MRP_L = \$360\) at the 3rd worker, and $240 < $360 at the 4th worker, so hire 3 workers.

c) At \(w = \$240\): \(MRP_L = \$240\) at the 4th worker, which just covers the wage, so hire 4 workers.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Labor Market Equilibrium
docs.text:
The labor market for registered nurses in a metro area is described by:

\[L^d = 5000 - 100w \qquad L^s = 500 + 150w\]

a) Find the equilibrium wage and employment level. b) If a new nursing school graduates an additional cohort, shifting labor supply to \(L^s = 1000 + 150w\), find the new equilibrium. c) Explain intuitively why the wage changed as it did.

Solution

a) Set \(L^d = L^s\): \(5000 - 100w = 500 + 150w \Rightarrow 4500 = 250w \Rightarrow w^* = \$18, \; L^* = 5000 - 100(18) = 3200\).

b) Set \(5000 - 100w = 1000 + 150w \Rightarrow 4000 = 250w \Rightarrow w^* = \$16, \; L^* = 5000 - 100(16) = 3400\).

c) Labor supply shifted right (more nurses available at every wage), creating a temporary surplus at the old wage of $18. The wage falls to $16 to clear the market, and equilibrium employment rises from 3200 to 3400.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Monopsony
docs.text:
A monopsonist coal mine is the only employer in an isolated town. It faces labor supply \(w = 15 + 0.01L\) and has \(MRP_L = 95 - 0.02L\).

a) Derive the marginal cost of labor (MCL) curve. b) Find the profit-maximizing level of employment. c) Find the wage the monopsonist actually pays. d) Compare this wage to the value of the marginal worker's output (\(MRP_L\)) at that employment level, and explain the gap.

Solution

a) \(TLC = wL = (15 + 0.01L)L = 15L + 0.01L^2 \Rightarrow MCL = 15 + 0.02L\).

b) Set \(MRP_L = MCL\): \(95 - 0.02L = 15 + 0.02L \Rightarrow 80 = 0.04L \Rightarrow L^* = 2000\).

c) \(w^* = 15 + 0.01(2000) = \$35\).

d) \(MRP_L\) at \(L = 2000\) is \(95 - 0.02(2000) = \$55\). The monopsonist pays workers $35 but each generates $55 in value — a $20 gap per worker. This gap is the essence of monopsony power: because the firm is the only buyer, it can pay workers less than their marginal contribution to revenue, and it also hires fewer workers than a competitive market would.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Present Value and Investment
docs.text:
A firm is considering a machine costing $50,000 today. It will produce a single payoff of $58,000 one year from now.

a) If the interest rate is 8%, should the firm buy the machine? Show the present value calculation. b) If the interest rate rises to 20%, should the firm buy the machine? c) Explain, in words, why rising interest rates reduce investment.

Solution

a) \(PV = \dfrac{58{,}000}{1.08} = \$53{,}703.70\). Since \(PV > \$50{,}000\) cost, the firm should buy the machine (positive NPV of $3,703.70).

b) \(PV = \dfrac{58{,}000}{1.20} = \$48{,}333.33\). Since \(PV < \$50{,}000\) cost, the firm should not buy the machine (negative NPV of -$1,666.67).

c) A higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of tying up funds in a project (or raises the cost of borrowing to finance it), so it discounts future payoffs more heavily. Projects that were profitable at a low interest rate become unprofitable at a higher one, so investment demand falls as interest rates rise.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Economic Rent
docs.text:
A unique beachfront lot can only be used for one restaurant. Three restaurant chains bid for the annual lease: Chain A values it at $200,000/year, Chain B at $150,000/year, Chain C at $90,000/year. The lot has no alternative use and costs the owner nothing to maintain.

a) What is the equilibrium annual lease payment, assuming competitive bidding? b) How much of this payment is economic rent? Explain why. c) Suppose a new highway exit dramatically increases foot traffic near the lot, raising each chain's valuation by $50,000. What happens to the rent, and why does supply play no role?

Solution

a) Competitive bidding drives the lease price up to the second-highest valuation (since Chain A will outbid Chain B by any amount up to $150,000, but has no reason to pay more than necessary to win) — approximately $150,000/year (the lot goes to Chain A at a price just above Chain B's valuation).

b) Because the lot's supply is fixed (there is exactly one such lot and no cost of maintaining it), the entire $150,000 payment is economic rent — it does not reflect any production cost, only the value of controlling a scarce resource.

c) All valuations rise by $50,000 (Chain A to $250,000, Chain B to $200,000), so the equilibrium rent rises to approximately $200,000/year. Supply plays no role because the lot's supply curve is vertical — the quantity of this specific lot cannot increase no matter how valuable it becomes; the entire effect of increased demand falls on price (rent), not quantity.

You Just Priced Every Factor of Production

Labor, capital, and land each have their own market, their own logic, and their own quirks — monopsony power, present value, fixed supply — and you worked through all of them. You can now explain why wages differ, why interest rates matter for investment, and why a beachfront lot commands a premium that has nothing to do with the cost of building on it.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 12: Market Failures, we step back from well-functioning competitive markets to examine why markets sometimes fail to deliver efficient outcomes — and what role government can play in response.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
