After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the conditions required for competitive markets to be efficient, and identify when those conditions break down
  2. Distinguish negative and positive externalities and explain why each leads markets away from the efficient outcome
  3. Define public goods and common-pool resources using the non-excludability and non-rivalry criteria, and explain the free-rider problem and the tragedy of the commons
  4. Explain how information asymmetry can cause markets to fail, including adverse selection and moral hazard
  5. Explain how market power causes inefficiency distinct from the other sources of market failure
  6. Compare taxes, regulation, property rights, and public provision as government responses to market failure
  7. Explain the concept of government failure and why government intervention does not automatically fix market failures

When the Invisible Hand Needs a Nudge

Every choice has a trade-off — and so far this book has mostly shown you markets getting that trade-off right on their own. This chapter is about the cases where they don't: pollution nobody pays for, goods nobody can be excluded from, deals where one side knows something the other doesn't. Understanding exactly why a market fails is the first step toward knowing whether — and how — to fix it.

docs.title: 12.1 When Do Markets Fail?
docs.text:
Chapter 2 showed that competitive markets, left alone, maximize total surplus — they are allocatively efficient. This is sometimes called the First Welfare Theorem: under certain conditions, competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. But those conditions are demanding, and in the real world they frequently do not hold. A market failure occurs whenever the free market, on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently — that is, whenever the price system does not lead to the surplus-maximizing quantity.

The conditions required for market efficiency — and the ways each can break down — are summarized below. This chapter surveys each category at a broad level; Chapter 13 returns to externalities and public goods in much greater depth.

Required Condition for Efficiency What Happens When It Fails Market Failure Category All costs and benefits are borne by buyers and sellers Costs/benefits spill onto third parties Externalities Goods are excludable and rival Goods can be consumed free, or use by one prevents use by others Public goods / common-pool resources Buyers and sellers have equal, sufficient information One side knows more than the other Information asymmetry Many small buyers and sellers, no one with pricing power A single firm (or few firms) controls price Market power

Efficiency is the benchmark, not a guarantee

None of these conditions is guaranteed to hold. Markets for haircuts, running shoes, and most restaurant meals come close to satisfying all four and function efficiently without intervention. Markets for pollution, lighthouses, vaccines, and used cars do not — and that is precisely where this chapter focuses.

Efficiency Was Never Magic — It Was a Checklist

Here's the mental model for this whole chapter: the First Welfare Theorem holds only when all four conditions in that table hold at once. Every topic between here and Section 12.6 is really just "which line of the checklist failed, and what does that specific failure look like?"

docs.title: 12.2 Externalities: Negative and Positive
docs.text: An externality exists when a transaction between a buyer and seller imposes costs or benefits on a third party who is not part of that transaction and whose interests are not reflected in the market price.

docs.title: Negative Externalities
docs.text:
A negative externality imposes a cost on third parties. The classic example is pollution: a factory's private cost of production does not include the cost of the air pollution it imposes on nearby residents. Because the firm does not pay for this cost, its private marginal cost curve lies below the true social marginal cost curve, and the market produces more than the efficient quantity.

\[\text{Social Marginal Cost} = \text{Private Marginal Cost} + \text{External Cost}\]

docs.title: Positive Externalities
docs.text:
A positive externality generates a benefit for third parties. Education is a common example: when you get vaccinated or become more educated, you benefit personally, but society also gains (lower disease transmission, a more informed citizenry, higher productivity of coworkers) in ways the market price does not capture. Because the market ignores this external benefit, the market produces less than the efficient quantity.

\[\text{Social Marginal Benefit} = \text{Private Marginal Benefit} + \text{External Benefit}\]

Everyday externalities

  • Negative: A loud late-night party (noise imposed on neighbors); a factory dumping waste in a river (harm to downstream users); vehicle emissions (climate and health costs borne by everyone).
  • Positive: A beekeeper's bees pollinating a neighboring orchard; a homeowner's beautiful garden raising neighborhood property values; getting a flu vaccine (reduces the chance others get sick).

Chapter 13 develops the full graphical and mathematical apparatus — including Pigouvian taxes, the Coase theorem, and cap-and-trade — for correcting externalities. For now, the key takeaway is the direction of the distortion: negative externalities cause overproduction, positive externalities cause underproduction, relative to the socially efficient level.

docs.title: 12.3 Public Goods: Non-Excludable, Non-Rival
docs.text:
Economists classify goods along two independent dimensions:

  • Excludable: Can the seller prevent people who do not pay from consuming the good?
  • Rival: Does one person's consumption reduce the amount available for others?
Rival Non-Rival Excludable Private goods (a sandwich, a haircut) Club goods (cable TV, a gym membership) Non-Excludable Common-pool resources (ocean fisheries, groundwater) Public goods (national defense, basic research, lighthouses)

Two Yes/No Questions, Four Boxes, No Ambiguity

Here's a fast way to classify any good on an exam: ask two questions in order. "Can the seller stop a non-payer from using it?" settles excludability. "Does my use leave less for you?" settles rivalry. Two yes/no answers drop you straight into the right box of that table.

A pure public good is both non-excludable (you cannot stop someone from consuming it even if they do not pay) and non-rival (one person's use does not diminish another's). National defense is the textbook example: protecting the country protects every resident, whether or not they paid taxes toward it, and one additional resident being "defended" does not reduce the defense available to anyone else.

Because no one can be excluded from enjoying a public good, private firms generally cannot profitably produce it — people have an incentive to free ride, consuming the benefit without paying. This is why public goods are typically funded through taxation and provided by government. Chapter 13 develops the free-rider problem and voting mechanisms for public goods provision in detail.

docs.title: 12.4 Common-Pool Resources and the Tragedy of the Commons
docs.text:
A common-pool resource is rival (one person's use depletes what is available to others) but non-excludable (no one can easily be stopped from using it). Ocean fisheries, groundwater aquifers, and unregulated grazing land are classic examples.

Same 'Non-Excludable' Label, Opposite Problem

Don't let the shared "non-excludable" label fool you into treating public goods and common-pool resources as the same problem. A public good (Section 12.3) is non-rival — my use doesn't reduce yours, so underfunding is the danger, not overuse. A common-pool resource is rival — which is exactly what makes overuse, not underfunding, the central threat here.

The tragedy of the commons describes what happens when a resource is open to all: because no individual user bears the full cost of their own extraction (part of that cost — the depleted resource — is spread across all other users), each person has a private incentive to overuse the resource even though collectively everyone would be better off with restraint. The result is systematic overexploitation and, in extreme cases, collapse of the resource.

Historical and modern tragedies of the commons

  • Atlantic cod fisheries: Decades of unrestricted fishing collapsed cod stocks off Newfoundland in the early 1990s, devastating an industry that had operated for centuries.
  • Groundwater aquifers: Farmers pumping from a shared aquifer have no individual incentive to conserve, since water they leave in the ground may simply be pumped by a neighbor instead.
  • Traffic congestion: Each additional driver on a congested highway imposes delay on all other drivers but bears only a small fraction of that cost personally.

Chapter 13 revisits common-pool resources with specific policy tools (catch shares, water rights, congestion pricing).

docs.title: 12.5 Information Asymmetry
docs.text: Information asymmetry exists when one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other. This can prevent markets from reaching efficient outcomes even when goods are perfectly rival, excludable, and free of externalities.

docs.title: Adverse Selection
docs.text: Adverse selection occurs when the party with less information ends up disproportionately transacting with the "worse" types from the other side, because information about quality is hidden before the transaction. The classic case is George Akerlof's "market for lemons": in a used-car market, sellers know whether their car is reliable or a "lemon," but buyers cannot tell. Buyers, unwilling to pay top price for a car that might be a lemon, offer only an average price — which then drives owners of genuinely good cars out of the market, leaving a disproportionate share of lemons for sale.

docs.title: Moral Hazard
docs.text:
Moral hazard occurs when one party changes their behavior after a transaction in ways the other party cannot observe or verify, because they no longer bear the full consequences of that behavior. A driver with comprehensive insurance may drive somewhat less carefully than an uninsured driver, since the insurer — not the driver — bears most of the cost of an accident.

Before the Deal, or After It? That's the Whole Distinction

Notice that timing is the entire difference between these two ideas: adverse selection is about hidden information before the deal is struck (who you're really dealing with), while moral hazard is about hidden behavior after the deal is struck (what they do once the incentives change). Ask yourself "before or after the contract?" and you'll never mix the two up again.

Looking ahead

Adverse selection and moral hazard, along with signaling and screening as partial solutions, are developed fully in Chapter 14: Information Economics.

docs.title: 12.6 Market Power as a Source of Failure
docs.text:
Chapters 7–9 showed that monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly all involve firms with some ability to set price above marginal cost. This market power is itself a distinct source of inefficiency, separate from externalities, public goods, or information problems.

A monopolist restricts output below the competitive level to raise price, creating deadweight loss: transactions that would make both the firm and some consumers better off simply do not happen, because the monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity is lower than the surplus-maximizing quantity.

\[Q_{monopoly} < Q_{competitive} \implies \text{Deadweight Loss} > 0\]

Unlike externalities, this failure does not require any third party at all — it can occur in a two-party market with no spillovers whatsoever, simply because the seller is not a price-taker. Policy responses include antitrust enforcement, price regulation of natural monopolies, and encouraging entry.

Quantifying the deadweight loss from market power

A market has demand \(P = 100 - Q\) and constant marginal cost \(MC = 20\) (the same cost a competitive industry would face).

Competitive outcome: Price-taking firms produce until \(P = MC\): \(100 - Q = 20 \implies Q_{competitive} = 80\).

Monopoly outcome: A monopolist produces until \(MR = MC\). With linear demand \(P = 100 - Q\), marginal revenue is \(MR = 100 - 2Q\). Setting \(MR = MC\):

\[100 - 2Q = 20 \implies Q_{monopoly} = 40, \qquad P_{monopoly} = 100 - 40 = \$60\]

The monopolist restricts output from 80 units to 40 units and raises price from $20 to $60. The deadweight loss is the triangle between the demand curve and \(MC\), between \(Q_{monopoly}\) and \(Q_{competitive}\):

\[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_{competitive} - Q_{monopoly}) \times (P_{monopoly} - MC) = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 40 = \$800\]

This $800 of surplus is destroyed — not transferred to anyone — purely because output is restricted below the efficient level. Chapter 7 develops this result in full.

docs.title: 12.7 Government Responses to Market Failure
docs.text:
Governments have four broad policy tools for addressing market failures. The right tool depends on which type of failure is present.

Policy Tool Best Suited For Example Taxes (Pigouvian) Negative externalities Carbon tax, cigarette tax Subsidies Positive externalities Vaccine subsidies, R&D tax credits Regulation Externalities, market power, information gaps Emissions standards, mandatory product labeling Property rights Common-pool resources Fishing quotas, tradable water rights Public provision Public goods National defense, public roads, basic research funding Antitrust enforcement Market power Breaking up or blocking anticompetitive mergers

Matching the tool to the failure

A city with heavy traffic congestion (a common-pool resource problem — roads are rival but hard to exclude people from) might use congestion pricing (a form of Pigouvian tax) rather than an R&D subsidy, which would do nothing to address the externality. Conversely, underfunded basic scientific research (a public good with positive externalities) is better addressed through direct public funding than through a tax, since the problem is underprovision, not overprovision.

docs.title: 12.8 Government Failure
docs.text: Government intervention is not automatically an improvement over the market outcome. Government failure occurs when a policy intended to correct a market failure instead makes outcomes worse, or fails to improve them, due to poor information, political incentives, or unintended side effects.

docs.title: Rent-Seeking
docs.text: Rent-seeking is the use of resources to obtain a larger share of existing wealth through the political process, rather than by creating new wealth. Firms may lobby for tariffs, subsidies, or regulations that benefit them specifically, at a cost borne by consumers or taxpayers generally. Because the benefits of rent-seeking are concentrated on a small group (who have a strong incentive to lobby) while the costs are spread across many people (each of whom has little individual incentive to oppose it), rent-seeking policies can persist even when they reduce total surplus.

docs.title: Other Sources of Government Failure
docs.text:
• Imperfect information: Regulators often know less about industry-specific conditions than the firms they regulate.
  • Principal-agent problems: Elected officials and bureaucrats may pursue their own re-election or budget-maximizing incentives rather than the public interest.
  • Unintended consequences: A policy designed to fix one problem may create new distortions elsewhere (e.g., a price ceiling intended to help consumers can create shortages, as seen in Chapter 2's extensions).
  • Regulatory capture: Regulated industries may come to influence or control the agencies meant to regulate them.

Market failure does not imply government success

The existence of a market failure is a necessary but not sufficient condition for government intervention to improve welfare. Economists compare the costs of the market failure against the costs of likely government failure before recommending intervention — sometimes "do nothing" is still the best available option.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Market Failure A situation in which the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently Externality A cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on a third party Negative Externality An external cost; leads to market overproduction Positive Externality An external benefit; leads to market underproduction Excludability Whether non-payers can be prevented from consuming a good Rivalry Whether one person's consumption reduces what is available to others Public Good A good that is both non-excludable and non-rival Common-Pool Resource A good that is rival but non-excludable Tragedy of the Commons Overexploitation of a shared resource because no user bears its full cost Information Asymmetry One party to a transaction has more/better information than the other Adverse Selection Hidden information before a transaction skews the market toward "worse" types Moral Hazard Hidden behavior after a transaction changes incentives because consequences are shared Market Power A firm's ability to set price above marginal cost, causing deadweight loss Pigouvian Tax A tax designed to correct a negative externality Rent-Seeking Using resources to capture existing wealth via politics rather than create new wealth Government Failure A policy intervention that fails to improve, or worsens, an inefficient outcome

docs.title: Problem 1 — Classifying Market Failures
docs.text:
For each scenario, identify the primary type of market failure (externality, public good/common-pool resource, information asymmetry, or market power).

a) A pharmaceutical company is the sole producer of a patented life-saving drug and charges a price far above its marginal cost. b) A chemical plant discharges waste into a river used by downstream fishing communities. c) A health insurance applicant knows about a pre-existing condition that the insurer cannot easily verify. d) A small town's fireworks display can be watched by everyone in town, whether or not they contributed to pay for it.

Solution

a) Market power — a single seller with no competition sets price above marginal cost, independent of any externality or information problem.

b) Negative externality — the plant's private cost of production does not include the harm imposed on downstream users.

c) Information asymmetry (adverse selection) — the applicant has hidden information about their own risk that the insurer lacks.

d) Public good — the fireworks display is non-excludable (anyone in town can watch) and non-rival (one person watching does not reduce what others see), creating a free-rider problem for funding it.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Excludability and Rivalry
docs.text:
Classify each good into one of the four categories (private good, club good, common-pool resource, public good) based on excludability and rivalry, and justify your answer.

a) A Netflix subscription b) Open-ocean tuna stocks c) A slice of pizza d) Street lighting on a public road

Solution

a) Club good — excludable (you need a paid subscription), non-rival (your friend watching doesn't reduce your access).

b) Common-pool resource — non-excludable (hard to stop anyone from fishing international waters), rival (fish caught by one boat are unavailable to others).

c) Private good — excludable (the seller can refuse to give it to you without payment) and rival (once you eat it, no one else can).

d) Public good — non-excludable (anyone walking the street benefits from the light) and non-rival (one pedestrian benefiting doesn't reduce the light available to another).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Matching Policy to Failure
docs.text:
For each market failure below, recommend the most appropriate government response from Section 12.7 (tax, subsidy, regulation, property rights, public provision, or antitrust) and briefly justify your choice.

a) Overfishing in a shared coastal fishery. b) A factory emitting air pollution with no regulation. c) Underfunded basic scientific research with broad social spillover benefits. d) A proposed merger between the only two firms in a local cable market.

Solution

a) Property rights (e.g., individual transferable fishing quotas) — assigning each fisher an enforceable share of the total allowable catch gives them a private incentive to conserve the resource's long-run value, directly addressing the common-pool resource problem.

b) Pigouvian tax or regulation (e.g., an emissions tax or an emissions cap) — forces the factory to internalize the external cost of its pollution, or legally limits the externality directly.

c) Subsidy or public provision — since the social benefit of research exceeds the private benefit captured by the researcher, the government should subsidize or directly fund research to increase it toward the efficient level.

d) Antitrust enforcement (block or restrict the merger) — combining the only two firms would create a monopoly, which would restrict output and raise prices; antitrust review protects against this specific type of market-power failure.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Government Failure
docs.text:
A city government, concerned about a shortage of affordable housing (which it attributes to market failure), imposes strict rent control, capping rents well below the market-clearing level.

a) Is a shortage of affordable housing, by itself, necessarily evidence of a market failure? Explain. b) Using the supply-and-demand framework from Chapter 2, predict the effect of the rent cap on the quantity of housing supplied and demanded. c) Explain how this policy could be an example of government failure.

Solution

a) Not necessarily. High rents might simply reflect high demand relative to a scarce resource (land in a desirable location) rather than any failure of the market mechanism itself — the market may be functioning efficiently even though the equilibrium price is high. A true market failure would require, e.g., an externality, information problem, or market power specific to the housing market (such as zoning-driven monopoly power among developers).

b) A rent cap set below the equilibrium rent creates a shortage: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price, exactly as in Chapter 2's price-ceiling analysis. Landlords have less incentive to maintain or build new rental housing, and more renters want apartments than are available.

c) This is a textbook case of government failure: a policy intended to make housing more "affordable" instead reduces the quantity supplied, worsens the shortage, and can lead to under-maintenance of existing units and inefficient allocation of apartments (e.g., to those with longest tenure rather than greatest need) — the intervention makes the underlying problem worse rather than correcting a genuine market failure.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Market Power and Deadweight Loss
docs.text:
A city grants an exclusive franchise to a single cable provider. Market demand for cable service is \(P = 80 - Q\), and the constant marginal cost of providing service is \(MC = 20\).

a) Find the quantity and price that would prevail if the market were competitive (\(P = MC\)). b) Find the monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity and price (recall \(MR = 80 - 2Q\) for linear demand \(P = 80 - Q\)). c) Calculate the deadweight loss created by the exclusive franchise. d) Suppose a lobbying firm could spend up to the entire gain in monopoly profit to keep the franchise exclusive. Relate this to the concept of rent-seeking from Section 12.8.

Solution

a) \(80 - Q = 20 \implies Q_{competitive} = 60, \; P_{competitive} = \$20\).

b) Set \(MR = MC\): \(80 - 2Q = 20 \implies Q_{monopoly} = 30, \; P_{monopoly} = 80 - 30 = \$50\).

c) \(DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (60 - 30) \times (50 - 20) = \frac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 30 = \$450\).

d) The monopolist's profit from the franchise is \((P_{monopoly} - MC) \times Q_{monopoly} = (50-20) \times 30 = \$900\) above the competitive (zero-profit) benchmark. Because this $900 is a prize created purely by restricting entry, the firm (or a lobbyist acting for it) has an incentive to spend resources — up to nearly $900 — on lobbying to preserve the exclusive franchise. Those lobbying expenditures produce no new goods or services; they are pure rent-seeking, and the resources spent on them are a further social loss layered on top of the original $450 deadweight loss from restricted output.

You Can Now Diagnose Why a Market Is Failing

Externalities, public goods, information asymmetry, market power, and even the ways government intervention can backfire — you worked through every major category economists use to explain why markets don't always deliver efficient outcomes on their own. That diagnostic skill is exactly what Chapter 13 builds on, going deep on the tools that fix externalities and fund public goods.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods, we return to externalities and public goods in much greater depth — deriving the Pigouvian tax mathematically, working through the Coase theorem, and analyzing cap-and-trade and public-goods voting mechanisms.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish private (internal) costs and benefits from social costs and benefits, and identify the deadweight loss from negative and positive externalities
  2. Calculate the efficient output level and the optimal Pigouvian tax or subsidy for a market with an externality
  3. State the Coase theorem and work through a private-bargaining example to an efficient outcome
  4. Explain how cap-and-trade systems achieve efficient pollution reduction at least cost
  5. Define public goods and derive the condition for their efficient provision
  6. Explain the free-rider problem using a simple game-theoretic example
  7. Compare voting mechanisms for public-goods provision and analyze common-pool resource solutions (quotas, pricing, and property rights)

Welcome to Market Failure, Part II

Every choice has a trade-off! And that's true for markets too, even when the costs and benefits spill onto people who never agreed to the deal: the fishery downstream of a factory, the neighbor who benefits from your flu shot, everyone who enjoys a fireworks display they didn't pay for. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a toolkit -- Pigouvian taxes, Coasean bargains, cap-and-trade, and public-goods financing -- for nudging private incentives back in line with what's best for society as a whole.

docs.title: Private vs. Social Cost
docs.text:
When a firm's production imposes costs on third parties, the private marginal cost (PMC) that the firm pays diverges from the social marginal cost (SMC) borne by society as a whole:

\[SMC = PMC + MEC\]

where \(MEC\) is the marginal external cost imposed on third parties. Because the firm only considers \(PMC\), not \(SMC\), when deciding how much to produce, the market supply curve (which reflects \(PMC\)) lies below the true social cost curve.

The Wedge That Breaks Markets

Notice what's really going on here: the firm's supply curve was never wrong about the firm's own costs -- it's just answering the wrong question. Every externality problem in this chapter boils down to this same wedge between what a decision-maker pays (or receives) and what society as a whole pays (or receives). Once you can spot that wedge, you can predict which direction the market will miss the efficient outcome.

docs.title: Finding the Efficient Quantity
docs.text:
The market reaches its (private) equilibrium where private marginal cost equals private marginal benefit (\(PMC = PMB\), which for a competitive market is simply \(S = D\)). But the efficient quantity is where social marginal cost equals social marginal benefit: \(SMC = SMB\). Because \(SMC > PMC\) with a negative externality, the efficient quantity is always less than the market quantity.

Worked example: a steel mill polluting a river

A steel mill's private marginal cost is \(PMC = 2Q\), and demand (= private and social marginal benefit, since there's no externality on the buyer side) is \(P = 100 - Q\). The mill's pollution imposes a constant marginal external cost of \(MEC = 20\) per unit on a downstream fishery.

Market (unregulated) equilibrium: Set \(PMC = PMB\):

\[2Q = 100 - Q \implies 3Q = 100 \implies Q_{market} = 33.3, \quad P_{market} = \$66.67\]

Efficient quantity: \(SMC = PMC + MEC = 2Q + 20\). Set \(SMC = SMB\):

\[2Q + 20 = 100 - Q \implies 3Q = 80 \implies Q_{efficient} = 26.7\]

The market overproduces by \(33.3 - 26.7 = 6.6\) units relative to the efficient level.

docs.title: Deadweight Loss from a Negative Externality
docs.text:
Every unit produced beyond \(Q_{efficient}\) costs society more than it is worth (since \(SMC > SMB\) for \(Q > Q_{efficient}\)). The deadweight loss is the triangle between the \(SMC\) and \(SMB\) curves, from \(Q_{efficient}\) to \(Q_{market}\):

\[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_{market} - Q_{efficient}) \times MEC = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.6 \times 20 \approx \$66\]

Efficient Doesn't Mean Zero

A common trap: assuming the "efficient" response to pollution is to eliminate it entirely. It isn't -- \(Q_{efficient}\) in the steel mill example is still a healthy 26.7 units, not zero. The efficient quantity is wherever \(SMC = SMB\), and some pollution is efficient as long as the good produced is worth more than the social cost of making it.

docs.title: Private vs. Social Benefit
docs.text:
With a positive externality, the social marginal benefit (SMB) exceeds the private marginal benefit (PMB):

\[SMB = PMB + MEB\]

where \(MEB\) is the marginal external benefit enjoyed by third parties. Because buyers only consider their own \(PMB\), the market demand curve lies below the true social benefit curve, and the market underproduces relative to the efficient quantity.

Worked example: flu vaccinations

Private demand for flu shots is \(P = 60 - Q\) (reflecting each individual's own protection), and private marginal cost (= social marginal cost, since there's no externality on the supply side) is \(PMC = Q\). Vaccination generates a constant marginal external benefit of \(MEB = 10\) per unit (reduced disease transmission to others).

Market equilibrium: \(PMB = PMC \implies 60 - Q = Q \implies Q_{market} = 30\).

Efficient quantity: \(SMB = PMB + MEB = 60 - Q + 10 = 70 - Q\). Set \(SMB = SMC\):

\[70 - Q = Q \implies Q_{efficient} = 35\]

The market underproduces by \(35 - 30 = 5\) units of vaccination relative to the efficient level. The resulting deadweight loss is \(\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10 = \$25\).

docs.title: Correcting a Negative Externality: The Pigouvian Tax
docs.text:
A Pigouvian tax is a tax set exactly equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity. It forces producers to "internalize" the externality by making their private cost equal to the true social cost.

\[t^* = MEC(Q_{efficient})\]

Setting the optimal tax (continuing the steel mill example)

From Section 13.1, \(MEC = \$20\) per unit (constant), so the optimal Pigouvian tax is simply \(t^* = \$20\) per unit.

With the tax, the firm's effective marginal cost becomes \(PMC + t = 2Q + 20\). Setting this equal to demand:

\[2Q + 20 = 100 - Q \implies Q = 26.7\]

This exactly reproduces the efficient quantity found in Section 13.1 — the tax has fully corrected the externality. Tax revenue collected is \(t^* \times Q_{efficient} = 20 \times 26.7 = \$534\), which can (in principle) be used to compensate the affected downstream fishery or for other public purposes.

A Shortcut for Spotting the Right Tax

Here's a time-saver for any Pigouvian tax problem: if \(MEC\) is already stated as a constant (like the $20 here), you don't need to re-derive \(Q_{efficient}\) to find \(t^*\) -- the optimal tax is just that constant. You only need to solve for \(Q_{efficient}\) when you're asked to verify the tax restores it, or when \(MEC\) itself varies with \(Q\).

docs.title: Correcting a Positive Externality: The Pigouvian Subsidy
docs.text:
Symmetrically, a Pigouvian subsidy set equal to the marginal external benefit induces the efficient, higher quantity when there is underproduction.

\[s^* = MEB(Q_{efficient})\]

Setting the optimal subsidy (continuing the vaccination example)

From Section 13.2, \(MEB = \$10\) per unit, so \(s^* = \$10\). With the subsidy, buyers face an effective price \(P - s\), so their willingness to pay a market price rises, shifting effective demand up. Supplying \(PMC = Q\) against effective demand \(PMB + s = 60 - Q + 10 = 70 - Q\):

\[70 - Q = Q \implies Q = 35\]

This matches the efficient quantity exactly — the subsidy corrects the underproduction.

docs.title: General Formula
docs.text:
\[\boxed{t^* \text{ or } s^* = \text{Marginal External Cost or Benefit, evaluated at } Q_{efficient}}\]

The tax/subsidy must target the externality, not the transaction

A Pigouvian tax is not simply "a tax on a harmful-looking good" — its size must be calibrated to the actual marginal external cost. A tax set too high overcorrects (causing underproduction, a new deadweight loss); set too low, it undercorrects.

Yes, This One Trips Everyone Up

If the Coase theorem feels slippery on a first read, that's completely normal -- it's one of the most counterintuitive results in this course. The trick is to stop asking "who's at fault?" and start asking "is there a trade both sides would accept?" Work through the numbers in both bargaining directions below, slowly, and the logic will click into place.

docs.title: 13.4 The Coase Theorem and Private Bargaining
Statement of the Theorem
docs.text:
Taxes and subsidies require the government to measure the externality and intervene. The economist Ronald Coase argued that under certain conditions, externalities can instead be resolved privately, without government action at all.

The Coase Theorem: If property rights are clearly defined, transaction costs are low, and bargaining is possible, private parties can negotiate their way to the economically efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the legal right.

The key insight is that the party suffering the externality and the party causing it can bargain: whichever arrangement produces more total surplus will be reached, because any surplus left on the table creates room for a mutually beneficial deal.

docs.title: Worked Numerical Example
docs.text:
A factory's production generates noise that annoys a neighboring resident. The factory earns $500/week in profit from its current activity. The noise is worth $300/week to the resident to eliminate (i.e., the resident would be willing to pay up to $300/week to make the factory quiet, or alternatively, suffers $300/week of harm from the noise).

Case A: The resident has the legal right to quiet (the factory must get consent to make noise).

The factory can offer to pay the resident for the right to continue operating noisily. Since the factory earns $500/week — more than the resident's $300/week cost of enduring the noise — a bargain exists: the factory offers, say, $350/week to the resident, who accepts (better than $0, and the factory still nets $500 − $350 = $150 profit, better than shutting down). The factory continues operating, which is efficient because its value (\(500) exceeds the harm it causes (\)300).

Case B: The factory has the legal right to make noise (no consent needed).

The resident could try to pay the factory to stop. But the resident would only be willing to pay up to $300/week, while the factory would need at least $500/week to be compensated for stopping. No price exists that makes both sides better off, so no deal happens — the factory continues operating.

The efficient outcome is the same either way

In both cases, the factory continues operating — the economically efficient outcome, since its value ($500) exceeds the harm ($300). The assignment of the legal right only changes who pays whom, not what happens: with resident's rights, the factory pays the resident; with factory's rights, no payment occurs. This is the heart of the Coase theorem — efficiency does not depend on the initial allocation of rights, as long as bargaining is costless.

docs.title: Why the Coase Theorem Often Fails in Practice
docs.text:
Coasean bargaining breaks down when:

  • Transaction costs are high — negotiating and enforcing an agreement (lawyers, monitoring) may itself be costly.
  • Many parties are affected — a factory's pollution may affect thousands of people, making coordinated bargaining prohibitively difficult (a free-rider problem among the victims, discussed in Section 13.8).
  • Property rights are unclear or unenforceable — if it's unclear who legally "owns" clean air, there is nothing to bargain over.

Why air pollution is rarely solved by Coasean bargaining

A coal plant's air pollution affects an entire city of residents. Even if the plant has a clearly assigned legal right to pollute, organizing hundreds of thousands of residents to collectively negotiate and pay the plant to reduce emissions is essentially impossible — the transaction costs of coordinating that many people swamp any potential gains. This is precisely why externalities affecting large, diffuse groups are usually handled through Pigouvian taxes or regulation (Section 13.3) rather than private bargaining.

docs.title: How Cap-and-Trade Works
docs.text: A cap-and-trade system is a market-based alternative to a Pigouvian tax for correcting a negative externality. The government sets a cap — a maximum total quantity of pollution (emissions permits) — and issues (or auctions) permits up to that cap. Firms are then free to trade permits among themselves.

docs.title: Why Trading Achieves Efficiency at Least Cost
docs.text:
Firms differ in how costly it is for them to reduce emissions (their marginal abatement cost). A firm with a low cost of reducing emissions will find it cheaper to cut its own pollution and sell its spare permits than to keep polluting; a firm with a high cost of reducing emissions will prefer to buy permits rather than cut back. Trading continues until every firm's marginal cost of abatement is equalized to the market permit price \(p^*\):

\[MAC_1 = MAC_2 = \cdots = MAC_n = p^*\]

This achieves the overall emissions target (set by the cap) at the lowest possible total cost — exactly the same total abatement is achieved as a uniform Pigouvian tax of \(p^*\) per unit would achieve, but the cap guarantees the quantity of pollution directly, whereas the tax guarantees the price directly.

Cap-and-trade numerical example

Two firms each currently emit 100 tons of pollution. Firm A's marginal abatement cost is \(MAC_A = 2x\) (where \(x\) is tons abated); Firm B's is \(MAC_B = 8x\). The regulator caps total emissions at 150 tons, requiring 50 tons of total abatement, and issues 150 permits.

Efficient abatement requires \(MAC_A = MAC_B\) at the margin:

\[2x_A = 8x_B, \quad x_A + x_B = 50\]

Substituting \(x_A = 4x_B\): \(4x_B + x_B = 50 \implies x_B = 10, \; x_A = 40\).

Firm A (which can abate cheaply) does most of the abatement (40 tons), while Firm B (which finds abatement expensive) does little (10 tons) and instead buys permits from Firm A. The market-clearing permit price equalizes marginal costs: \(p^* = MAC_A(40) = 2(40) = \$80 = MAC_B(10) = 8(10) = \$80\). Total abatement cost is minimized compared to, say, requiring both firms to cut emissions by 25 tons each.

docs.title: 13.6 Public Goods: Definition and the Efficient Provision Condition
Recap: Non-Excludable and Non-Rival
docs.text: As introduced in Chapter 12, a public good is both non-excludable and non-rival. Classic examples include national defense, lighthouses, basic scientific research, and public fireworks displays.

docs.title: The Samuelson Condition
docs.text:
Because a public good is non-rival, everyone who values it can simultaneously enjoy the same unit — so the efficient quantity is found by summing each person's marginal benefit (vertically adding demand curves), not by the usual horizontal summation used for private goods.

\[\text{Efficient Quantity: } \sum_{i=1}^{n} MB_i = MC\]

This is often called the Samuelson condition for public goods, in contrast to the private-good efficiency condition \(MB_i = MC\) for each individual.

Why You Add, Not Choose

This is the moment this chapter asks you to unlearn a habit from earlier chapters: for a private good, you add up quantities at a given price (horizontal summation); for a public good, where everyone consumes the same unit simultaneously, you add up what each person is willing to pay for that unit instead (vertical summation). Same word, "add," but a completely different operation -- mixing them up is the single most common Samuelson-condition mistake.

Worked example: a neighborhood fireworks display

Three neighbors value a fireworks display as follows: Neighbor 1's marginal benefit is \(MB_1 = 30 - Q\), Neighbor 2's is \(MB_2 = 20 - Q\), Neighbor 3's is \(MB_3 = 10 - Q\) (where \(Q\) is display size/intensity). The marginal cost of a bigger display is \(MC = 2Q\).

Because fireworks are non-rival, sum the marginal benefits vertically:

\[\sum MB_i = (30 - Q) + (20 - Q) + (10 - Q) = 60 - 3Q\]

Set \(\sum MB_i = MC\):

\[60 - 3Q = 2Q \implies 60 = 5Q \implies Q^* = 12\]

The efficient display size is \(Q^* = 12\) — far larger than what any single neighbor would privately fund alone (Neighbor 1 alone would set \(MB_1 = MC \implies 30 - Q = 2Q \implies Q = 10\), and Neighbors 2 and 3 would fund even less, or nothing, on their own).

docs.title: Why Public Goods Are Underprovided
docs.text: Because a public good is non-excludable, no individual can be forced to pay for it, and each person has an incentive to free ride: let others pay for the good while still enjoying its benefits. If everyone free rides, the good may not get funded at all, even though its total social value exceeds its cost.

docs.title: A Simple Game-Theoretic Example
docs.text:
Suppose two neighbors are each deciding whether to Contribute $60 toward a $100 streetlight that benefits both of them equally (each values the streetlight at $80 if it is built, regardless of who paid). The streetlight gets built if at least one neighbor contributes $60 (the other contributing $40 to cover the rest) — but to keep this simple, suppose the light is built if and only if both contribute $50 each, totaling the required $100.

Neighbor 2: Contribute ($50) Neighbor 2: Free Ride ($0) Neighbor 1: Contribute ($50) Light built. Each nets \(80 - 50 = \$30\) Light not built. N1 nets \(-\$50\), N2 nets $0 Neighbor 1: Free Ride ($0) Light not built. N1 nets $0, N2 nets \(-\$50\) Light not built. Both net $0

This is a prisoner's dilemma structure (Chapter 10): mutual contribution ($30, \(30) is better for both than mutual free-riding (\)0, $0), but each neighbor's individually dominant strategy is to free ride — if the other contributes, free riding yields $80 (full benefit, no cost) which is better than $30; if the other free rides, contributing alone yields \(-\$50\), which is worse than $0. The dominant strategy for both is Free Ride, so the Nash equilibrium is (Free Ride, Free Ride) — the light does not get built, even though building it ($30 + $30 = \(60 net total surplus) is better than not building it (\)0 total).

The free-rider problem is exactly why public goods need government provision

Private, voluntary contribution systematically underprovides public goods for the same reason underlying every prisoner's dilemma: individually rational behavior produces a collectively inefficient outcome. This is the central economic argument for financing public goods through compulsory taxation rather than voluntary donation.

docs.title: 13.8 Providing Public Goods: Voting and Public Choice
docs.text: Because public goods are typically funded through government rather than markets, how government decides how much to provide becomes an economic question in its own right — the field of public choice theory.

docs.title: Majority Voting and the Median Voter
docs.text:
Under simple majority rule with a single issue (e.g., "how large should the public park budget be?"), and if voters' preferences are single-peaked (each voter has one preferred amount, and support falls off as proposals move further from it in either direction), the median voter theorem predicts that the outcome of majority voting will match the preference of the median voter — the voter exactly in the middle of the preference distribution.

Median voter theorem in action

Five town residents have the following preferred annual park budgets: $10,000, $30,000, $50,000, $70,000, $200,000. Under pairwise majority voting between any two proposals, the $50,000 proposal (the median) will defeat any other proposal, because it can always attract support from the voters on the side closer to it. The outcome converges to the median voter's preferred amount, regardless of the mean (which here is $72,000) — a very wealthy or very frugal outlier does not dominate the outcome the way it would in a market purchase decision.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Majority voting can still produce inefficient outcomes relative to the Samuelson condition (Section 13.6) — the median voter's preferred quantity generally does not equal the surplus-maximizing quantity, because voting does not weight preferences by intensity (a voter who cares passionately gets the same one vote as someone who barely cares). This is one reason public-goods provision remains a persistently debated area of policy.

docs.title: 13.9 Common-Pool Resources: Fisheries, Groundwater, and Congestion
docs.text:
Chapter 12 introduced the tragedy of the commons; here we examine concrete policy tools used to prevent it.

Resource Problem Policy Tool How It Works Ocean fisheries Overfishing collapses fish stocks Individual Transferable Quotas (ITQs) Each fisher is allocated a tradable share of the total allowable catch, creating a property right that rewards conservation Groundwater aquifers Over-pumping depletes the water table Water rights / pumping permits Usage rights are defined and limited, often tradable, so users bear the cost of their own extraction Road congestion Each driver imposes delay on others Congestion pricing Tolls that rise with congestion force drivers to internalize the delay they impose on others, similar to a Pigouvian tax

Congestion pricing as a Pigouvian tax on a common-pool resource

A congested highway lets 10,000 cars through per hour for free, but average delay rises sharply with each additional car — a cost each driver imposes on every other driver but does not personally pay. A congestion toll of $8 during peak hours, calibrated to the marginal external delay cost each driver imposes, reduces traffic to the efficient volume, exactly paralleling the Pigouvian tax logic of Section 13.3 applied to a common-pool resource instead of ordinary pollution.

The common thread across all three tools is the same insight from Section 13.4's Coase theorem and Section 13.3's Pigouvian taxes: assigning well-defined, enforceable property rights (or their price equivalent) forces users to internalize the costs they impose on others, converting a tragedy-of-the-commons problem into one where private incentives align with social efficiency.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Social Marginal Cost (SMC) Private marginal cost plus the marginal external cost Social Marginal Benefit (SMB) Private marginal benefit plus the marginal external benefit Marginal External Cost (MEC) The cost of one more unit of production imposed on third parties Marginal External Benefit (MEB) The benefit of one more unit of consumption enjoyed by third parties Pigouvian Tax A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost, correcting a negative externality Pigouvian Subsidy A per-unit subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit, correcting a positive externality Coase Theorem With clear property rights, low transaction costs, and bargaining, private parties reach the efficient outcome regardless of who holds the rights Cap-and-Trade A system capping total pollution and allowing firms to trade permits, equalizing marginal abatement costs Marginal Abatement Cost (MAC) The cost of reducing pollution by one more unit Samuelson Condition Efficient public-goods provision requires the sum of individual marginal benefits to equal marginal cost Free-Rider Problem The incentive to let others pay for a non-excludable good while still enjoying its benefits Median Voter Theorem Majority voting on a single issue with single-peaked preferences yields the median voter's preferred outcome Individual Transferable Quota (ITQ) A tradable property right to harvest a fixed share of a common-pool resource Congestion Pricing A toll that rises with congestion, forcing drivers to internalize the delay they impose on others

docs.title: Problem 1 — Pigouvian Tax for a Negative Externality
docs.text:
A paper mill has private marginal cost \(PMC = 3Q\) and faces demand \(P = 150 - 2Q\). Each unit of paper produced imposes a constant marginal external cost of \(MEC = \$15\) on a downstream community (water pollution).

a) Find the market (unregulated) equilibrium quantity. b) Find the socially efficient quantity. c) Find the optimal Pigouvian tax, and verify that it induces the efficient quantity. d) Calculate the deadweight loss of the unregulated market outcome.

Solution

a) Set \(PMC = P\): \(3Q = 150 - 2Q \implies 5Q = 150 \implies Q_{market} = 30\).

b) \(SMC = 3Q + 15\). Set \(SMC = P\): \(3Q + 15 = 150 - 2Q \implies 5Q = 135 \implies Q_{efficient} = 27\).

c) \(t^* = MEC = \$15\). With the tax, firms face \(PMC + t = 3Q + 15\), and setting this equal to demand reproduces exactly \(Q = 27\) from part (b) — confirmed.

d) \(DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (30 - 27) \times 15 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 15 = \$22.50\).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Pigouvian Subsidy for a Positive Externality
docs.text:
Private demand for a job-training program is \(P = 80 - Q\), and marginal cost is \(MC = Q\). Each unit of training generates a marginal external benefit of \(MEB = \$20\) (employers and the broader economy benefit from a more skilled workforce).

a) Find the market equilibrium quantity. b) Find the efficient quantity. c) Find the optimal per-unit subsidy.

Solution

a) \(80 - Q = Q \implies Q_{market} = 40\).

b) \(SMB = 80 - Q + 20 = 100 - Q\). Set \(100 - Q = Q \implies Q_{efficient} = 50\).

c) \(s^* = MEB = \$20\). The subsidy raises effective demand to \(100 - Q\), which (as shown in part b) yields \(Q = 50\), confirming the efficient outcome.

docs.title: Problem 3 — The Coase Theorem
docs.text:
A dry cleaner's machine vents fumes that bother a bookstore next door. Operating the machine is worth $400/week to the dry cleaner. The fumes cost the bookstore $250/week in lost business (customers avoid the smell).

a) Suppose the bookstore has the legal right to clean air. Will the dry cleaner continue to operate? Describe a possible bargain. b) Suppose instead the dry cleaner has the legal right to operate without restriction. Will the dry cleaner continue to operate? c) Is the outcome efficient in both cases? Explain why or why not. d) Now suppose operating the machine is only worth $200/week to the dry cleaner (less than the $250/week harm). Redo parts (a) and (b).

Solution

a) The dry cleaner can offer to pay the bookstore for the right to operate. Since $400 > $250, a bargain exists (e.g., the dry cleaner pays the bookstore $280/week): the bookstore is better off than with $0, and the dry cleaner still nets $400 − $280 = $120, better than shutting down. The dry cleaner continues operating.

b) The bookstore could try to pay the dry cleaner to stop, but would only pay up to $250, while the dry cleaner needs at least $400 to accept. No deal is possible. The dry cleaner continues operating (since it has the right to, and no one pays it to stop).

c) Yes, efficient in both cases — the dry cleaner's operation generates $400 of value against only $250 of harm, so continued operation maximizes total surplus regardless of who holds the legal right. This illustrates the Coase theorem: the assignment of property rights affects who pays whom, not the efficient outcome.

d) Now the machine is worth only $200, less than the $250 harm. (a) With the bookstore holding the right: the dry cleaner cannot offer enough (its maximum willingness to pay is $200, less than the bookstore's $250 minimum to accept), so no deal is struck — the dry cleaner stops operating. (b) With the dry cleaner holding the right: the bookstore can now profitably pay the dry cleaner to stop (the bookstore is willing to pay up to $250, more than the $200 needed to compensate the dry cleaner for lost value) — e.g., bookstore pays $220, the dry cleaner stops operating. In both cases the efficient outcome (stop operating, since harm $250 > value $200) is reached.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Public Goods and the Samuelson Condition
docs.text:
Four households are considering funding a shared community garden. Their marginal benefits are \(MB_1 = 40 - 2Q\), \(MB_2 = 30 - 2Q\), \(MB_3 = 20 - 2Q\), \(MB_4 = 10 - 2Q\). The marginal cost of expanding the garden is \(MC = 5Q\).

a) Write the condition for efficient provision of this public good. b) Solve for the efficient size \(Q^*\). c) If only Household 1 funded the garden alone, what size would they choose? Compare to \(Q^*\) and explain the discrepancy.

Solution

a) Since the garden is non-rival, sum marginal benefits vertically and set equal to marginal cost: \(\sum MB_i = MC\).

b) \(\sum MB_i = (40 - 2Q) + (30 - 2Q) + (20 - 2Q) + (10 - 2Q) = 100 - 8Q\). Set \(100 - 8Q = 5Q \implies 100 = 13Q \implies Q^* \approx 7.69\).

c) Alone, Household 1 sets \(MB_1 = MC\): \(40 - 2Q = 5Q \implies 40 = 7Q \implies Q = 5.71\). This is well below the efficient \(Q^* \approx 7.69\), because Household 1 ignores the benefits the garden provides to Households 2, 3, and 4 — a textbook illustration of why voluntary private provision underprovides public goods relative to the socially efficient quantity.

docs.title: Problem 5 — The Free-Rider Game
docs.text:
Two roommates are deciding whether to clean their shared apartment. Cleaning costs each roommate 2 hours of effort (valued at $20/hour, so $40 of cost) if they do it. A clean apartment is worth $50 to each roommate, regardless of who cleaned it. If at least one roommate cleans, the apartment is clean; if neither cleans, it stays dirty (worth $0 to both).

a) Construct the payoff matrix for (Clean, Don't Clean) for both roommates. b) Find the Nash equilibrium (or equilibria). c) Is the outcome efficient? What does this illustrate about public goods?

Solution

a) Payoffs (Roommate 1, Roommate 2), net of cleaning cost where applicable:

R2: Clean R2: Don't Clean R1: Clean \((50-40, 50-40) = (10, 10)\) \((50-40, 50) = (10, 50)\) R1: Don't Clean \((50, 50-40) = (50, 10)\) \((0, 0)\)

b) Each roommate's best response is to let the other clean: if R2 cleans, R1 prefers Don't Clean (50 > 10); if R2 doesn't clean, R1 prefers Clean (10 > 0)... wait — check carefully: if R2 doesn't clean, R1 comparing Clean (10) vs. Don't Clean (0) prefers Clean. So there is no single dominant strategy here; instead there are two pure-strategy Nash equilibria: (Clean, Don't Clean) and (Don't Clean, Clean) — in each, exactly one roommate free rides on the other's cleaning, earning $50 while the cleaner earns only $10. (Note: unlike the streetlight example in Section 13.7, here a single contributor suffices to provide the good, so this is a "volunteer" coordination game rather than a strict prisoner's dilemma.)

c) Both equilibria are efficient in the sense that the apartment does get cleaned (total surplus \(10 + 50 = 60\) far exceeds the \((0,0)\) outcome), but they are inequitable — one roommate free rides entirely while the other bears the full cost. This illustrates that even when a public good does get provided, free-riding incentives can create an unfair distribution of who bears the cost, and in larger groups (more than two) or with higher cleaning costs relative to the benefit, this type of game can easily collapse to the inefficient (Don't Clean, Don't Clean) outcome instead, just as in the streetlight example.

You've Tamed Market Failure

Take a moment -- you just worked through Pigouvian taxes, the Coase theorem, cap-and-trade, the Samuelson condition, and the free-rider problem, five of the trickiest ideas in microeconomics, and came out able to solve all of them numerically. Every choice has a trade-off, and now you know how to find the one society as a whole should make, even when markets alone won't get us there.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 14: Information Economics, we examine how asymmetric information — introduced briefly in Chapter 12 — shapes markets for insurance, used cars, labor, and credit, and what tools (signaling, screening, and contracts) can mitigate adverse selection and moral hazard.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric information and identify which side of a market holds the informational advantage
  2. Explain adverse selection using Akerlof's "market for lemons" and derive its effect on market outcomes
  3. Distinguish moral hazard (hidden actions) from adverse selection (hidden information)
  4. Explain how signaling can allow informed parties to credibly reveal private information
  5. Explain how screening allows uninformed parties to sort informed parties by type
  6. Analyze principal-agent problems and the incentive contracts used to mitigate them
  7. Apply these tools to real markets: health insurance, used cars, credit, and labor contracts

When Someone Knows More Than You

Every choice has a trade-off -- but some trades are riskier than others, because one side of the deal knows something the other side doesn't. In this chapter you'll meet the used-car seller who knows their car is a lemon, the insurance applicant who knows their own health better than any insurer, and the clever tools -- signaling, screening, and incentive contracts -- that markets have invented to cope. This is the economics of trust, and of what happens when trust alone isn't enough.

docs.title: 14.1 Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Information
docs.text:
The supply-and-demand model of Chapter 2 assumed that buyers and sellers know everything relevant about the good being traded: its quality, the risk involved, the effort behind it. Economists call this symmetric information — both sides of a transaction have the same relevant knowledge.

In many real markets, this assumption fails. Asymmetric information exists when one party to a transaction knows something relevant that the other party does not. Asymmetric information is not a minor wrinkle — it can prevent mutually beneficial trades from happening at all, and it is one of the central reasons markets fail to reach the efficient outcomes described in Chapter 12.

Economists sort problems of asymmetric information into two broad categories, distinguished by when the information gap matters relative to the transaction:

Problem Nature of the hidden information Timing Example Adverse selection Hidden characteristic (type) Exists before the contract is signed A used car's owner knows if it's a lemon before selling it Moral hazard Hidden action (behavior) Arises after the contract is signed A driver with insurance drives less carefully after buying the policy

Before or After the Ink Dries

Here's the one question that sorts every problem in this chapter: did the hidden information exist before the contract was signed, or does the hidden behavior only happen after? Before means adverse selection -- a type that was always there; after means moral hazard -- a choice the contract itself changed. Get the timing right, and the correct tool follows almost automatically.

Why this distinction matters

Adverse selection is a problem of selection — who chooses to participate in a market or contract. Moral hazard is a problem of incentives — how a contract changes behavior after it is signed. The policy tools that address each are different: signaling and screening address adverse selection; monitoring and incentive-compatible contracts address moral hazard.

The economists George Akerlof, Michael Spence, and Joseph Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics for developing the theory of markets with asymmetric information — the framework this chapter builds on.

docs.title: 14.2 Adverse Selection: The Market for Lemons
Akerlof's Insight
docs.text:
In his famous 1970 paper, George Akerlof asked a deceptively simple question: why are used cars that have barely been driven often sold for so much less than their "true" value? His answer launched an entire field of economics.

The Lemons Math Looks Scarier Than It Is

If the back-and-forth of buyers revising their expectations downward feels dizzying at first, you're not alone -- this unraveling logic is genuinely one of the hardest ideas in microeconomics, which is exactly why it won Akerlof a Nobel Prize. Go slowly through each round of the price-quality spiral below, and notice it's really the same simple calculation -- expected value given who actually shows up to sell -- repeated until nothing changes.

Consider a market for used cars. Each seller knows the true quality of their own car; buyers cannot observe quality before purchase — they can only see the average quality of cars offered for sale. Suppose there are two types of used cars:

  • High-quality cars ("peaches"): worth $10,000 to sellers and $12,000 to buyers
  • Low-quality cars ("lemons"): worth $4,000 to sellers and $5,000 to buyers

Assume half of all used cars on the market are peaches and half are lemons, and buyers cannot tell which is which at the time of purchase. Because buyers cannot distinguish quality, they will only pay a price based on the average quality they expect to receive.

Buyers' expected value, if both types are offered for sale in equal proportion:

\[E[\text{Value}] = 0.5(12{,}000) + 0.5(5{,}000) = \$8{,}500\]

At a price of $8,500, what happens? Owners of peaches (worth $10,000 to them) will not sell — $8,500 is less than what the car is worth to them. Owners of lemons (worth $4,000 to them) are happy to sell at $8,500. So only lemons come to market.

But if buyers anticipate this, they revise their expectations: if only lemons are sold, buyers should only be willing to pay the value of a lemon.

\[E[\text{Value} \mid \text{only lemons offered}] = \$5{,}000\]

docs.title: The Death Spiral
docs.text:
This process can cascade. At $8,500, only lemons sell. Rational buyers anticipate this and lower their offer to $5,000 (lemon value). At $5,000, sellers of lemons (valuing their car at $4,000) are still willing to sell. The market settles at a price reflecting only lemon quality — the peaches are permanently driven out of the market even though peach buyers and peach sellers could have found a mutually beneficial trade (anywhere between $10,000 and $12,000) if information had been symmetric.

Market collapse

In the most extreme version of this model, adverse selection can cause a market to disappear entirely — even though there are gains from trade available to every participant if only quality could be verified. The inefficiency comes not from bad intentions but from the simple fact that buyers cannot distinguish good from bad before purchase.

docs.title: A General Formulation
docs.text:
Let a fraction \(\lambda\) of sellers have high-quality goods worth \(V_H\) to buyers, and \((1-\lambda)\) have low-quality goods worth \(V_L\) to buyers, with \(V_H > V_L\). If sellers of high quality require a minimum price \(S_H\) to sell, and the market-clearing price must reflect average expected quality:

\[P = \lambda V_H + (1-\lambda) V_L\]

The high-quality sellers participate only if \(P \geq S_H\). If \(S_H > \lambda V_H + (1-\lambda)V_L\), high-quality sellers exit, \(\lambda\) falls, and \(P\) falls further — a feedback loop that can unravel the market completely.

docs.title: Other "Lemons" Markets
docs.text:
Adverse selection extends well beyond used cars:

  • Health insurance: People who know they are likely to get sick are more eager to buy generous insurance than healthy people are. If insurers cannot distinguish risk types, they must price policies based on the average risk of their applicant pool. This can drive healthy, low-risk people out of the market (they find the average-risk price too expensive), raising the average risk of those who remain, which raises prices further — the same unraveling dynamic.
  • Credit markets: Borrowers know their own likelihood of repayment better than lenders do. If a bank cannot distinguish safe from risky borrowers, it must charge an interest rate reflecting average default risk. This can discourage safe borrowers, leaving a riskier pool — a phenomenon Stiglitz and Weiss (1981) showed can lead banks to ration credit (deny loans) rather than simply raise interest rates indefinitely.
  • Labor markets: Workers know their own skill and work ethic better than employers do at the hiring stage.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Moral hazard arises when one party's actions, taken after a contract is signed, are not fully observable to the other party, and those actions affect the outcome of the contract. The classic illustration is insurance: once you are insured against a loss, you bear less of the cost of that loss yourself, so you have less incentive to prevent it.

Moral hazard illustrations

  • A driver with full collision coverage may drive less cautiously than one with no insurance (less incentive to avoid accidents, since the insurer bears the cost).
  • A renter who has posted no security deposit may take worse care of the apartment.
  • An employee on a flat salary (not tied to performance) may exert less effort than one paid by the piece.
  • A borrower who is not personally liable for a loan (e.g., behind limited liability) may take on riskier projects with the bank's money.

docs.title: Why Moral Hazard Is Different from Adverse Selection
docs.text: Adverse selection is about who shows up to a market (a hidden type that existed before the contract). Moral hazard is about what people do once insured, employed, or lent to (a hidden action that occurs after the contract). Both stem from asymmetric information, but the timing and the remedy differ.

docs.title: A Simple Model
docs.text:
Suppose a worker can choose high effort (\(e_H\)) or low effort (\(e_L\)), where \(e_H\) costs the worker a disutility of \(c\) but raises the probability of a good outcome (e.g., project success) from \(p_L\) to \(p_H\) (\(p_H > p_L\)). If the firm cannot observe effort — only the outcome — and pays a flat wage \(w\) regardless of outcome, the worker will always choose \(e_L\) (the effort that minimizes cost), because pay does not depend on effort. This is the moral hazard: the firm would prefer high effort, but cannot contract on it directly, only on the (noisy) outcome.

Incentive-compatible solution: Pay a wage that depends on the outcome, e.g., \(w_{\text{success}} = w_H\) and \(w_{\text{failure}} = w_L\), with \(w_H > w_L\), chosen so that the expected gain from exerting high effort exceeds its cost \(c\):

\[p_H w_H + (1-p_H)w_L - c \; \geq \; p_L w_H + (1-p_L)w_L\]

Rearranging:

\[(p_H - p_L)(w_H - w_L) \geq c\]

This is the incentive compatibility condition: the pay gap between success and failure, weighted by how much effort changes the probability of success, must be large enough to cover the cost of effort. This is why many real-world contracts tie pay to performance — commissions, bonuses, stock options, tips, and piece rates are all attempts to solve moral hazard by linking pay to observable outcomes that are correlated with unobservable effort.

Solving Incentive Compatibility in One Line

Whenever you're asked for the minimum pay gap that induces high effort, skip straight to \((p_H - p_L)(w_H - w_L) \geq c\) and divide: the minimum gap is just \(c\) divided by the change in success probability. You almost never need to set up the full expected-utility comparison from scratch once you recognize the problem as an incentive-compatibility question.

docs.title: Mitigating Moral Hazard
docs.text: Tool How it works Example Deductibles and co-pays Insured party bears part of the loss, restoring some incentive to prevent it Auto and health insurance deductibles Monitoring Reduce the information asymmetry directly Employer supervision, telematics devices that track driving behavior Performance pay Tie compensation to observable outcomes correlated with effort Sales commissions, bonuses, stock options Reputation / repeated interaction Future business depends on current behavior Online seller ratings, repeat customers Liability rules Make the agent bear some cost of bad outcomes Not allowing full discharge of debt in bankruptcy

docs.title: 14.4 Signaling: Letting the Informed Party Speak
docs.text: When adverse selection threatens to destroy a market, the informed party sometimes has an incentive to find a credible way to reveal their private information. This is called signaling.

docs.title: Spence's Education Model
docs.text:
Michael Spence's classic (1973) model asks: why do employers pay more for workers with college degrees, even in jobs where the specific material learned in college is never used? His answer: a degree can function as a signal of underlying (unobservable) ability, if it is less costly for high-ability workers to obtain than for low-ability workers.

Suppose there are two types of workers, High ability (H) and Low ability (L), and the cost of acquiring \(y\) years of education is \(c_H(y)\) for high types and \(c_L(y)\) for low types, with \(c_H(y) < c_L(y)\) for any \(y > 0\) (education is relatively less costly/painful for high-ability workers — they learn faster, find it less unpleasant). Employers cannot observe ability directly but can observe years of education, \(y\).

For signaling to work (a "separating equilibrium"), the signal must satisfy two conditions:

  1. High types want to signal: the wage premium for acquiring education \(y^*\) must exceed its cost to a high type.
  2. Low types do NOT want to mimic: the same wage premium must not be worth it for a low type, i.e., it would cost them more than the wage gain.
\[c_L(y^*) > w_H - w_L > c_H(y^*)\]

If such a \(y^*\) exists, education can separate the two types in equilibrium even though a college education, in Spence's stylized model, teaches no job-relevant skill at all — its value is purely in being a cost that only high-ability types find worthwhile to incur.

A 'Useless' Signal That Says Everything

Sit with this for a second: in Spence's model, the education itself teaches the worker nothing useful on the job. Its entire value comes from being expensive enough that a low-ability worker wouldn't bother faking it. That's the mental shift signaling asks of you -- a credential's power to inform can come purely from its cost, not from its content.

Other signals

  • Warranties: A manufacturer confident in its product's reliability can profitably offer a long warranty (few claims will be filed); a manufacturer of unreliable products cannot afford to, because claims would be too costly. The warranty length signals quality.
  • Reputation: An established restaurant with years of good reviews signals quality that a brand-new restaurant cannot yet demonstrate.
  • Dividends: A firm that pays a stable dividend signals confidence in its future cash flows, since cutting a dividend later would be costly to its reputation.
  • Collateral: Offering more collateral on a loan signals that a borrower genuinely expects to repay (since a borrower planning to default would not want to risk losing valuable collateral).

docs.title: Requirements for an Effective Signal
docs.text:
For a signal to credibly convey private information, it generally must be:

  • Costly — a costless signal could be sent by anyone, so it would convey no information
  • Differentially costly across types — it must be cheaper for the type it's meant to reveal (otherwise everyone, or no one, would send it)
  • Observable to the uninformed party

docs.title: 14.5 Screening: Letting the Uninformed Party Sort
docs.text: Screening is the mirror image of signaling: instead of the informed party revealing information, the uninformed party designs a menu of options that induces different types to reveal themselves by the choices they make.

docs.title: Insurance Deductibles as a Screening Device
docs.text:
An insurance company cannot observe which applicants are high-risk and which are low-risk. Instead of a single policy, it can offer a menu:

Policy Premium Deductible Policy A High premium Low deductible Policy B Low premium High deductible

High-risk individuals, who expect to file claims, prefer Policy A (low deductible matters more to them, and they're willing to pay the higher premium to avoid a large out-of-pocket cost). Low-risk individuals, who rarely expect to file a claim, prefer Policy B (why pay a high premium for low-deductible protection they are unlikely to use?). By choosing between the two policies, customers reveal their type even though the insurer never directly observes risk.

This is an example of a self-selection constraint: the menu must be designed so that each type prefers the option intended for them over the option intended for the other type.

A Menu Isn't Screening Unless It Actually Sorts

A common mistake is assuming that offering any menu of contracts automatically screens customers by type. It doesn't -- if both types end up preferring the same option (as happens in Problem 5 at the end of this chapter), you've learned nothing about who's who. Always check the self-selection constraint directly: does each type's own expected-cost calculation actually favor the option meant for them?

docs.title: Job Interviews and Screening
docs.text: Employers use interviews, tests, probationary periods, and tiered job offers (e.g., offering a lower base salary with a large bonus for proven performers) as screening devices. A candidate's willingness to accept a performance-contingent contract can itself reveal information: a candidate confident in their own ability is more willing to accept pay tied to performance than a candidate who is not.

docs.title: Screening vs. Signaling — Who Moves First?
docs.text: Who acts first Who designs the mechanism Example Signaling Informed party Informed party chooses a costly action Worker chooses how much education to get Screening Uninformed party Uninformed party designs a menu of contracts Insurer designs a menu of deductible/premium combinations

docs.title: 14.6 Principal-Agent Problems
docs.text:
A principal-agent problem arises whenever one party (the principal) hires or delegates authority to another party (the agent) to act on their behalf, but the agent's interests are not perfectly aligned with the principal's, and the principal cannot perfectly monitor the agent's actions.

\[\text{Principal-Agent Problem} = \text{Misaligned incentives} + \text{Imperfect monitoring}\]

Principal-agent relationships

Principal Agent Potential conflict Shareholders CEO CEO may prefer prestige projects or perks over maximizing shareholder value Patient Doctor Doctor may recommend more (or less) treatment than is medically optimal, especially under fee-for-service pay Homeowner Contractor Contractor paid hourly has less incentive to finish quickly Client Lawyer billing by the hour Lawyer may have an incentive to prolong a case Voters Elected officials Officials may pursue re-election or personal goals over constituents' interests

docs.title: Solving the Principal-Agent Problem
docs.text:
Principals use several tools, many of which we've already encountered as tools against moral hazard (the principal-agent problem is, formally, a generalization of the moral hazard problem):

  1. Incentive contracts that tie the agent's pay to outcomes correlated with the principal's goals (stock options for CEOs, commissions for salespeople).
  2. Monitoring to reduce the information gap (audits, boards of directors, performance reviews).
  3. Bonding — requiring the agent to post a stake that is forfeited for poor performance (a security deposit, a performance bond).
  4. Competition and reputation — repeated interactions and outside options discipline agents who cannot be perfectly monitored in any single period.

The agency cost tradeoff

Perfect incentive alignment is usually impossible (or prohibitively expensive) to achieve, so real-world contracts accept some agency cost — the loss in value from imperfect alignment — in exchange for lower-powered, simpler, or less risky incentive schemes. A CEO cannot bear 100% of the risk of the firm's performance (she would demand enormous compensation to accept that risk), so boards settle for incentive contracts that only partially align her pay with shareholder value.

docs.title: Health Insurance
docs.text:
Health insurance markets combine both adverse selection and moral hazard:

  • Adverse selection: People who expect to need more care are more likely to buy generous coverage, raising the average cost of the insured pool.
  • Moral hazard: Once insured, people may consume more healthcare than they would if paying full price out of pocket (since the marginal cost to them is lower).

Policy responses include mandates (requiring everyone, healthy and sick, to buy insurance, preventing the healthy from opting out and causing the death-spiral dynamic of Section 14.2), subsidies, community rating regulations, and cost-sharing tools like deductibles and co-pays (which address moral hazard, per Section 14.3).

docs.title: Used Cars
docs.text: Modern used-car markets have developed institutions specifically to combat the lemons problem: certified pre-owned programs (manufacturer-backed signals of quality), vehicle history reports like Carfax (reducing the information asymmetry directly), warranties (a costly signal, per Section 14.4), and independent mechanic inspections (a buyer-initiated screening device).

docs.title: Credit Markets
docs.text: Lenders screen borrowers using credit scores, collateral requirements, and down payments (all of which are costlier for borrowers who expect to default, making them effective screens). Interest rates that are "too good to be true" can themselves be adversely selected — a lender who simply raised rates to cover the risk of its average borrower might find that doing so drives away its safest borrowers, worsening the pool it's left with, which is part of why credit rationing (denying some loans altogether rather than raising their price) can be the profit-maximizing response for a lender facing asymmetric information.

docs.title: Labor Contracts
docs.text: Employers use probationary periods, performance bonuses, stock vesting schedules, and non-compete or training-repayment clauses to manage both moral hazard (motivating effort once hired) and adverse selection (screening for the right hires before offering a permanent role).

docs.title: Key Terms
