docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text: Course: ECON 1101: Principles of Microeconomics Assessed: 2026-10-26 Skill version: course-description-analyzer v0.05

docs.title: 2. Quality Rating
docs.text:
Fair (40–59) — Significant gaps to address.

The course description has a strong, well-organized topic outline (16 chapters across 6 units) but is missing an explicit target audience statement, an excluded-topics section, and most of the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy outcome levels. These gaps will noticeably limit the breadth and reliability of the 200+ concept learning graph this description is meant to drive.

docs.title: 3. Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Possible Points Earned Notes Title 5 5 Clear and specific: "ECON 1101: Principles of Microeconomics" Target Audience 5 2 Implied by the "ECON 1101" course code and university context, but never stated explicitly (e.g., "college undergraduate, no prior economics required") Prerequisites 5 5 Explicit: "No prior economics knowledge is required. Basic algebra is used throughout; calculus appears in optional advanced sections." Main Topics Covered 10 10 Comprehensive — 16 chapters across 6 units, well beyond the 5–10 topic target Topics Excluded 5 0 No section stating what the course does not cover (e.g., macroeconomics, econometrics, advanced general equilibrium theory) Learning Outcomes Header 5 2 "By the end of the course, students will be able to:" exists, but isn't framed around Bloom's Taxonomy levels Remember 10 0 No recall/define/list-style outcomes present Understand 10 0 No explain/describe/summarize-style outcomes present Apply 10 6 Two outcomes use "Apply," but fewer than the 3 needed for full credit Analyze 10 3 One outcome ("Analyze how different market structures affect prices, output, and social welfare") Evaluate 10 3 One outcome ("Evaluate the causes and consequences of market failures") Create 10 0 No synthesis/design/capstone-style outcome present Descriptive Context 5 4 Course Overview paragraph explains the course's purpose and the analytical skills it builds Total 100 40

docs.title: 4. Gap Analysis
docs.text:
• Target Audience (2/5): The audience is inferable (undergraduate, intro-level, university course numbering) but never stated outright. A generated learning graph could skew toward the wrong depth without this.
  • Topics Excluded (0/5): No boundaries are set. Without this, concept generation has no signal for where to stop (e.g., should it reach into macro policy, international finance, or econometrics?).
  • Learning Outcomes Header (2/5): The outcomes are listed as a flat bullet list rather than organized under the six Bloom's levels, so it's unclear which cognitive level each outcome targets.
  • Remember (0/10) and Understand (0/10): Entirely absent. These lower-order levels typically generate the foundational vocabulary and definitional concepts (terms, laws, relationships) that a learning graph needs as prerequisite nodes for the higher-order concepts.
  • Apply (6/10), Analyze (3/10), Evaluate (3/10): Present but thin — only 1-2 outcomes each, below the 3-outcome threshold for full credit. Each only hints at one topic area rather than spanning the course's six units.
  • Create (0/10): No synthesis-level outcome (e.g., a capstone project, policy brief, or original model) is present. This is often where the richest, most interconnected concepts come from.

docs.title: 5. Improvement Suggestions (prioritized by impact on concept generation)
docs.text:
1. Add explicit Remember and Understand outcomes — these are completely missing and will have the single largest impact on reaching 200+ concepts, since they seed the vocabulary/definition layer of the graph. Example additions:
  2. Remember: "Define key terms including opportunity cost, marginal utility, price elasticity, deadweight loss, and Nash equilibrium."
  3. Understand: "Explain how changes in supply or demand shift market equilibrium" and "Describe the distinguishing features of perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly."
  4. Add a Topics NOT Covered section — list exclusions such as macroeconomics (GDP, inflation, monetary/fiscal policy), econometrics/statistical methods, and advanced general equilibrium or welfare theorems, to bound concept scope.
  5. State the target audience explicitly — e.g., "College undergraduates, typically first- or second-year students, with no prior economics coursework required."
  6. Expand Apply, Analyze, and Evaluate to at least 3 outcomes each, spanning more of the 6 units rather than 1-2 topics. Example:
  7. Apply: add an outcome tied to game theory ("Apply game-theoretic reasoning to predict outcomes in oligopoly and strategic settings") and one tied to factor markets.
  8. Analyze: add outcomes for elasticity ("Analyze how elasticity affects the incidence of taxes and subsidies") and for information economics (adverse selection/moral hazard).
  9. Evaluate: add outcomes judging policy trade-offs (e.g., tariffs vs. free trade, Pigouvian taxes vs. cap-and-trade).
  10. Add a Create-level outcome — e.g., "Design and justify a policy proposal that addresses a specific market failure, using supply-and-demand and welfare analysis to support the recommendation" (ties well to a capstone/final project).
  11. Reframe the outcomes section under explicit Bloom's headers (Remember / Understand / Apply / Analyze / Evaluate / Create) rather than one flat list, so each level's coverage is unambiguous.

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text: Score is 40/100, below the 85 threshold. Recommend addressing the gaps above — especially adding Remember, Understand, and Create outcomes and a Topics Excluded section — before running learning-graph-generator. Running it now would likely under-generate concepts in the foundational-vocabulary and synthesis layers of the graph.

docs.title: 7. Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
• Topic breadth: Strong — 16 chapters across 6 units gives wide topical coverage and should support concept generation across most sub-areas of microeconomics.
  • Topic depth: Good — the "Key Topics" column per chapter already lists 3-6 sub-concepts per chapter (e.g., Chapter 13 alone lists externalities, Pigouvian taxes/subsidies, Coase theorem, public goods, common-pool resources), suggesting real depth once content is written.
  • Bloom's diversity: Weak — 3 of 6 levels (Remember, Understand, Create) are entirely unrepresented, and the other 3 are thin. Bloom's level diversity is a strong driver of concept type diversity (facts/terms vs. processes vs. relationships vs. design artifacts), so this is the main risk area.
  • Estimated concept yield at current state: Likely in the 100-150 range, concentrated in topic/process concepts, with under-representation of foundational definitions and no synthesis/capstone-driven concepts — short of the 200+ target.
  • Recommendation: Address items 1, 2, and 5 above (Remember/Understand outcomes, Topics Excluded, Create outcome) before generating the learning graph; those three changes alone should meaningfully close the gap toward 200+ concepts.

docs.title: About This Section
docs.text: This section provides curated AI prompts you can use with Claude or other large language models to deepen your understanding of microeconomics. The prompts are organized by chapter and learning objective.

docs.title: How to Use These Prompts
docs.text:
1. Open Claude (or your preferred AI assistant) in a new tab.
  2. Copy and paste a prompt below.
  3. Read the response critically — AI can make mistakes. Use your textbook and lecture notes to verify.
  4. Follow up with your own questions to dig deeper.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics
docs.text:
• "Explain the concept of opportunity cost using an example from my daily life as a college student."
  • "What is the difference between a movement along a PPF and a shift of the PPF? Give a real-world example of each."
  • "Give me three examples of sunk cost fallacies from business history."

docs.title: Chapter 2: Supply and Demand
docs.text:
• "Walk me through how to find market equilibrium algebraically, step by step."
  • "What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity in the market for coffee if both the price of coffee beans rises and a health study finds coffee reduces cancer risk? Which effect dominates?"
  • "Explain why a price ceiling below equilibrium causes a shortage, using a concrete example like rent control."

docs.title: Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: About MicroSims
docs.text: MicroSims are interactive, browser-based simulations that let you explore microeconomic models by changing parameters and observing how the model responds. No installation required.

docs.title: Planned Simulations
docs.text:
Simulation Chapter Description Production Possibilities Frontier Ch. 1 Adjust resources and technology; see how the PPF shifts Supply & Demand Ch. 2 Shift supply and demand curves; observe equilibrium changes Elasticity Explorer Ch. 3 Change elasticity; see how total revenue responds to price changes Budget Constraint Ch. 4 Adjust income and prices; find consumer optimum Cost Curves Ch. 5 See how fixed/variable costs shape ATC, AVC, MC Competitive Market Ch. 6 Entry and exit in the long run Monopoly Pricing Ch. 7 Set price or quantity; see deadweight loss Prisoner's Dilemma Ch. 10 Play strategic games against an AI opponent Externality Ch. 13 Compare private vs. social optimum; apply a Pigouvian tax Nudge Lab Ch. 15 Design choice architectures and see how behavior changes

Simulations are built using Python (Panel/Bokeh) or JavaScript (Observable Plot). Source code will be available in the GitHub repository.
